Commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou.
This commentary on the sutra is divided into three major sections: first, a general introduction to the essential meaning; second, the opening of chapters and explanation of the text; and third...

This concludes the explanation of the intent of the mantra. It is intended to accord with the three divisions of the sūtras—preface, main body, and dissemination—and to conform to pure karma, faith, practice, and aspiration.
First, the general meaning of the common preface (five sections): first, clarifying the nature; second, praising the sūtra; third, responding to the time; fourth, describing...
The Mind invites the fivefold empowerment.
First, the clarification of its nature:
It is luminous and penetrating, profoundly still and eternally constant; neither turbid nor clear, without back or front. How great is this true essence!
That which cannot be grasped by thought—can it be anything other than self-nature?

This general introduction to the meaning of the sutra consists of five major sections. From the beginning, which clarifies self-nature, up to the fifth section, which requests the bestowal of empowerment; now, first, we clarify self-nature.
This sutra fully reveals self-nature, and furthermore, all sutras do not depart from self-nature; therefore, it is placed at the outset.
This is the definition. "Spiritual" (ling) refers to spiritual awakening; "luminous" (ming) refers to manifest clarity. Although the sun and moon are luminous, they cannot be called spiritual.

Now, within ultimate luminosity, there is a divine understanding that is unfathomable; luminosity alone is insufficient to exhaust its meaning. Therefore, it is called "spiritual luminosity" (lingming).

"Penetration (*che*)" means to pass through. "Piercing clarity" (*dong*) is the ultimate limit of penetration. Although the sun and moon pervade all things, they do not illuminate objects covered by a basin;

this is penetration that is not yet fully penetrating. Now, this numinous luminosity shines upon heaven and earth and penetrates metal and stone; throughout the four quarters and the zenith and nadir, there is never any obstruction.
This is indeed a state of piercing clarity where there is nothing that is not penetrated; it is not a penetration defined merely as the passage through opposition and separation.

"Cloud" (*yun*) means to be thoroughly penetrating. "Luminous stillness" (*zhan*) means being unstained. "Quiescence" (*ji*) means being unshakable. Although the great earth is quiescent, it cannot be called luminously still.
Now, within ultimate quiescence, there is brilliant purity without dregs; quiescence alone is insufficient to exhaust its meaning, hence it is called "luminously still and quiescent.
"Perpetual" (*heng*) means long-lasting. "Constant" (*chang*) is the ultimate limit of the perpetual. Although the great earth is firm, it cannot escape destruction.
The *kalpa* is eternally constant yet not [merely] constant. This present profound stillness, when traced back, has no beginning; when extended forward, it has no end.
Spanning from antiquity to the present, it has never undergone change. It is the constancy of that which is naturally so—a constancy that is neither constant nor non-constant;

it is not a "long-lasting" constancy spoken of in contrast to the "temporary. As for being "not turbid": it is said that if there were anything, not even a single speck of dust could be received. It is not...
"Pure" means that if one says it is non-existent, not a single dharma can be discarded. "Without aversion" means that even if one lets it go, there is nowhere for it to depart.
"Without inclination" means that even if one meets it, there is nowhere from which it comes.

To say that this very luminous and profoundly tranquil state cannot be sought through purity or turbidity, or through inclination and aversion—by raising the concepts of purity, turbidity, inclination, and aversion, the intent encompasses both good and evil, as well as the holy and the ordinary.
There are [concepts such as] arising and ceasing, increase and decrease, unity and difference, and so forth. "Great" (Mahā) refers to these two phrases; it is a term of praise.

"Great" is named according to its essential nature (*dharmatā*); it possesses the two meanings of pervasiveness and permanence. Because it extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically to the limits of the three periods of time, there is no other dharma with which it can be compared.
This is not a "greatness" defined merely in contrast to the small. "True" (*tattva*) means non-delusory. By means of the three...
The realms are false; only this is true. That is to say, it is not an illusion and is not subject to extinction;

it cannot be destroyed, and is therefore called "True. As for its "essence" (*tǐ*): all myriad phenomena do not transcend the essence of the one mind. This essence encompasses both appearances and function; taken as a whole, it is termed the "True Essence.
It is "inconceivable" because, as clarified above, it is tranquil within clarity, and clear within tranquility.
Furthermore, when clarity and turbidity do not manifest, and facing or turning away cannot be discerned, then the path of mind and speech is severed, leaving no room for conceptualization.
That which is inconceivable is what is called the Dharma without marks or conceptions; to think of it gives rise to confusion. As the Sūtra says:

"If you momentarily raise your mind, the dust of affliction arises first. This is precisely it. Moreover, since the Dharma is without marks or conceptions, thinking of it is merely a futile labor. As the Sūtra says...
It is said: "This Dharma cannot be reached by thought or discrimination. This is precisely it. Therefore, it is said that when the mind seeks to take it as an object, deliberation vanishes.
That which cannot be discussed means that while the principle is perfect, words are partial; when words give rise to the principle, the principle is lost. As the Sūtra says:
"All verbal expressions constitute frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). This is it. Furthermore, because the principle is perfect and words are partial, words are unable [to fully express it].
"Exhausted. As the Sūtra says: "Each and every body possesses immeasurable mouths; from each and every mouth issue immeasurable sounds.

Even as the celestial maiden Śubhavyūha might speak for the duration of an eon, she could never reach the end. This is what is meant. Therefore it is said: "The mouth desires to speak, yet words fail.
Furthermore, this sūtra was originally titled *Acintya* (Inconceivable); thus, these four characters are used to summarize and praise what precedes.
[This is] the prose. This is indeed the ultimate designation for the supreme principle. The final sentence provides the conclusion, asking: "What, then, is this 'inconceivable'?
It is simply the self-nature (*svabhāva*) that is thus. It is said that there are two kinds of nature: when including the category of the insentient, it is called *dharmatā* (dharma-nature);
when referring exclusively to the category of sentient beings, it is called *buddhatā* (Buddha-nature). Now, when we speak of "self-nature," it refers to the former.
This refers to Buddha-nature. As for its being "self," it is so by its very nature; it is not something produced through effort.
It is "my own self" because it does not belong to another. This self-nature has many names; it is also called the original mind.
It is also called primordial awakening (*mūla-awakening*), true knowledge, true consciousness, and suchness (*tathatā*). These various names are inexhaustible;
yet, to summarize them, they refer to the one mind that is inherently possessed by every person—the numinous knowledge and numinous awareness.
What is now clarified as "inconceivable" is precisely this mind; there is nothing else that possesses such inconceivability.
The essence is identical to the mind. According to this very scripture: the first phrase refers to Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*), because it penetrates all things with unimpeded clarity;
the second phrase refers to Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*), because it is eternally constant and unchanging;

the third and fourth phrases refer to the numinous mind that transcends all relativity, wherein light and life are fused, such that all merits are immeasurable; the fifth phrase is a general praise, which is the [title of the] scripture.

It says: "Just as I have praised the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha," the final phrase concludes by returning [to the source], stating that Amitābha Buddha’s entire body is the self-nature of the person themselves. Furthermore, the first phrase clarifies that there is nothing it does not illuminate;

this is the Greatness of Function (*vṛtti-mahattva*). The second phrase clarifies that in its stillness, there is nothing it does not contain; this is the Greatness of Aspect (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*). The third and fourth phrases transcend both [extremes].

The final phrase refers to the Greatness of Essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*). These five phrases constitute a comprehensive praise: namely, that which is both three and one, where both are simultaneously negated and both are simultaneously preserved;
where words fail and thought ceases; and which is inconceivable. The final phrase likewise concludes by returning to self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the first phrase speaks of "illumination," which is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*); the second phrase speaks of "quiescence," which is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*); and the third and fourth phrases speak of "quiescent illumination."
Non-duality is the virtue of the Dharmakāya. These five phrases constitute a general praise, with the final phrase serving as a concluding summary;

this may be understood by analogy with what precedes. Furthermore, when analyzed through the four dharma realms: the distinction between clarity and turbidity, or orientation and aversion, constitutes the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); the numinous luminosity and profound stillness [constitute the realm of principle].

This is the Dharma-realm of principle (*li-fajie*). It is luminous and profoundly tranquil, remaining immutable while responding to conditions; it remains immutable while responding to conditions amidst the variations of clarity and turbidity, or approach and aversion.

This is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wuai fajie*), which is inconceivable. This is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wuai fajie*).
Because this section of the sutra subsumes the Perfect [Teaching], it also attains a partial realization of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. [End of] Section.
Regarding the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): this also serves to bind [the teachings] to the four dharma-realms and return them to the one mind.
II. Praising the Sūtra (in two parts): first, a general praise; second, a specific praise.
I. General Praise:
It clarifies the turbid and turns the averse toward [the truth]; it transcends three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* in a single thought-moment and brings one into equality with all the sages in a few words.
How sublime is this wondrous function! It is truly beyond the reach of conceptual thought—this is none other than the Buddha’s teaching of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Indeed. The preceding passage spoke of the essence of numinous clarity and profound stillness, which fundamentally has no distinction between clarity and turbidity, nor between facing toward or away; it is ultimately equal and is solely the one mind.

Now, it is said that from the perspective of the gate of arising and ceasing, because phenomena are not known as they truly are, they do not accord with reality. Thus, although the Dharma is one, [sentient beings] fail to realize it as such.
When the mind arises without awareness and thoughts emerge, one is shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*). One loses the source and flows toward the branches, muddying the true essence;

thus it is called "turbidity. Just as when one settles silt and sand to restore clarity, this is what is meant by "purity"—referring specifically to the transformation of the five turbidities into pure tranquility.
Led by ignorance, one abandons awakening to pursue sensory dust, becoming estranged from the truth.
Because it is the true essence, it is called "back. To turn back from the path one has traveled and cause one to return is what is meant by "facing.

This specifically refers to turning one's back on Saṃsāra and facing toward Sukhāvatī. However, this is merely spoken of in terms of sentient beings attaining enlightenment from delusion during a single lifetime;
while there appear to be traces of clearing away and returning, in the self-nature (svabhāva), there is in fact nothing to be attained.

There is neither loss nor increase or decrease. Therefore, whether the times are turbid or clear, the nature of the water does not change; it is simply that at one moment it flows away and at another it turns toward [the source].
A person likewise has no second body. What is meant is this: cultivation and realization are indeed not non-existent, yet defilement is never attained.

As for the "three *kalpas*," they refer to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. The explanation of *saṃkhyeya* will be found in the subsequent text. Regarding the mention of "three," this refers to Śākyamuni.
Attaining enlightenment: from the ancient Śākyamuni to Śikhin, one passes through seventy-five thousand Buddhas;
from Śikhin to Dīpaṃkara, one passes through seventy-six thousand Buddhas; and from Dīpaṃkara to Vipaśyin, one passes through seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.
These are called the "three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Having fully undergone many kalpas, traversing further and further, yet even now, one has not transcended a single [moment].
"Contemplate. This means to swiftly transcend birth and death. "A single thought-moment" refers precisely to that single thought-moment of contemplating Amitābha Buddha.
"The various sages" refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. From the perspective of an ordinary person looking toward the sages, the distance is vast and ever-increasing;

yet now, without departing from a single word, one directly ascends to the stage of non-retrogression. "A single word" refers precisely to this single [thought] of the Amitābha Buddha whom one contemplates.
These are the words. The two phrases beginning with "Ultimate" (*zhì*) are words of praise. "Ultimate" (*zhì*) means the extreme limit; it is the ultimate limit beyond which nothing can be added.

"Subtle" (*miào*) refers to the comprehensive elucidation of the subtle meaning within the aforementioned four phrases. "Function" (*yòng*) refers to its dynamic power and efficacy. Now, the defiled mind is difficult to purify.
Turbid as the Yellow River, delusive thoughts are difficult to restrain; wild as a galloping horse, they have revolved without ceasing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Though one studies the texts of the Tripiṭaka and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon, the path to awakening grows ever more distant.

Yet, it is possible to clarify what is turbid and turn those who have turned their backs toward the truth—to transcend all at once in a single thought and realize it in a single word. Such is the wondrous efficacy of its power.
How inconceivable! Since [this] emerges from the essence and its characteristics, it is simply called "wondrous function" (*miao-yong*).

The final sentence concludes by asking: to which sutra should such wondrous function be attributed? Only the *Sutra of Amitābha* spoken by the Buddha is sufficient to correspond to it. Someone may ask:
setting aside the Hīnayāna for a moment, even among the Mahāyāna sutras, they are as vast as a mountain of accumulated earth. What do you say?
Question: Why do you single out this sutra to praise its wondrous efficacy? Answer: Although these meanings are contained within the *sūtras*, none are as clear and concise as this sutra.
Thus, it speaks in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and teaches with directness;

it is neither incomplete nor gradual, yet it clarifies what was turbid and reverses what was contrary, whereas the skillful means (*upāya*) in other dharma-gates have not been fully revealed. Furthermore, those other dharma-gates are either vast and extensive...
Yet it is difficult to maintain; at times its profundity leaves one at a loss for what to do. Now, by means of even a few words or a name, one immediately enters single-mindedness.
Having attained rebirth there, one proceeds directly to Buddhahood. Thus, through these skillful means, the sudden and perfect path is realized—a divine efficacy and supreme power.

If one does not take refuge in this sutra, in whom else shall one take refuge? Furthermore, the former refers to the virtue of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), while the present refers to the virtue of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*).

The former is the purity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśuddhi*), while the present is the purity free from defilement (*vimala-viśuddhi*). Thus, from the exhaustion of nature to the exhaustion of hindrances, they are mutually fused and non-dual, as explained in the teachings.
II. Specific Praise (four parts): First, explaining the reason for preaching this sutra; second, a general discussion of the merits of the Pure Land;
third, specifically indicating that upholding the name is the essential requirement; fourth, extensively revealing the scope of those for whom upholding the name is intended.
First, I shall set forth the reason for expounding this sutra.
Thus, our World-Honored One initially taught the Three Vehicles, yet ultimately returns to the Single Reality; he distributes precious gifts equally and bestows extraordinary grace.
Continuing from above: This sutra possesses such inconceivable merit; therefore, there is a profound reason why the Buddha preached this sutra.
"Zha" (乍) means temporary; it refers to a provisional teaching and is not the ultimate truth. As for the "Three Vehicles":
The vehicles are originally threeless; they are spoken of as three by way of expedient means—namely, the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Bodhisattva.

"Ultimate" is said in contrast to "sudden," and "real" is said in contrast to "expedient. It is said that when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he expounded the *Avataṃsaka*.

Because this Great Teaching was difficult for beings to receive, he taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles in accordance with the faculties of sentient beings, and only later did he bring the expedient back to the real.
[The Buddha] bestowed great chariots upon all; hence it is said that he distributed precious gifts equally. This is the general purport of the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his entire life.
Within this, there further emerges the single gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection).

Whether one possesses great or small faculties, anyone who merely recites the Buddha’s name shall attain rebirth. Nor does one wait for the faculties to ripen before realizing the ultimate reality; it is simply thus.

Those who attain rebirth immediately achieve non-retrogression; this is like a promotion that bypasses the regular order of succession, where an official receives a hereditary rank through extraordinary favor—this is termed "extraordinary grace" (*shu-en*).
Furthermore, this extraordinary grace contains two meanings: first, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is itself an extraordinary grace among all graces;
second, the recitation of the Buddha's name is the most extraordinary grace among these extraordinary graces.
II. A General Discussion of the Merits of the Pure Land:
It points to the forty-eight gates of vows and unfolds sixteen methods of contemplation; every vow returns to the goal of universal salvation.
Contemplation observes the fundamental principle of the wondrous mind.
Above, the excellence of the Pure Land Dharma-gate was praised; now, regarding the Pure Land, first the other sutras are presented, and then this sutra is compared as being even more sublime.
The Vows and the Contemplation of the Dharma are fully contained within these two sutras. As for the words "beginning from the original vow":
Until the fulfillment of these vows, there is nothing that does not fully encompass all sentient beings so that they may be reborn together in the Pure Land.
From the beginning of the contemplations to their conclusion, everything is the perfect, ultimate single mind of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way.

From this single mind, great vows are produced and perfect enlightenment is attained; then, by means of those original vows, one returns to deliver sentient beings back to the single mind of the Pure Land.
Regarding the Dharma-gate: the general purport of these two sutras is essentially as follows.
III. Specifically showing that holding the name is the essential (2): first, comparing and discussing the essentials and brevity; second, thoroughly investigating and clarifying the benefits.
First, a summary of the essential points of comparison:
Furthermore, because the gate of vows is vast, it is vital to know what comes first; because the contemplation of dharmas is profound and mysterious, one should especially adhere to simplicity.

To know what comes first is to strive for rebirth in that land; to adhere to simplicity is to devote oneself solely to the practice of holding the Name. When one utters that Name, all virtues are encompassed therein.
It is fully complete; it is dedicated solely to upholding [the Name]. It encompasses all practices without exception.
Comparing this with the aforementioned *Amitābha Sūtra* (the Larger Sūtra), one knows that the practice of holding the Name is especially essential and concise.

As for its vastness: through the Forty-eight Vows, it provides shelter and protection for both the hidden and the manifest, encompassing all who are holy and ordinary; thus, it is vast, expansive, and magnificent.

Vast and boundless, yet there must be a gradual progression for one who enters it; therefore, knowing what comes first is prized. The Master said: "To maintain what is concise while extending its application broadly is the way of the sages. How do we know this priority? It is because by being born in that land, one draws near to the Tathāgata;
such a great vow can then be hoped for. If one merely obtains the sight of Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
Therefore, seeking rebirth through aspiration is the most urgent of all duties. What does it mean to 'maintain what is concise'?"
This is because, although there are sixteen contemplations, speaking of the Buddha encompasses them all; and although the Buddha is the ultimate reality, he is simply the mind itself.

Now, hearing the name of the Buddha and single-mindedly upholding it can be called most simple and easy; its efficacy is not applied through complexity, yet since all phenomena are but the mind, and because the mind is pure, what task cannot be accomplished?
In a single kṣaṇa, through the movement of thought, the environment and its inhabitants appear vividly as they truly are.
As soon as the thought arises, one immediately ascends to that land; this is a visualization difficult to accomplish, yet it is achieved without practice.

Therefore, by means of mindfulness through the recitation of the name, what is maintained is especially essential and concise. Tianru remarked that the Great Sage felt compassion and pity [for sentient beings].

This refers precisely to the exhortation to single-mindedly uphold the Name. As for the invocation of the Name: although the Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues, these four characters alone are sufficient to encompass them all.
For Amitābha is the very embodiment of the One Mind; this mind encompasses all virtues—permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
original enlightenment and initial enlightenment; true suchness and buddha-nature; bodhi and nirvāṇa—and hundreds of thousands [of other qualities].

The ten thousand names are all subsumed within this single name without exception. As for "exclusive recitation": when sentient beings study the Buddha, there are likewise immeasurable methods of practice;
yet now, by merely upholding the single dharma of the Name, it is sufficient to encompass them all. This is because upholding the Name is itself upholding this one mind.
The mind encompasses the hundred practices, the Four Truths, the Six Perfections, and even the eighty-four thousand [dharmas] of the Bodhisattvas.
All subtle dust-like practices and gateways are subsumed therein without exception; therefore, it is called "guarding the essential. II.
Thoroughly investigating and clarifying the benefits (three parts): first, the accomplishment of the cause; second, the realization of the fruit; third, the general conclusion.
First, regarding the accomplishment through causes:
from this point onward, all myriad thoughts come to rest, culminating in the state of "one mind without distraction.

Prior to the practice of nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name), every thought was one of worldly toil; that is to say, within a single kṣaṇa, there are nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing. Arising...

The phases of abiding, changing, and ceasing, along with their divisions and enumerations, are immeasurable and boundless; even the divine eye cannot perceive them, and thus they are called "ten thousand anxieties.
These ten thousand anxieties—wherein one thing perishes as another arises, and what has just departed suddenly returns—cannot ultimately be eliminated no matter how many schemes one employs.
Now, by the power of holding the name, as soon as right mindfulness is raised, these miscellaneous thoughts are naturally dispelled. It is like this:

When the lion emerges from its cave, the hundred beasts hide their tracks; when the bright sun shines upon the frost, the thousand forests lose their whiteness. This is what is meant by "all names are stilled. Thus, Yongming said:

"If one counts the breaths, discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) do not cease; if one recollects the Buddha and calls his name, one immediately breaks through discursive thought and investigation.
This is the verification of it. To still them again and yet again, one exhausts their source and root; hence it is called "reaching the ultimate. Upon reaching this point—
Within this state of single-minded non-distraction, one achieves the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection.
Second, regarding the realization of the fruit:
one then knows that it is not more than a few steps away that the jeweled ponds surge with flowers of four colors; nor does one need to leave the courtyard for the golden lands to surround them.
Within seven tiers of trees, Amitābha preaches the Dharma at every turn; from time to time, beings are born by transformation within lotus buds.
Exquisite birds and common fowl harmonize their songs, while jade palaces and thatched huts share a common splendor.
Once one has attained the state of single-mindedness without distraction, one finally realizes that the lotus ponds, the walking paths, and the various adornments are not external to the mind.
Why, then, must one listen with one's ears to the golden words before they constitute Amitābha preaching the Dharma? Only when the seal of the Sahā world is broken can it be called the Pure Land;
only then do the texts truly come to fruition. If this is so, then what is inferior and what is superior between the rare birds and common fowl, or the jade halls and the thatched cottages?
"Excellent. What is pure and what is defiled? Therefore it is said that the Western Land is before one's very eyes.
III. Conclusion:

It is because by means of the true mindfulness of emptiness, birth enters into non-birth; the mindfulness of the Buddha is itself the mindfulness of the mind, and being born there is not separate from this.

Born herein, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are of one essence; abiding neither on this shore nor the other, it is therefore called the Amitābha of Self-Nature and the Pure Land of Mind-Only.

Building upon the aforementioned sublime causes and wondrous fruits, when mindfulness of the Buddha reaches the state of single-mindedness, then through the culmination of mindfulness, all becomes emptiness.

The mindfulness of non-mindfulness is called true mindfulness. Furthermore, since the essence of mindfulness is fundamentally empty, mindfulness is in reality non-mindfulness; this is termed true mindfulness.
As for "arising without arising," it means that when one realizes the essence of arising is unattainable, then one arises while not arising, and does not arise while arising.

This is what is meant by entering the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) with a mind of buddha-recollection, as will be explained in detail in the subsequent section on the Arising of the Teaching. Therefore...
Know that throughout the day one recollects the Buddha; throughout the day one recollects the mind. There is a fervent rebirth, yet in its ultimate stillness, there is no going.
Regarding the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, the Sūtra says: "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Indeed, the mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is sentient beings. Sentient beings are within the minds of all Buddhas; one recollects the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings.

Therefore, it is said to be "one essence. Regarding the two banks of the middle stream: *Sahā* (this world) is a metaphor for this [shore], and *Sukhāvatī* (the Land of Ultimate Bliss) is a metaphor for that [shore].

At the beginning, one feels weary of suffering and rejoices in bliss; subsequently, both suffering and bliss are simultaneously extinguished; and in the end, one does not even dwell in that which is neither suffering nor bliss.
This is what is meant by "not clinging to the two extremes" and "not abiding in the middle way. The Amitābha of self-nature is but the mind itself.

The Pure Land—this is the intended meaning. Thus, the Chan school and the Pure Land school take different paths but reach the same destination, because that which does not depart from one’s own mind is itself the Buddha, and is itself Chan.
To cling to Chan while slandering the Pure Land is to slander one’s own fundamental mind;
it is to slander the Buddha; it is to slander one’s own Chan. This is simply due to a lack of reflection.

This [method] is, in principle, the single mind that is entirely directed toward those of superior intelligence; yet it also extends to the level of phenomenal phenomena, being specifically designed for those of dull faculties.

The unity of principle and phenomena within the one mind is detailed in the subsequent text. Here, however, "the self-nature is but mind" specifically refers to the passage in the sutra concerning the "one mind not being distracted" in terms of principle.
Only those of superior intelligence are able to take this up; those of dull faculties have not yet been able to receive and bear it.
Therefore, this "one mind" does not exclusively refer to principle but also encompasses phenomena, for through the "one mind of phenomena," all people are capable of practice.
It is said that even the ignorance and unworthiness of ordinary husband and wife possess both knowledge and capability;
for like heaven universally covering all, and like earth universally supporting all, within the great creation there is no discarded thing.
III. The Threefold Response to the Times (3). First, a general eulogy; second, a specific eulogy; third, a concluding eulogy. I. The General Eulogy.
Alas, those who cling to ignorance attend only to phenomena while remaining deaf to principle; those of limited wisdom cling only to principle while neglecting phenomena.
Consequently, [the former] was abandoned. To cling to phenomena while being deluded about principle is like a young child reading the books of the ancient sages;
to grasp at principle while neglecting phenomena is comparable to a poor man obtaining a promissory note from a wealthy family.
The previous statement said that the Buddha’s compassion extends equally to both the wise and the foolish; the present statement says that sentient beings do not realize the Buddha’s intention.

There are skillful teachings, yet there is no skillful learning; thus, it is lamentable. Those who cling to ignorance remain ignorant while sweetly relishing their ignorance; those with meager wisdom possess wisdom yet lack true wisdom.

This is truly because phenomena arise based on principle, and when principle is attained, phenomena are manifested. Since phenomena and principle mutually support one another, they must not be treated as partial or separate.
To abandon this while clinging to that, the resulting弊 (calamities/defects) are equal. The "ignorant child" is a metaphor for one who is utterly foolish;

being dark and immature, their minds are not yet opened, such that they can merely read the words but do not understand the meaning at all. This is what is meant by "reciting the Buddha's name all day long without knowing the Buddha who is being recited."
The parable of the poor man illustrates small wisdom. Long ago, there was a destitute man who found a discarded deed on the road.
Seeing the various figures recorded therein for fields, gardens, palaces, houses, gold, silks, rice, and grain, he rejoiced beyond all expectation and declared himself a man of great wealth.

He did not realize that while he was enumerating the treasures of another, they had no bearing upon himself. This is what is meant by the saying: "Though one knows that Buddha is identical to mind, [if one does not realize it,] it remains distinct."

The mind is not the Buddha. Therefore, from the perspective of principle (*li*), there is nothing to be contemplated; yet from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), one contemplates within that which has nothing to be contemplated.
Because contemplation is itself non-contemplation, one cultivates both principle and phenomena simultaneously, seeking the Buddha-wisdom through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Only then can it be called "Great Wisdom."

However, if one clings to phenomena while maintaining mindfulness, the merit of entering this stage will not be in vain;
yet, if one grasps at principle while the mind remains truly unenlightened, one conversely incurs the calamity of falling into emptiness.

The preceding passage identified two types of illness; now, among these two, we shall specifically cite the most egregious. First, there is the attachment to mundane phenomena where faith is not earnest—this truly requires no further discussion.

Even if one were to single-mindedly recite the Name with continuous mindfulness, uninterrupted at every moment, though they may not understand the profound principle of reality, they will already be able to achieve a pure body. Although their rank may be low, they will [attain rebirth].
Success is certain. What is called a scholar appearing at the bottom of the examination list and passing is not necessarily a bad thing; one simply fears not having one's name on the list at all.
How can you condemn me for being "stupidly persistent"? It is that I adhere to principle while my mind remains truly clear and lucid.
This need not even be discussed. Suppose one gallops about with wild wisdom and indulges in stubborn emptiness;
if they have never awakened to their own fundamental mind, yet they speak lightly of the Pure Land and hold in contempt rebirth there, the harm is no small matter.
This is what is meant by "vaguely embracing emptiness while negating cause and effect," or "roaming wildly and recklessly, inviting calamity. Question: For what reason do you not blame [them]?

[Question: "The dull-witted person, conversely, suppresses the sharp-witted one. [Answer: The sharp-witted person relies on their talent and holds themselves aloft, constantly claiming to be far superior to the dull-witted.
Now, this teaching is presented so that they may realize that attempting to paint a tiger without success results in the reverse—a loss of a single tally.

○ Third, the lamentation:

Thus it comes to pass that stretching out one's hand is but a labor in vain, and leaning upon the gate is but a hollow longing. Above, one fails the Buddha’s transformation; below, one betrays one’s own spirit.
From this life through many lifetimes, a single error becomes a hundred errors. One consents to the bitter realms and binds one’s hands at the gate of death—there is no salvation.
They have no refuge; they are pitiable and tragic.

Regarding "reaching out the hand," the ancients said: "If one's sister-in-law is drowning, one should rescue her by reaching out the hand. Regarding "leaning on the gate," the mother of Wangsun Jia said: [She leaned on the gate, weeping, when her son had gone to serve the state.]
If you had gone out in the morning and not returned, I would have leaned against the gate and gazed toward you. Now, it is said that sentient beings are submerged in the realms of suffering;
the Buddha rescues them as one reaches down a hand from a deep abyss. Sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of delusion;

the Buddha pities them as one leans against a gate and gazes for a son. Though his rescue is earnest and his pity is intense, they remain deeply submerged and do not rise, fleeing far away without end.
This, indeed, is the solitary Buddha’s transformation. As for those who fall short: all who possess a mind are certain to become Buddhas.

Therefore, the Buddha taught the holding of the name, desiring that people contemplate their own minds and realize their own Buddhahood. To remain indifferent and disbelieve—how could this not be to betray one's own spirit?
As for those born now and those born in many future lives, they will fall into the realms of suffering birth after birth, without end.

To err once is to err a hundred times; this is a missed opportunity in this life that will be difficult to encounter again for many kalpas. Entering the realms of suffering is like flies and maggots wallowing in a latrine;
rushing toward the gates of death is like cattle and sheep being led to a slaughterhouse—there is no one to rescue you.
There is nothing to rely upon; how tragic this is! ○ IV.

Exposition of the Intent (in three parts): First, expressing regret for one’s own lack of virtue; second, clarifying what one holds in high esteem; third, explaining the intent behind the commentary on the sutra.
First, I feel ashamed of my own lack of virtue.
I, Zhuhong, am a lowly ordinary person in the Dharma-ending age, a latecomer to learning from a remote corner. I have not mastered the profound principles and have always despised empty talk;
what benefit can painted cakes provide to a hungry stomach? And how could a "swallow-stone" deceive the eyes of a merchant?

The above clarifies that by practicing *nien-fo* (recollection of the Buddha), one obtains such benefits; conversely, by failing to practice *nien-fo*, one incurs such losses. Therefore, I set forth my own intention to solely honor and uphold *nien-fo*.
First, at the outset, I shall assess my own capacity as one of dull faculties. In this age of the Final Dharma (*mofa*), birth occurs at an untimely moment;
as a lowly ordinary person (*xiangfan*), my karmic retribution is insufficient; living in a remote corner, my vision is not broad; and being a latecomer to the study, my wisdom is...

Their [understanding] is not deep; they are not yet capable of even practicing the matter, much less knowing its underlying principle. This makes it clear that what they say is insufficient to command the trust of others.

As for those who are naturally humble, they recognize their own shallowness and inferiority, feeling ashamed of their empty talk—this is what is meant by "being ashamed of one's words while exceeding in one's actions.
A painted cake serves as a metaphor for empty talk. "Yan-shi" (a stone from Yan) refers to something that resembles jade but is not.
This is jade. As for the "barbarian merchant," he is a trader from the Western Regions who is skilled at discerning precious gems.

Long ago, there was one who obtained a piece of "Yan stone" (ordinary rock from the Yan region) and, believing it to be a *yujin* (a high-quality jade), flaunted it before the eyes of commoners, hoping to sell it for a high price. He showed it to the barbarian merchant and said:
It was merely a stone. He returned in great shame. This is like one who has a vague glimpse of the Way, yet remains indistinct and not true;
before those with clear eyes, it is fit to be laughed at.
II. Clarifying what one personally esteems.
I reverently uphold the former edict and faithfully serve this sutra. I look toward the Land of Bliss as my hometown and gaze upon the Compassionate Honored One as my parents.

Since I am aware of my own dull faculties, I must surely follow the ancients. "Reverently" (祇) means respect. The jade-like voice of the Worldly Lord and the golden mouth of the Dharma King are both termed an "edict" (勅).
"Faithfully serving" (篤奉) refers to the utmost devotion. Describing the Land of Bliss as one's "hometown" refers to the realm of tranquility.
The pure land of cessation is precisely where a person establishes their dwelling and sustains their life;

yet, having abandoned one's native village to wander aimlessly in a foreign land, the traveler stands alone and solitary, possessing nothing but the single thought of longing for home. Thus, the Compassionate Honored One spoke of "parents" as those upon whom one relies.
The father says, "He is my protector. The mother says, "He is my reliance. The Buddha, through his great kindness and great compassion, receives and guides sentient beings;

he nurtures me within the womb of the holy and feeds me with the milk of the Dharma. Thus, at this very moment, there is nothing—neither internal nor external, neither body nor mind—that has not been established by the power of his grace.
His virtue of arduous toil is as vast as the great heavens and without limit, yet I have instead rebelled against and abandoned him.

Regarding the *Jātaka*: though the *mínglíng* (the caterpillar) is of a different species, it should only harbor admiration for its foster parent throughout its life; it has no other means of assistance, being content with merely attending to its needs and never failing in its service.

"Personal. "Superficial vision" refers to that which remains on the surface of the skin; it does not penetrate deeply, serving as a metaphor for shallow insight. Regarding "mental effort": the function of the mind is thought. Even the sages Yao and Shun exhausted their mental efforts; what kind of person am I that I should [not do so]?... [The text continues: ...how could I dare to remain idle? I must strive with all my heart. Thus, he took up his brush and paper to record these words. Although he lacked the capacity of a sage, he possessed the aspiration of a sage. He did not seek fame or profit, nor did he wish to be known by the world. His sole purpose was to transmit the Dharma to future generations. Therefore, he recorded this account. It is said: "If one wishes to know the Way, one must first know oneself. This is why he called himself "one of shallow vision. Furthermore, he said: "I am merely a man of humble talent, yet I have received the grace of the Buddha. Because of this, he dared to compose this work. May those who encounter it take it to heart and practice accordingly. This is the intention behind his writing. Thus ends the preface. As for the main text: "The Buddha’s teaching is vast and profound; its principles are subtle and difficult to fathom. This means that the Buddha’s doctrine is expansive and deep, and its underlying truths are refined and hard to comprehend. "Yet, through the power of his great compassion, he appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings. This means that by the force of his supreme mercy, he manifested in this realm to rescue all living beings. "His wisdom is like the ocean, and his vows are as vast as space. This means that his enlightened insight is as boundless as the sea, and his compassionate aspirations are as expansive as the cosmos.
