attracting elevates their indolence, causing them to produce joyful aspiration (*prāmodya*). Only after this can they remain long [in the path].
Like one smeared with mud who initially loathes filth and foulness, yet upon suddenly hearing of purity and wondrousness, stirs up a profound aspiration and seeks it out;

seeing this great mass of fire and that cool pond, and observing how flames scorch sentient beings, one cannot help but avoid the former and hasten toward the latter. Such is the natural course of the Dharma when employing skillful means to deliver beings.
Once born in that land, having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and only then does one realize.
This mind is originally equal.

As for the transformation and guidance of those of the two vehicles who cling to emptiness and do not cultivate the Pure Land: it is because they have suddenly attained the realization of self-emptiness and immediately become attached to it;
when they hear it said that one should purify Buddha-lands and teach and transform sentient beings, their hearts find no joy. Therefore, they are caused to turn back from the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding those who aspire for rebirth in the Great [Vehicle] and have just attained the realization of self-emptiness (*pudgala-nairātmya*): the followers of the Lesser Vehicle merely awaken to the absence of a self within the aggregates (*skandha*), yet they do not know that the aggregates themselves are also empty.
Grasping at objects as truly existent, they seek only to avoid sensory realms and pursue quiescence; thus, upon hearing of rebirth by transformation in the Pure Land, their hearts find no joy.

Like the śrāvakas, they do not perceive the spiritual power of Śākyamuni nor participate in the great assemblies of bodhisattvas, because the pure merits and virtues of the buddha-fields in the ten directions were never praised or explained to them.
It is said by the ancients that in the Hīnayāna there is no other Buddha.

Regarding this teaching: the Great Teachings (Mahāyāna) contain discourses on oceans of *kṣetra* (buddha-fields). Those who hold such views are merely a class of "self-benefiting" practitioners; they are also termed "dull-witted arhats.
Therefore, the teachings command them to turn away from and sever the mind of nihilistic extinction (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) and to cultivate practices for the Pure Land.

Only then do they come to know that the compassion, wisdom, conduct, and vows of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are thus vast and thus inexhaustible. Their minds are not obstructed by objects, nor are objects...
To obstruct the mind [with the thought that] all dharmas are empty by their very nature, such that one spends the whole day saving sentient beings yet spends the whole day with no one saved,
while practicing meditative concentration alone and refusing to aspire for rebirth— this is a great failure.

Fifth, regarding the encouragement for bodhisattvas at the stage of the initial resolve to draw near to the Tathāgata: although a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment has established the great mind, their supreme patience (*kṣānti*) is not yet perfected.
As the saying goes, "A fledgling with weak wings can only cling to a branch; an infant must still rely on its mother.

Only by entering the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and drawing near to that World-Honored One can they finally realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) and attain the fruit of Buddhahood, riding upon the power of the great vow.

A raft for crossing over sentient beings from the sea of suffering, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Furthermore, the six types of those who fall back and the śrāvakas of kalpas as numerous as dust motes—like fish eggs and mango blossoms—are sufficient to serve as clear mirrors.
Thus we know that the Buddha is the father of bodhisattvas, giving birth to the Dharma-body.
From the first stage up to the tenth stage, one never departs from mindfulness of the Buddha. How could the initial resolve alone be sufficient to dispense with the aspiration for rebirth?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "An ordinary person bound by all fetters may possess great compassion and desire to be born in an evil world to save suffering sentient beings."
This is impossible. Why? Because their afflictions are powerful; having not yet attained the power of patience (*kṣānti*), their minds follow after sense objects.

Bound by sounds and forms, they fall of their own accord into the three miserable realms—how then could they save others? Even if they were to be born among humans, the Noble Path would be difficult to attain.
By the power of the merit of giving and precepts, they might become kings, ministers, or those with wealth, status, and autonomy; yet even if they encounter a [Buddha],...
The consciousnesses refuse to believe and follow [the teaching]; they become deluded and negligent, committing manifold transgressions, and by means of this, they fall.
It is further illustrated by the analogy of two people attempting to rescue someone drowning: those who enter the water directly to save him both drown together.

However, one who possesses skillful means goes to fetch a boat or raft and rescues them by means of it, so that all escape the calamity. A bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind is also like this; they must...

One must stay close to the Buddha; only after attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) can one rescue sentient beings from the ocean of suffering, like one who has obtained a boat.
It is further said: for example, it is as if an infant were separated from its mother—it might fall into a pit or well, or die of thirst for milk.

Or again, it is like a fledgling with weak feathers that can only cling to the branches of a tree; only when its wings and plumage are fully developed can it fly through the air with ease and mastery.
Obstruction. Ordinary beings lack the power [to achieve this on their own]; they should simply focus their mindfulness exclusively on Amitābha Buddha so as to bring about samādhi.

At the time of death, with right mindfulness, they will certainly attain rebirth there. Upon seeing the Buddha, they will attain patience (*kṣānti*) and return to the triple world to save and deliver sentient beings.

Those in the stage of "right determination" (*samyaktva-niyāma*) are distinguished from those in the stages of "false determination" or "indetermination," for ordinary beings, heterodox practitioners, and outsiders are already fixed in their respective courses; it is only the beginner who advances [toward the right].
Whether they have regressed or not is not yet fixed; however, having now been born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), they are all non-retrogressive regardless of their rank.

"Assembly" (*ju*) means a gathering; it refers to the assembly of the various superior virtuous persons mentioned in the text. It means that by entering this assembly, one sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma.
Regarding those who fell from the sixth mind: Śāriputra gave rise to the bodhicitta and had already realized the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
Because they encountered those begging for their eyes, they subsequently withdrew from the Great Resolve (mahācitta) and sank into the five realms of existence.

Those who have been Śrāvakas for aeons as numerous as motes of dust all originated by developing the resolve during the era of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; it was solely because they withdrew from the Great [Vehicle] that, since the kalpa of "dust-points," they fell into the rank of Śrāvaka.
Thus the Sūtra says: "The eggs of fish and the flowers of the mango—these three things are many in their causal state; yet when..."
The results are few. This is cited to clarify that even a bodhisattva at the initial stage should remain close to the Tathāgata to find a refuge upon which to rely, so as never to fall back.
Regarding the "Father of Bodhisattvas," in the eleventh fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the youth Tejaprabha beholds the marks of the Tathāgata and attains ten kinds of benefit;
the first is stated as attaining the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), named "Boundless."

Regarding the "Sea-Treasury Gate" (*Sāgaragarbha-mukha*): the commentary states that because the samādhi of buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo san-mei*) is the father of bodhisattvas, it is explained first.
This is truly because bodhisattvas take skillful means (*upāya*) as their father, and since buddha-remembrance is the actual engagement with phenomena, it is a skillful means.

Furthermore, buddha-remembrance is the direct seed for attaining buddhahood. As for the beginning and end of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), within the text on the ten stages, from the very beginning...
At the conclusion [of each stage], it is stated for every ground that all actions are not separate from the mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

It further states that although Bodhisattvas on the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (the Far-Reaching Ground) know that all buddha-fields are like empty space, they are nonetheless able to adorn those buddha-fields with pure and wondrous practices.
The *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand all Buddhas..."

Furthermore, all phenomena are merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). Having attained the patient acceptance that accords with reality (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), one either enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) or, upon casting off the body, is swiftly reborn in the world of Abhirati or within the pure Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī. Therefore, Nāgārjuna maintains that rebirth occurs at the first stage.
Māmakṣama attained the stage of patience (kṣānti) and was reborn there. As for the great bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, those who made vows to be reborn there are beyond counting;

how much more so for those at the initial stage of the path? Yongming said that those who wish to entrust their essence to the lotus throne, forever leave the womb, and sport with supernatural powers in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and other Buddha-lands, all [must do so].
One who is able to thoroughly comprehend their own mind can go anywhere without exception. Tianru said:

"If you awaken to the mind, then rebirth in the Pure Land is something that ten thousand oxen could not pull back from. Thus, although a bodhisattva at the initial stage may be said to have attained clear understanding, they are still far from the Buddha;
it is precisely for this reason that one must seek birth [in the Pure Land] and cannot delay.

Regarding the sixth point, "completely encompassing those of both sharp and dull faculties so that all are delivered": as for other Dharma gates, if they are elevated, those of inferior capacity are excluded;
if they are lowered, they do not reach those of superior faculties. Thus, the Flower Treasury [Sūtra] is like a blind man, and the light of a firefly only increases his delusions.
This single Dharma alone encompasses both the high and the low; it may be said that myriad illnesses are cured by *agada* medicine, and a thousand vessels are forged in a great furnace.
How could its gate of compassion not be vast and expansive, universally delivering all without exception?

It is like the case of the blind. When the Tathāgata was expounding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in the Jeta Grove, the śrāvakas of superior virtue, such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, were like the blind and the deaf—their vision blocked and their hearing cut off—even the bodhisattvas who had accumulated long-standing practice were said to be “exposing their cheeks.
This is because, while the Dharma is lofty and the Path is vast, their spiritual capacities (*indriya*) were small. As for those with increased fetters, it refers to Vimalakīrti.
The Sūtra states: "There were two bhikṣus who had violated a root precept. They confessed their transgressions and sought repentance.
Upāli, relying on the Vinaya, determined their offenses for them, yet their doubts remained unresolved. Viśuddhamati said: 'Do not disturb their minds with conventional dharmas.'"
This further increases the offenses of these two bhikṣus. Yongjia compared them to the light of fireflies, meaning they cannot dispel the darkness of delusion but instead augment it.
Mingbei [stated] that their faculties are profound while the teaching is shallow;

thus, if others apply impurity to the furnace and bellows, or if counting the breaths is not beneficial for those who dwell among tombs, each of these approaches serves as a gateway, yet they remain distinct from one another.

Furthermore, as for the shallow and deep, the small and great, their capacities cannot all be accommodated simultaneously. Only this Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance delivers all through its three grades and nine ranks.

Reaching upward, the three minds are fully developed and one enters directly into the state of non-arising; reaching downward, even ten recitations successfully accomplished lead to birth in that land.
This is what is meant by not departing from a single dharma while skillfully adapting to various faculties—truly a method for the heroic and eminent.
There is no shame in being inferior, for even the mediocre and ignorant gain the benefit of looking up and reaching toward it.

Indeed, there is no capacity that is not accommodated, and all sentient beings are gathered within its embrace. *Agada* is a name for a medicine in the Western Regions (India) that can cure all ailments with a single drug;

it serves as a metaphor for merely upholding the Buddha’s name, whereby the five desires, the three poisons, immeasurable afflictions, and even the partial vehicles and external paths [are all overcome].
The Way: because it completely severs and eliminates all the maladies of views. The Great Smelter: within a single smelting, it molds and casts the myriad things, each becoming its own vessel;
this is a metaphor for how by merely holding the Buddha’s name, beings are reborn in the nine grades according to their faculties and conduct, all of whom are non-retrogressive.
Vastness: in the *Zhou Yi*, Qian is said to "give birth to the great" and Kun is said to "give birth to the vast. Now, there is nothing...

It does not exclude anyone. It is likened to heaven covering and earth supporting, nurturing all beings and embracing all with equal compassion without discrimination; this is called the Universal Gate (Pumen).
Seventh, it protects and sustains practitioners who face many obstacles so that they do not fall away. In practicing during the final age, there are many hindrances and difficulties.

If one’s right view falters even slightly, one immediately falls into the midst of various evils. Through the power of that Buddha’s vows and his majestic spiritual authority, he bestows his protection upon the practitioner;

amidst the great radiance, they shall not encounter demonic obstacles, and he will be able to provide protective mindfulness until the very site of enlightenment. Thus, we know that the *Zetú* (Sacred Diagram) wards off strange anomalies.
A precious mirror hides away demons; when right mindfulness is clear and distinct, none can cause disturbance.
As for those with many obstacles and difficulties, the practitioner may provoke the *ābhāsvara-māra* (shadows of the aggregates) within meditative contemplation.

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* enumerates fifty kinds, it states that if one does not conceive the thought of attaining sainthood, these are called "auspicious realms"; however, if one interprets them as signs of sainthood, one will immediately be afflicted by them.

Because of these various evils, it is known that when right view slightly declines, demonic influences then flourish; what was not beneficial becomes further detrimental, and those seeking to ascend instead sink downward.
Due to this, those of shallow roots fear the Path and do not study it. Now, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are received by the great vows of the Buddha.
Great power upholds and rectifies; its majesty is such that none dare to interfere. Its spirit is unfathomable; even if demonic affairs arise, they will naturally vanish on their own.

Furthermore, a sutra states: "Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha possess a radiance forty *li* in extent that illuminates their bodies, such that demons cannot violate them, for Amitābha Buddha and the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly protect and mind them. From this moment, resolve your mind and proceed directly.
From the arrival at the place of practice until its conclusion, there is auspiciousness and nothing that is not beneficial. This is truly because right mindfulness is clear and distinct;

even if demons should come, they are easily recognized and easily dispelled. This is unlike those who indulge in stillness or cling to emptiness, who lack a sovereign master within and thus fail to perceive the demons when they encounter them, allowing them to eventually enter the mind.
To illustrate this with the metaphor of the precious mirror: by means of these two analogies, it is made clear that it is not merely...

The power of the Buddha is none other than the power of one’s own mindfulness. There was a divine beast named Bái-zé (White Zé) that could speak human language and discern the true nature of all things;
all malevolent spirits would flee upon seeing its shadow. Thus it is said: "If a household possesses the Bái-zé Diagram, such demons and monsters will certainly not exist.
Furthermore, mountain spirits and wild ghosts can assume various forms to deceive and delude people.
Yet it cannot alter the forms within the mirror. This is a metaphor for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha:
when right mindfulness manifests before them, their wisdom-illumination is refined and brilliant, so that all celestial Māras and mental Māras find no opportunity to gain the upper hand.

The eighth refers to those who, by means of a mind possessing mindfulness, enter into the state of non-mindfulness. The mind is fundamentally without thought; the arising of thought is a departure from its true nature.
Yet, since beginningless time, sentient beings have been habituated to deluded conceptualization, which is not easily dispelled all at once.

Teaching them now to recite the Buddha’s name is like using poison to counteract poison or employing soldiers to stop soldiers. Once the illness has healed and the enemy has been pacified, one abandons the diseased body and there is no longer any self.
The body is originally my own child who has become a robber.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "The essence of the mind is free from thought; yet one gives rise to thoughts to recite the Buddha's name. Does this not, rather than helping, disturb the mind?

The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "To be without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) is called mindfulness of the Buddha; to be without perception (*saṃjñā*) and without speech is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
Yet, to give rise to thoughts while practicing mindfulness of the Buddha—would this not be to turn one's back on the Buddha?

Now, it is true in principle that the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha through the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) consists in extinguishing all applied and sustained thoughts. However, although the mind may be free from conceptualization, the mind remains defiled by ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, [the practitioner] continues to think.
The continuity of thought is like a seven-year illness or a long-disordered populace; hence it is called "habituation.

Now, if one wishes to force a suppression and suddenly establish emptiness and stillness, yet movement ceases only to return to movement, and stillness becomes even more intense as movement increases—even if coarse thoughts temporarily subside while subtle thoughts persist—one might claim to have attained "correspondence" (*yoga*).
Such an error is no small matter. Since one still dwells in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), [one has not yet realized the truth].
If one can sever deliberation and forget objects of perception, why not take those very perceptions and deliberations as the basis for cultivation and progress?
Therefore, use mindfulness to counteract mindfulness itself: by reciting the name of a single Buddha, replace those hundreds of thousands of millions of miscellaneous thoughts.
Since delusion arises from the True, like waves following the water, that which is perceived is immediately empty; it is the manifest fundamental essence, not something separate from mindfulness.

Because one attains Bodhi, it is said that the myriad dharmas are illusory and false, and that there is only this single mind. To fully awaken to one's own mind is to realize that everything encountered is Bodhi.
This is like calling a body "healthy" once an illness has been cured, or designating a person a "good citizen" after civil unrest has subsided.
To seek the mind by removing thoughts is like a physician who must first destroy his own body to cure a disease, or one who intends to slaughter an entire nation.
Yet to seek to pacify the people [in this way]—how could that be reasonable?

Those who skillfully demonstrate the cause for rebirth while truly awakening to non-arising (anutpāda) find that at the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) they merely manifest signs, whereas it is only at the eighth stage that they attain non-arising.
To urgently desire to extinguish arising in order to seek non-arising is to go further and further away from it the more one seeks. Now, having come here...
Born into the Pure Land, one then awakens to non-arising; entering existence to attain emptiness, one transforms from an ordinary person into a sage.
This may be called the secret manual for penetrating the profound mystery, the divine elixir for transforming the bones.

Regarding the mere manifestation of names: although in the *Avataṃsaka* each stage (*bhūmi*) is said to be "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), it is only upon reaching the eighth stage that one truly attains it.

As for the seventh stage, it is said: "One purifies the immeasurable body, speech, and mind, and attains the radiance of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The commentary states that the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is what is attained at the eighth stage; thus, in this seventh stage, one merely perceives the signs of clarity within that patience.

Though it manifests before one, it is not yet truly attained, as explained in the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*. Since non-arising (*anutpāda*) belongs to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the underlying intent is roughly the same here.
This continues up to the eighth stage, where one is free from all conceptual discriminations of mind, thought, and consciousness;

only then is it called the true attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thus we know that even for the sages, non-arising is difficult to realize; how much more so for ordinary people? It is therefore exceedingly remote.
One grows weary of birth as a source of affliction and urgently desires to extinguish it in order to return to non-existence;

yet this extinction is not true extinction, which only increases one's toil, ultimately resulting in the cycle of saṃsāra—like an ox that destroys its own cart, as there is a clear analogy for in antiquity. Now, focus exclusively on the Buddha’s name and make the vow to be reborn in that land.
Once reborn in that realm, the lotus flower will open and you shall behold the Buddha, thereby realizing your own original mind: that it is fundamentally unborn.
What hindrance is there even to birth? That which is called "vigorously seeking birth" does not contradict the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
To be born throughout one's entire life yet never truly born—this is precisely what constitutes true non-arising. One realizes non-arising while within birth;
therefore, it is said that by entering existence, one attains emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Birth belongs to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), yet through birth one reaches non-arising; hence it is said:

Thus, one becomes a sage from an ordinary person; following the path, one returns home. Secretly transcending the dense veil [of ignorance], it is inconceivable and beyond discussion. Hence it is said:
"To penetrate the profound, one suddenly shifts [realms]," like ascending to immortality on level ground, or a commoner suddenly attaining noble rank. Therefore, it is called "changing the bones.
To discard the secret instructions and cultivate empty words, to cast away the divine elixir and take wild drugs—is this not truly a matter of great lamentation?
Tenth, to further clarify the path of cultivation—the path within paths—there are two meanings.

First, while practicing the Way through other gates is a journey of ten thousand miles, the recollection of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land has been called the "direct path" since antiquity. Yet, within this single method of recollecting the Buddha, there are many approaches;
the present practice of holding the name is the most direct among these direct paths, like a crane soaring or a great Peng bird.
Exemplified: A galloping horse or a soaring dragon does not move swiftly, yet arrives with speed; it takes the direct path of paths. Regarding these two meanings:
first, it is a comparison among various types of pure practices; second, it is a distinction within the primary division of this Great Canon.
Thus, it is called "the direct path of paths. As for "direct path," a path that is small yet swift is termed a "direct path" (*jing*).
The "small" analogy illustrates the simplicity of the power of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation); the "swift" analogy illustrates the rapidity with which success in *nien-fo* is achieved.
As Great Master Shandao’s verse says: "There is only this direct path for practice: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. This is precisely what it means.

Therefore it is said: practicing the Way through other gates is called "ascending out of the triple world," whereas reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth in the Pure Land is called "transversely exiting the triple world.
It is like a worm inside a bamboo stalk: if it moves vertically, it passes through the nodes with difficulty; if it moves horizontally, it emerges all at once.
Compared to other gates, the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name is swifter. Furthermore, there are many gates within the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name, as will be explained below.

Within this text, four types of *buddhānusmṛti* (mindfulness of the Buddha) based on the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) are revealed, extending even to the dedication of the myriad practices and so forth.

Although it is said that the Buddha of true reality is inherently possessed by all, sentient beings are heavily burdened by obscurations, and those who attain realization and understanding are rare; therefore, these several gates are taught for those below that level.

If one contemplates the image, the image vanishes upon being removed, resulting in interruptions in practice. If one contemplates the visualization (*bhāvanā*), the mind is coarse while the object is subtle, making it difficult to achieve profound contemplation.
If one practices the myriad deeds, they are so numerous that one inevitably falls into partiality toward those deemed more important.

Only this single method of holding the Name is concise, essential, and direct; by merely maintaining mindfulness, one attains rebirth in the Pure Land. As the ancients said: "Once you have attained this vision..."
Amitābha—how could one worry about not attaining enlightenment? Thus, without seeking the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one accords with it.
Therefore, mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) is the path for spiritual practice, and the recitation of the name (*chiming*) is the path within mindfulness of the Buddha.

A crane may already surpass ordinary birds, yet how can it compare to the soaring of the great Peng? A galloping horse may indeed outstrip the herd, yet it has not yet reached the flight of the dragon. All [of these]...
The upper part is a metaphor for mindfulness of the Buddha; the lower part is a metaphor for mindfulness of the Buddha by reciting the name.

Regarding "not swift and not acting," the *Appended Statements* of the *I Ching* say: "The *I Ching* has no thought and no action. It is still and unmoving, yet when stimulated, it immediately penetrates the affairs of the world.
Were it not for the ultimate divinity of the world, who could participate in this? Only through divinity can one act without haste and yet..."
"Swift. It arrives without traveling. This means that what is "fast" (ji) is followed by "swift" (su). That which travels and then arrives is the constant nature of things.
The essence of the milfoil stalks and the hexagrams is quiescent and devoid of volition or action, yet when there is a resonance, they penetrate immediately. This is to be swift without being fast.
"To arrive without traveling" refers to that which is called "spiritual" (*shen*), as it wondrously transforms all things.

Citing this to clarify the various gateways of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), although they are all equally termed "rebirth," their efficacy is somewhat more difficult and the duration somewhat longer;

thus, one must practice and proceed with speed, even to the point of being swift. Now, however, there is no waiting for months or years, nor is there any need for artificial effort; in seven days, one [attains it].
The mind immediately gives birth in that land; how marvelous and wondrous it is to reach such a state! Thus, the *Commentary on the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra* states:
"Among the several hundred volumes in the Great Canon—whether sutras or treatises—that explain the cultivation of those causes, all require diligent accumulation before one may attain rebirth there.
Yet now, by merely reciting the name, one ascends directly to the stage of non-retrogression. Is this not a shortcut?"
How direct this path is!

Second, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* extensively details the environment and its inhabitants, and fully records the methods of practice; whereas this present sūtra honors brevity by eliminating redundancy, and through a concise approach, encompasses the vast.
It offers no other teaching, pointing solely to the holding of the Name. Provided one attains single-mindedness, one shall immediately be born [in that land].
That land may be described as increasingly simple and concise, increasingly subtle and profound—the very path within the path.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Immeasurable Life Sūtra) is found in detail within the two sections on classification and translation and commentary; when compared with the present sūtra, it is commonly called the "Large Version.

This is because while the textual division is the same, they differ in their brevity and detail. That [sūtra] was taught for those who delight in the extensive, whereas this [sūtra] is for those who delight in the concise.
Thus it is said. Yet, while the phrasing is concise, the principle becomes even more clear; while the matters are summarized, the merit is doubled and superior.

For instance, whereas the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (the "Great Root") speaks extensively of various merits, this sutra states that merely holding the name constitutes great merit and great goodness.

Furthermore, whereas the "Great Root" still distinguishes between three grades of rebirth, this sutra states that by merely being born in that land, one attains non-retrogression from bodhi for all alike. This is...
Thus, it is not only the essential among the various gates of Buddha-recollection; it is even more essential within its own school.
It may be called the most sublime of the sublime, the most profound of the profound, and the most direct of the direct.
As explained above regarding the ten meanings within the specific [sections], the first nine are taken as general and the last one as specific;
together with the preceding general meaning, these constitute the causes for the arising of this scripture’s teaching.

"General" refers to the general clarification that all Pure Land sutras share this same cause. "Specific" refers to the specific clarification that this sutra alone emphasizes the recitation of the name, taking the recitation of the name as its cause.
"Comprehensive" refers to the previous comprehensive clarification that all sutras take the One Great Matter as their cause.
When it is said that the Buddha preached this sutra, it was to teach sentient beings to be mindful [of the Buddha].
The Buddha taught sentient beings to practice mindfulness by holding the name in order to lead them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
he did so solely to bring about the realization of this great matter of the one mind. This constitutes the reason for the arising of the teachings of this sutra.
III. The Inclusion within the Two Pitakas, the Teachings, and so forth (3). First, inclusion within the Pitakas; second, inclusion within the teachings; third, inclusion within the divisions.
Regarding the first, inclusion within the Pitakas:
it is already known that the Buddha spoke this sutra for such causes; however, it is not yet known which of the Pitakas, the teachings, or the divisions this sutra belongs to.
Regarding the categories of inclusion, there are two types of "piṭakas": first, the three piṭakas; second, the two piṭakas.
As for the former, the three piṭakas are: first, the Sūtra Piṭaka; second, the Vinaya Piṭaka; and third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
This present sutra is included within the Sūtra Piṭaka. Although various sutras may also mutually include one another, this is not the case here.
In Sanskrit, *sūtra*; here it is translated as "Sutra" (契經). It is called the Sūtra Piṭaka. An explanation can be found later in the commentary on the title.
*Vinaya* means "Discipline" (調伏); this is the Vinaya Piṭaka. *Abhidharma* means "Higher Dharma" (對法); this is the Śāstra Piṭaka.
The former two possess many meanings, which will not be cited here as they are not urgent. As for that which is subsumed under the Sūtra Piṭaka, this refers to the present sutra.
Among the three collections of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, this belongs to the Sūtra-piṭaka. Regarding their mutual inclusion:

for instance, the *Avataṃsaka* is subsumed under the Sūtra-piṭaka while simultaneously encompassing the Vinaya and Abhidharma, because chapters such as the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika*) manifest the precepts and discipline, while chapters such as the "Questions of Samantabhadra" (*Samantabhadraparipṛcchā*) manifest the discourses of the Abhidharma.

The *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, however, is subsumed under the Vinaya-piṭaka while simultaneously encompassing the Sūtra-piṭaka, because the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" (*Cittabhūmi-parivarta*) extensively discusses the bodhicitta.
Because this concerns the stages of the Bodhisattva path, the rest may be understood by analogy. This sutra does not incorporate the Vinaya, nor does it engage in dialectical discussion;
from beginning to end, it exclusively teaches mindfulness of the Buddha and the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land. Therefore, it is said: "The present [text] is not that one."
Regarding the two collections (*piṭaka*): first, the Bodhisattva Collection; second, the Śrāvaka Collection. This present sutra is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Collection.
Furthermore, there is mutual inclusion between them; however, this is not the case here.

The Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas are explained in detail in the subsequent commentary. Regarding the two divisions of the Piṭaka: because the sūtras comprise both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, they are subsumed within these two divisions of the Piṭaka.
If categorized by way of persons, there are three vehicles, and thus it would also be appropriate to divide them into three.

However, since Pratyekabuddhas for the most part do not rely upon formal instruction, they are subsumed under the Śrāvakas; therefore, there are only two Piṭakas. Now, this [text] is included within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
This sutra expounds upon the Mahāyāna, such as the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants, faith, aspiration, and rebirth in the Pure Land;
these are all the paths for Bodhisattvas to purify Buddha-lands and transform sentient beings for their own benefit and the benefit of others. Regarding mutual inclusion:
As it is subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the *Avataṃsaka*, it also extends to the Śrāvakas, because it is able to encompass immeasurable vehicles.

Since the seeds of the two vehicles do not arise in this present sutra, it is said that they are "not those. Someone may ask: "How can it be so when the text states that that Buddha had Śrāvaka disciples?
Answer: These exist only temporarily and ultimately do not; this shall be explained in detail below in the commentary on the text. Furthermore...

Question: One who loathes suffering and pursues happiness does so solely for their own benefit; how can such a person be called a bodhisattva? Answer: To seek rebirth in a pure land is precisely for the purpose of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma.
Once one has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), one returns to this world to rescue suffering sentient beings.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva, not the path of a śrāvaka. As it is said in the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (Shiyi lun) of Tiantai: [The text continues with the citation].
II. Inclusion by Teaching (*śāsana-saṃgraha*).
Regarding "teaching," according to Xianshou’s classification of the teachings, there are five divisions: namely, the Small, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect.
This present sutra is subsumed under the Sudden Teaching, while it also concurrently accords with the preceding two teachings (the Initial and Final).

Regarding the five teachings: first is the Hīnayāna teaching, which explains only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Even when it briefly mentions the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it does not do so clearly.
This is because it establishes the roots of defilement and purity based on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, and thus has not exhausted the source of all phenomena.
Second is the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna. From the second turning of the wheel, it clarifies only emptiness; from the third turning, it definitively explains [the Middle Way].

The Three Vehicles do not admit that those of fixed nature (niyata-gotra) who are icchantikas can attain Buddhahood; thus, they have not yet exhausted the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna and are therefore called "Initial" (ādikarmika).
Because they maintain that some will attain Buddhahood while others will not, they are further termed "Distinctive" (vibhāga-śāsana).

What they expound consists largely of a detailed discussion of *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) with little reference to *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena). Even what they call "nature" (*svabhāva*) is merely a category of characteristics, for it relies upon the eightfold [consciousness] of arising and ceasing.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because it establishes the various categories of meaning regarding the causes of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa, there are three [aspects].

The Mahāyāna Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-deśanā*) is so called because it reaches the ultimate limit of the Mahāyāna; for by emerging from the subtle existence of the Middle Way, it proclaims that even those of fixed nature who are icchantikas shall all become Buddhas.
Because it accords with the true principle (*tattva*), it is further called the "True Teaching" (*bhūta-deśanā*). As for its exposition, it speaks primarily of...
The Dharma-nature (dharmatā). It involves a slight engagement with the characteristics of phenomena (lakṣaṇa), yet these so-called characteristics ultimately converge back into the nature itself;

this is because the eight consciousnesses, based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, establish various categories of meaning according to conditions. Fourth is the Sudden Teaching (dun jiao): it does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena at all, but speaks only of true nature (*bhūtatathatā*).
The non-arising of even a single thought is itself called Buddhahood, as there is no gradual progression. Fifth is the Perfect Teaching (yuan jiao): it universally...
The preceding four [teachings] are fully perfected; what is taught therein is exclusively the inexhaustible *dharmadhātu*.

Its ocean of nature is perfectly interfused, its dependent origination is unimpeded, its characteristics are mutually identical and mutually inclusive, like a multi-layered net of Indra, with principal and satellites intermingling, inexhaustibly and infinitely so.

The details are as explained in the *Huayan Xuanzan* (Profound Commentary on the Avataṃsaka); fearing prolixity, they are not recounted here. As for that which is subsumed under the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*):
As will be explained in the subsequent section on doctrinal principles (*yili*), it also extends to both the preceding and succeeding [teachings].

It extends to the preceding Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*) because all sentient beings who practice *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha) are certain to attain Buddhahood; that is, even those of fixed nature who are *icchantikas* (those devoid of faith) will all become Buddhas.
Its extension to the succeeding Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is likewise explained in the section on doctrinal principles.
The threefold classification.
As for "classification," it refers to the twelve divisions of the teaching, such as the sūtra (sūtra), geya (geya), and so forth. This present scripture is a sūtra.
Udāna is subsumed under two categories.
As for "categories" (bhāga), this refers to a distinct limit; that is, the teachings of one lifetime are distinguished by their respective limits, each belonging to its own specific class.
Geya is translated here as "repeated verse. Udāna is translated here as "unasked self-exposition. [The full list of] twelve divisions is omitted for fear of being too cumbersome.
It is not categorized [under the *sūtra*]. As for what is said regarding its inclusion within two categories: first, it is included under the *sūtra*, because it is a *saṃyukta-āgama*;
second, it is included under the *udāna*, because it was spoken by himself to Śāriputra without waiting for a question.
III. The Profundity and Extensiveness of the Meaning and Principle (3). First, the subsumption of the Sudden [Teaching], the partial inclusion of the Perfect, and the secondary correspondence.
First, the subsumption of the Sudden:

It has already been known that this sutra subsumes the Sudden Teaching and partially belongs to the Perfect; however, the specific meanings and principles it possesses have not yet been understood, and thus they shall now be further [examined].

How so? First, to clarify that this sutra subsumes the *sudden* (dun) approach: it means that by merely holding the name, one is born [in the Pure Land] immediately and swiftly attains realization, for there is no detouring or circuitousness;
thus, it properly belongs to the sudden.

Regarding that which truly pertains to the meaning of the Sudden Teaching: for an ordinary person at the level of the mundane ground to wish to ascend to the ground of the sages is an exceedingly difficult matter;
the path is exceedingly remote. Now, by merely holding the Name, one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land; once reborn there, one immediately attains the stage of non-retrogression.

This may be called "perfecting in a single snap of the fingers" or "accomplishing everything in one lifetime. It is like bestowing the precious throne directly upon an ordinary person without passing through successive ranks;
it is not comparable to the gradual teachings that are circuitous and winding. Therefore, it belongs to the meaning of the Sudden (Dun).
Someone may raise this objection: "In the Sudden Teaching, it is said that when not a single thought arises, one is immediately called a Buddha;

the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty, and the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are both discarded. Now, to practice *nianfo* by reciting the name is to have 'thought' (*nian*). How, then, can this be called 'Sudden'? Answer:
"One mind without distraction" precisely refers to non-thought. If there is thought, it cannot be called "one mind.
Once one attains this one mind, what dharma would not be tranquil?
The five dharmas are: first, name; second, appearance; third, false imagination; fourth, correct gnosis; and fifth, suchness.

The three natures are as follows: name and appearance constitute the imagined nature; false imagination constitutes the dependent-arising nature; and correct gnosis and suchness constitute the perfected nature. The eight consciousnesses are:
the ālaya, the manas, and the six [consciousnesses] beginning with the visual, which together form the eight. (2)
Regarding selflessness: there is the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Both of these are likewise included within the five dharmas;

this is seen in detail in various sutras such as the *Laṅkāvatāra*. All are empty and all are relinquished. That which is called the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any numerical categories.
The principle that "the non-arising of a single thought is itself called Buddhahood" is the purport of the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*).

Now, when we speak of "reciting the Buddha's name," the name of the Buddha belongs to the category of names; the Buddha-body one faces belongs to the category of marks (*lakṣaṇa*); and the recollective mindfulness of that Buddha belongs to the category of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
Even if one’s pure mindfulness continues uninterrupted such that one enters *samādhi*, this still belongs to the realm of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*).

Yet, to further differentiate [this state] as "Buddha" belongs to the sphere of consciousness and emotion (*vijñāna-vedanā*). The subject who contemplates and the object contemplated belong to the categories of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*);

thus, the notion of a self (*ātman*) has not yet been eliminated, let alone the elimination of non-self (*anātman*). All these things—what is to be emptied and what is to be discarded—are present in that teaching, because it still possesses conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*).
Therefore, the objection is not immediate. What is truly meant by "no-thought" (amanasikāra) is precisely this:

because the single mind is undisturbed, one does not think with a mind that exists, nor does one think with a mind that does not exist, nor does one think with a mind that both exists and does not exist, nor does one think with a mind that neither exists nor does not exist.
Apart from these four propositions, what further thought could there be? Although it is called "recollection of the Buddha," it is in fact no-thought.
This is the thought of non-thought. To think without thinking is called "one mind. In such a mind, the mind has no mind; it is only forcibly named "one.
Since even the mark of "one" does not exist, how can one seek what are called five, three, eight, or two?
Thus, the non-distraction of one mind is no different from the non-arising of a single thought; how could this not be the Sudden [Teaching]?
○ Regarding the division into two parts, those belonging to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): the meaning of "Perfect" refers to the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Among these, the first three are common to all teachings, while the last one is uniquely possessed by the Perfect Teaching alone. This present sutra fully encompasses this [last realm]; as this part encompasses the Perfect, it attains the Perfect.
A small portion belongs to the Perfect [Teaching].

Regarding the four dharma-spheres (dharmadhātu): first, the dharma-sphere of phenomena; second, the dharma-sphere of principle; third, the dharma-sphere of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.

These three [teachings] are found in all the various scriptures. The fourth, the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*), exists only in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* alone;

it is called the "Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle" (*biejiao yicheng*). Because the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle (*shili wuai*) is identical to the sudden and the final [teachings], yet the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*) differs from those two, it is distinguished from the "Common Teaching of the One Vehicle" (*tongjiao yicheng*), and is therefore termed "distinct. This does not refer to the *zang*, *tong*, or *bie* [of the four teachings].

This is a distinction within the Perfect [Teaching]. Now, regarding the claim that the Partial [Teaching] is subsumed within the Perfect: since the *Avataṃsaka* represents the entirety of the Perfect Teaching, what we have now is but a small portion of it.
Briefly stated, there are ten aspects. First, in the *Avataṃsaka*, the vessel-world, atoms, hairs, and all things—whether with form or without form—all produce the sublime sounds of the Dharma;
thus, even waterfowl and forest trees all proclaim the dharmas of the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment.
First, because it is the gateway. Second, within a single atom of the *Avataṃsaka*, the infinite adornments of the dharma-realm of the ten directions are fully present.
This is as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya*: "Within the jeweled trees, one sees the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, like reflections in a mirror.
Third, because the immovable site of enlightenment in the *Avataṃsaka* pervades the entire dharma-realm, it is said that its essence and characteristics are as they originally were.
The distinctions are peerless and immeasurable, pervading everywhere. This is as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sutra]:
"Amitābha Buddha constantly resides in the western quarter, yet he also pervades the ten directions. Fourth, the *Avataṃsaka* uses the metaphor of the King of Medicine Tree:
if there are those who see it, their eyes attain purity; even so for the ears, nose, and the other six sense organs—there is nothing that does not attain purity. When sentient beings see...
The Buddha is likewise so. Because one sees the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment and hears the Dharma of the Universal Gate, his spiritual power is such as this.
This is because those who see or hear [the Buddha] at the jeweled trees of Amitābha Buddha’s place of practice have their six sense faculties purified. Five.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the eight difficulties transcend the stages of the ten bhūmis; for those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals who merely recite the Buddha’s name shall all attain rebirth there.

Sixth, because in the *Avataṃsaka* the one is identical to the all, the Tathāgata can manifest within a single body as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields. From each head emerge that same number of tongues, and from each tongue...
The sounds you produce, even down to the words, phrases, and meanings, fill the entire Dharma-realm. This is as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*:
"In that land, from each of the immeasurable jewel-flowers, thirty-six billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of rays of light emerge;
from each ray of light, thirty-six billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands [of further lights] emerge."
Because the Buddha universally expounds all dharmas for the sake of the ten directions. Seventh:
Vairocana and Śākyamuni of the *Avataṃsaka* both manifest two forms simultaneously. This is as stated in the *Contemplation Sūtra*:
"Amitābha Buddha manifests a body sixty quadrillion nayuta Ganges-sands of yojanas in height, yet is also seen with a body sixteen feet tall upon the waters of the pond."
Therefore, there are eight [points of correspondence]. Ninth, the *Avataṃsaka* takes Vairocana Buddha as its presiding teacher;

this is because, as Qingliang [Zongmi] stated, Amitābha Buddha is none other than the original teacher, Vairocana. Tenth, the *Avataṃsaka* is titled the "Great Inconceivable," while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and other sutras are titled the "Small Inconceivable";
this is because [the Pure Land teachings] are also named the "Inconceivable Merit."
Tenth: The *Avataṃsaka* as a teaching means that the mind of an ordinary person immediately becomes the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of all Buddhas.

This does not transcend the act of reciting the name, for the Buddha manifests before one. Thus, it is equal to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and other sutras, sharing the same category as the *Avataṃsaka*.
The Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) fully encompasses this sutra, while this sutra partially encompasses the Perfect Teaching by way of its limited meaning. Therefore.
This is called "Perfecting the Name.
○ Third, General Application (2). First, the *Amitābha Sūtra* and second, the various other sūtras.
○ First, the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

First, regarding the general interpretation of the sutra: some say that the sixteen contemplation gates are termed "concentrated goodness" (*samāhita-kuśala*), while the upholding of the Name is termed "scattered goodness" (*vikṣipta-kuśala*).
Now, we shall provide a general clarification of this, which consists of two parts: first, the general; second, the specific. First, the general is explained as follows:
That sutra’s sublime contemplation takes the single mind as its fundamental principle; this sutra’s single mind precisely accords with that intent.

To practice contemplation with the single mind and to recite the name with the single mind—how could these not both lead back to the single mind? To exalt the former while disparaging the latter is unfounded, as explained in detail in Jingjue’s Commentary.

Regarding "comprehensive penetration": this does not differentiate between the Sudden and the Perfect [teachings], but rather takes the principles of various Mahāyāna sūtras as being mutually compatible.
Because the *Sixteen Contemplations* is a specialized sūtra on the Pure Land, it is mentioned first. Regarding "concentrated and dispersed":

Mount Gushan judges the Sixteen Contemplations to be "concentrated goodness" (*samādhi-kuśala*), while the practice of upholding the Name in this sūtra is "dispersed goodness. Now, it is said that "one-pointed mind without distraction" involves both the phenomenal and...
This is logical. Even "one-pointedness regarding phenomena" (*shishi ichinen*) is not entirely free from distraction; how much more so is "one-pointedness regarding principle" (*rishichi*)?

That which precisely accords with the intent of that [other] sutra—where the three contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle transcend sequential order—is what constitutes "one mind.
In this present sutra, by upholding the Name with "one mind without distraction," both the subject who upholds and the object upheld become utterly unapprehendable. This is...

That which is called the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is precisely when, at the very moment of emptiness, the subject and object are clearly distinct; this is called the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
That which is neither provisional nor empty, yet is eternally empty and eternally provisional—this inconceivable state is called the Middle Contemplation (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*).

This is because by single-mindedly invoking the sacred name, one directly descends into a unified mind; what sequential order could there be? This is precisely the meaning of the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations. Thus, that sutra...
Taking contemplation as its primary principle, this sutra takes mental recollection as its primary principle. Contemplation is precisely recollection; recollection is precisely contemplation.
Since what is taught in both sutras is the same single mind, why should this sutra alone suppress it and label it "scattered"?

Therefore, this dharma-gate is called the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-remembrance samādhi), and it is also called the *i-hsing san-mei* (one-practice samādhi), and it is also called "the manifestation of all Buddhas before one."
It is called samādhi; it is also named prajñā-samādhi and also named universal equality samādhi (samantatulya-samādhi). The term "samādhi" means concentration (*dhyāna*).
Since it encompasses many kinds of samādhi, how could it be considered distracted? In essence, if visualization and contemplation are not performed with a single mind, [it is not samādhi].

Contemplation also becomes distracted. If one attains single-mindedness while reciting the name, the recitation itself constitutes concentration (*samādhi*). It is not a matter of whether one relies on contemplative visualization or the recitation of the name;
rather, it depends on whether the mind is single-minded or not. As stated in Master Jingjue’s commentary (*shu*), the commentary says:

"The Great Master Zhiyi, regarding the *Contemplation Sutra*, classified the three types of pure karma as belonging to distraction and the sixteen subtle contemplations as belonging to concentration. This has not yet been [fully addressed].
It is heard that reciting the name is categorized as "scattered" (dispersed) practice.孤山 (Gushan) judges this sutra to be for scattered goodness. I do not approve of his view.

Furthermore, in the *Commentary on the Universal Gate Chapter*, he explains that single-mindedly invoking the name has both a phenomenal and a noumenal aspect: maintaining mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara [is the phenomenal].

The absence of interruption is called "single-mindedness in practice" (*shi-ichinen*). If one penetrates this mind such that the four modes of being do not arise and it accords with the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), it is called "single-mindedness in principle" (*ri-ichinen*).
Regarding the two characters "unconfused" (*furan*) in the context of the Universal Gate, even the Great Master Chih-i (Chih-che) interpreted them as the wisdom of emptiness.
Now, when it is said "single-mindedly without confusion," how can it be disparaged as merely "scattered good"? According to my humble analysis, Chih-i entered...
He passed away. Zhiyi (Zhang’an) also invoked the names of Amitābha and the two Great Beings when he was nearing death.
Since such was the personal practice of both master and disciple, one must not categorically dismiss the practice of invoking the name; thus, our faith is further strengthened.
Next, to clarify the distinctions: some claim that this sutra merely involves hearing the Buddha’s name; some claim that the Buddha in this sutra is a subordinate response-body (hīna-nirmāṇakāya);

some claim that the lotuses in this sutra are restricted to the size of chariot wheels; some claim that those who commit the five grave offenses cannot be reborn [in the Pure Land] through this sutra;

and some claim that this sutra belongs exclusively to the lowest grade. This is because they do not know that the two sutras share the same essential meaning, nor do they realize that this sutra is particularly and uniquely essential.

Regarding "merely the name": some claim that while other sutras involve contemplating the teachings and visualizing the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of that Buddha, this sutra merely upholds the four characters of the empty name;

thus, one does not see the Buddha’s body, and it is therefore called "scattered goodness" (*vikṣiptakuśala*). However, the sutra states: "Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of sages, appears before one.
Since the Buddha has appeared, how could he lack the marks and signs? Moreover, since he is accompanied by the assembly, [how could they be absent?]

The principal and the attendant are both manifested together. This is because while the former involves seeing the Buddha through contemplation, the latter involves seeing the Buddha by holding his name; thus, while the causes differ, the vision of the Buddha is one and the same.

Regarding the "inferior response" (the *hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*), some may say that the *Amitābha-sūtra* states the Buddha’s body is sixty million billion nayutas of *gaṅgā*-sands of *yojanas* in height, whereas this sūtra does not mention it, and therefore suspect it must be the inferior response. For this reason...
This is called "scattered goodness. However, the *Mūla-sūtra* states: "At that time, Amitābha Buddha emitted a great radiance, universally illuminating all worlds.
Ānanda saw the Buddha’s countenance and body so majestic and towering, like a mountain of yellow gold, rising high above all the worlds.
Thus, while the *Contemplation Sūtra* describes it as being within a single world, the present text speaks of "all worlds."
As for his realm, it is even more vast and magnificent; how can it be said to be inferior?

Furthermore, the *Mūla-sūtra* states that the jewel trees in Amitābha Buddha’s place of enlightenment are composed entirely of various precious gems, naturally formed; they are not the wooden Bodhi tree beneath which [Śākyamuni] attained awakening.
How can it be said to be inferior? Moreover, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* says that this Buddha may manifest at a height of one zhang and six chi, or eight chi, or...

The great body fills the void of space; thus, according to what each person perceives, its size is not fixed. Therefore, the ancients said that it is simultaneously inferior and superior, for the arising and the dharma are non-dual.
How much more so in the present sutra, which does not exclude either the Great or the Small [Vehicles]. How can one definitively designate it as inferior?
As for the claim that the lotus is restricted to the size of a chariot wheel: some say that in the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching), the lotus is twelve yojanas in size, whereas in this sutra...

The wheel [of rebirth]. The *Huaju* (Flower Bureau) restricts this to the small scale, hence it is called "scattered goodness" (*saṃkīrṇakuśala*). It does not understand the meaning of the wheel; its size is not fixed.
In the *Daben* (Great Root), the wheel is as large as one hundred thousand *yojanas*. How could it stop at twelve? This is explained in detail later in the text.

Regarding those who do not produce the five heinous offenses (*pañcānantarya*): some claim that the *Guanjing* (Contemplation Sūtra) states that even those who commit the five heinous offenses can attain birth [in the Pure Land], whereas the *Daben* [states] only...
If one excludes only the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the merit of salvation is narrow; therefore, these are called "scattered virtues" (*vikṣiptakuśala*).

This is because it is not realized that beneath the phrase "excepting the five heinous crimes," there are the four characters "slandering the True Dharma. One who commits the five heinous crimes while also slandering the Dharma is among those excluded.

Even if one possesses all five heinous crimes, if they do not slander the Dharma, they will not necessarily fail to attain birth [in the Pure Land]. This is truly because to slander is to lack faith, and to lack faith...
It does not arise. Thus, it is as the saying goes: "If there is doubt, the flower will not open. The *Contemplation Sūtra* does not explicitly mention the slandering of the Dharma;

however, even those who slander it do not attain birth [in the Pure Land]. Furthermore, in the section on the lowest of the low grades (*adhamādhama-pudgala*) of the *Contemplation Sūtra*, which describes the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), it states that such a person attains rebirth by ten recitations of the Name.
This implies that while their visualization practice has not yet been perfected, they rely solely upon these ten recollections (*daśa-smṛti*). Five...

Regarding the arising [of beings] through the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*): it is precisely by invoking the Name that they attain birth. How much more so when the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: "Those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals shall also be born within my land.

○ First, the Exposition of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇānusāra*).
It has already been understood that this sūtra is universally applicable to all capacities; however, it remains unknown what the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the expressive medium is.

Following the successive ten gates of investigation into the source by the ancients, these are condensed into four. First, the Exposition of Characteristics, which itself contains two parts: the first concerns sound (*śabda*) and names (*nāman*).

"Phrases and words. The second refers to the meaning expressed (*artha*). Since both words and meaning belong to the category of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), these ten gates are presented in successive relation.

Thus, there are four gates. First, regarding sound (*śabda*), name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*):

sound is taken as the teacher of the doctrine, while "name" refers to the sequential arrangement that elucidates the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena. "Phrase" [refers to...]

The "syllables" (*vyañjana*) are the sequential arrangement that defines the distinctions among phenomena. The "phrases" (*pada*) are the sequential conjunctions that serve as the basis for the former two.

These three—name, phrase, and syllable—are the vocal sounds that function as expressive designations; yet, sound alone cannot express meaning, while name, phrase, and syllable alone lack intrinsic substance.
It is the combination of these four factors that constitutes the essence of the teaching (*deśanā*). This is established by way of designation (*prajñapti*).
The substance and function are mutually supportive. Second, regarding the meanings expressed:

if these sounds, names, phrases, and syllables lacked the meanings they express, they would be no different from mere rhyme books, utterly devoid of significance. Conversely, if there were only meaning without the written expression, by what means could the subtle principles be revealed?
This is because the expression follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the expression; thus, expression and meaning are interdependent.

The material basis thus constitutes the essence of the teaching. Therefore, in this present sutra, from the words "Thus have I heard" up to "having paid homage, they withdrew," there is the substance of sounds, names, phrases, and syllables;
meanwhile, the primary and secondary retributions, as well as faith, aspiration, and rebirth therein, which are explained within it, constitute the meaning to be expressed.
Because these two are mutually dependent, they together form the essence of the teaching.
Furthermore, if one relies on the meaning revealed by the Dharma, then there is nothing that is not a Buddha-activity, such as the fragrant food, the light, and so forth.
One should know that every phenomenon (dharma) serves as the essence of the teaching.

Thus, in this sutra, even the waterfowl and the forest trees all proclaim the sublime Dharma; accordingly, whichever phenomenon one mentions, it all constitutes the essence of the teaching.

VI. The Six Schools and Their Ultimate Aims (3): First, a general presentation of two divergent interpretations; second, the correct intention.
First, the general presentation:

We have already understood that the substance of this sūtra’s expressive medium encompasses all things in such a manner; however, we do not yet know which of these [interpretations] constitutes its primary tenet.
Now, that which is esteemed in discourse is called the "tenet" (zong). That to which the tenet returns is called the "destination" (qu). These have both general and specific aspects.

Generally speaking, the dependent origination of Buddhism is the tenet. Specifically, there are ten traditional gates, ranging from the co-existence of self and dharmas up to the perfect fusion of all virtues.
Each subsequent gate is deeper than the preceding one. Therefore, each sutra has its own respective tenet and destination.
"Shang" (尚) means "to honor. When the Sages established their teachings, what among the various expressions of a single scripture was held in highest honor?
That which is honored is called the *zong* (宗, school/essence). "Gui" (歸) means "to arrive at. Establishing this as the *zong* is for the purpose of seeking out that which is ultimately arrived at;

this ultimate destination is called the *qu* (趣, goal). "In-yuan" (因緣, causes and conditions) serves to distinguish [the teaching] from that which is causeless or possesses false causes. These constitute the temporal teachings of the One Vehicle.

It does not depart from causes and conditions. As it is said: by reason of causes and conditions there is arising and ceasing; by reason of causes and conditions there is emptiness; by reason of causes and conditions there is the provisional;

the first is the school that maintains the existence of both self and dharmas, which internally clings to a self and externally clings to dharmas.

The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is perfectly interfused. This present sutra takes this dharmatā as its fundamental principle; for the Pure Land, its environment and inhabitants, as well as faith, vows, and so forth, all ultimately converge within the one mind.

Regarding this sutra, there have been many interpretations in the past. Some maintain that the central theme (*śāstra*) is faith and aspiration;
others maintain that it is the two kinds of purity that transcend the triple world; and some hold that its destination (*prayojana*) is to cause all sentient beings to attain non-retrogression.
Regarding "taking faith and aspiration as the core principle," most commentaries agree on this, because the sutra repeatedly states:
"If there are those with faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land. Regarding the "two kinds of purity," the treatise says it refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The two retributions—the primary and the secondary—are pure and adorned, beyond the reach of the triple world; thus, this is taken as the central tenet.
Yet, regarding their ultimate purpose, it is to cause sentient beings to be born in that pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and once born in that land...

○ Third, the Correct Intention (in two parts): first, a general enumeration; second, a specific explanation.
○ First, the general enumeration.
This sutra takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as its primary tenet. Within this nature of phenomena, there is further differentiation between the general and the specific;
yet when these are unified in their totality, they are termed the purity of the environment and its inhabitants, with the aspiration for rebirth through faith and vow serving as its central purpose.
Taking the two preceding explanations and combining them constitutes the overall thesis.

This is because the former explanation does not encompass both the environment and its inhabitants (*śāsanadeśa* and *sattvadhātu*), while the latter explanation is not detailed regarding faith and aspiration (*śraddhā* and *praṇidhāna*). Therefore, they must be combined so that nothing is omitted.

This is truly because rebirth is attained through the mutual support of the complete presence of both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as faith and aspiration—all of which do not transcend one’s own mind. Thus, these constitute the overall thesis.

Regarding "aim" (*gati*): following the precedent of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, that scripture also incorporates various explanations, taking as its central aim the reality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the principle of dependent origination encompassing both cause and effect.
If one wishes to distinguish them, the upper phrase constitutes the "thesis" (*mata*), while the lower phrase constitutes the "aim."
The meaning is also self-evident. If one wishes to add further, that sutra adds "inconceivable," and this present sutra does likewise.

II. Specific Clarification: To clarify it specifically, there are five pairs: first, teaching and meaning; second, phenomena and principle; third, object and practice; fourth, practice and quiescence.
The five aspects of quiescent function constitute the fundamental aim.
First, regarding the correspondence between teaching and meaning: the teaching is taken as the primary principle (*mūla*), while the realization of its meaning is the ultimate goal (*prayojana*).
When it is said that this teaching of *buddhānusmṛti* and rebirth [in the Pure Land] is held in high esteem, what is its intent? It is precisely to clarify and comprehend the *Amitābha-sūtra*...
The primary and secondary rewards of Amitābha Buddha are pure and magnificently adorned. If one believes in them and aspires to them, one will be born in that land;
such is the meaning within the teachings, and this is their essential intent. It is not merely a matter of words and letters.
Regarding the first pair, "phenomena and principle" (*dharma* and *tattva*): phenomena are taken as the thesis (*pakṣa*), while making the principle manifest is the goal (*prayojana*).

Following the scriptural teachings of the preceding sutra, both are discussed in terms of their signified meaning (*lakṣya-artha*). Within that meaning, there are further distinctions between phenomena and principle.

When it is said that one reveres these matters such as reliance, right faith, and aspiration, what is the intended meaning? It is precisely to reveal the ultimate [principle] inherent within phenomena.
Principle (*li*) is its ultimate aim; it does not merely consist of the traces of phenomenal conditions. Regarding the "pairing of the three objects with the single practice":
the object is taken as the primary tenet, while the arousal of practice is the goal. The object is the principle that is contemplated;

it is called an "object" because it is contrasted with the wisdom that contemplates it. When it is said that one reveres this principle, what is the intended meaning? Since one already knows [it] extensively...
The self-nature of Dharma is that the Pure Land is mind-only; one truly intends to take this as the true realm and give rise to contemplative practice.
To hold fast to the Name with a single mind without distraction—this is the goal. It is not merely for the sake of understanding this principle alone. Regarding the "Four Practices and One Goal":
taking practice as the primary principle, one causes it to reach tranquility as the ultimate goal. This is what is meant by "veneration."

Furthermore, regarding this practice of the contemplation of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti-vipaśyanā*), what is its intended meaning? It is because although the mind is fundamentally quiescent, it has been defiled by habitual tendencies throughout many lifetimes;

thus, when encountering objects, the mind arises. If one does not cultivate contemplative practice, even if one forcibly suppresses the deluded mind, it will ultimately never achieve the equilibrium of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Now, by relying on correct contemplation and upholding the Name until one reaches single-mindedness, one returns once more to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The essence of quiescence (*śānti*) is its ultimate goal. It is not merely a matter of engaging in artificial conceptualizations. Regarding the "five aspects of quiescent function" as a single pair:
quiescence is taken as the fundamental principle (*mūla*), while the arousal of function is made the goal. When it is said that one reveres this quiescence, what is the intended meaning?
It is because liberation cannot be attained through the attachment of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*). Once delusion is exhausted and the mind becomes one, then purity reaches its ultimate limit.
"Radiant penetration" is like a mirror that is bright when dust is cleared away; there is no image that does not appear within it.

This means that once one has been born in the original land and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one returns to the realm of birth and death to perform great Buddha-works through countless skillful means, delivering and liberating sentient beings.
Its wondrous functions are as vast as the sands of the Ganges—this is its essential course. It is not merely a matter of sinking into emptiness or lingering in quiescence.
Thus, these ten gates arise in succession as the fundamental purport.
○ Section Seven: Distinctions among the Categories (Three). First, explaining the *piṭaka*; second, explaining the *nikāya*; third, explaining that which is neither *piṭaka* nor *nikāya*.
Section One: Clarifying the Textual Division.
It is already known that the essential purport of this sutra is profound and deep; however, it has not yet been determined how many types of divisions exist for its corresponding class.
To first clarify the divisions: there are two kinds. The first is the Great Root Text (Mūlasūtra); the second is this present sutra.

Regarding the "sections" (bù): these are all subsumed within a single collection, yet they differ in detail and brevity. The detailed version constitutes the Great Sūtra, while the abbreviated version is this present scripture.
The Great Sūtra consists of six [recensions]: first, the *Wúliàng píngděng qīngjìng jué jīng* (Sūtra of Immeasurable, Equal, and Pure Enlightenment), translated by Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han;
second, the *Wúliàngshòu jīng* (Sūtra of Immeasurable Life), translated by Kang Sengkai of the Cao Wei; third, the *Āmítuó*... [text truncated]
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* (Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra). It shares the same title as the present sūtra and was translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty.

Fourth, it is titled the *Sūtra on the Adornments of Immeasurable Life*, translated by Faxian of the Song dynasty. Fifth, it appears as the eighteenth sūtra in the *Ratnakūṭa*, titled the "Assembly of the Tathāgata Immeasurable Life."
Translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty; the sixth title is the *Buddhabhāṣita-mahā-amitābha-sūtra*.

The lay practitioner Wang Rixiu of Longshu during the Song Dynasty took the first four translations as a whole, collating and harmonizing them. He excluded only the *Ratnakūṭa*, as that was not within their scope.
However, among the aforementioned five translations, there are mutual differences and similarities. The two translations from the Han and Wu periods consist of forty [sections].
Of the eight vows, half remain, making twenty-four. The rest of the text is largely the same, with only minor differences.

That which was compiled by the Wang family, when compared with the five translations, is concise, clear, and easy to understand; it has circulated in the present age and its benefit is exceedingly great.
However, because it did not rely on a Sanskrit manuscript but was composed solely by approximating Chinese literary style, it did not conform to the rules of translation.
