Had it been retranslated from a Sanskrit manuscript to produce these six versions, there would have been no room for dispute; thus, he did not speak of "translation" but rather of "collation and correction."

Furthermore, among the texts selected and excerpted therein, there are also omissions. For example, regarding the three grades of those who attain birth [in the Pure Land], the Wei translation states that all "arouse the bodhicitta," whereas in the Wang family edition, only the middle grade arouses the bodhicitta, while the lower grade is said not to do so.

Since the preceding section concludes without mentioning it, the hierarchy of stages loses its proper order. Furthermore, within the text there are many roots of goodness, all of which reside in the arousal of the bodhicitta;
yet, although the three classes differ, they share the same arousal of the mind as the essential point for rebirth. That this is instead omitted is why it is said to be "incomplete.
Nevertheless, the meanings cited in the present commentary (*shū*) and sub-commentary (*shō*) incorporate all five translations, while the phrasing—

Most [versions] follow the Wén-běn (Text of King). Because this was the version commonly circulated in the world and people were already familiar with it, the other five were selected intermittently, yet all were generally designated by the title "Wén-běn.
Thus, the six types mentioned above are all called "Wén-běn. As for the present sutra:
It is called the *Shorter Version*. While the text varies in its elaboration and brevity, there is no difference in the superiority or inferiority of its meaning;

thus, it is judged to belong to the same division. Second, the clarification of related texts. Regarding the clarification of related texts, there are three types: first, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*; second, the *Ghoṣadatta-rāja-sūtra*; and third, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* (also known as the *Later-issued Amitābha Sūtra*).

Regarding the *Amitābha-gāthā-sūtra*, "of the same class" (*tonglei*) means that while they differ in their respective sections (*bu*), they are identical in their category. This is like brothers who, though having different fathers, share the same grandfather;

they are also called "shoulder-to-shoulder," meaning they are equals to one another. Therefore, it is said they are "of the same class. As for the *Contemplation Sūtra* (*Guan jing*), it is a contemplation...
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* fully expounds the sixteen sublime gates; for a detailed explanation of the "one mind and three contemplations," consult the original commentaries and sub-commentaries.
As for the *Ghoṣadatta-rāja Sūtra*, it was preached by the Buddha while at the Gaṅgā-linga Pond in the great city of Campā to a hundred bhikṣus.
Within it, it says: "If there are members of the fourfold assembly who receive and uphold the name of Amitābha Buddha, when their lives come to an end..."

At that time, the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones guided [beings] toward rebirth and so forth. Regarding those who later produced the verse-sūtra (*gāthā*), it consists entirely of verses from beginning to end;
thus, it belongs to the *gāthā* section. It states: "I shall make vows comparable to those of all Buddhas," consisting of twenty-four chapters.

Only half of these vows remain extant, which is consistent with the two Chinese translations from the Han and Wu periods. As for the forty-eight vows, they have been propagated from antiquity until the present day.
"Long ago. Twenty-fourth: it may be that the Sanskrit original is incomplete, so this remains uncertain. Someone asks:
'If the *Drum-Sound Sūtra* (*Dharmaghoṣa-sūtra*) also speaks of holding the name, why is it not of the same category as the present sūtra? Answer: Because it contains dhāraṇīs.
Although that sūtra speaks of holding the name, its primary emphasis is on holding the dhāraṇī."
Third, those that are neither [specific] divisions nor categories.

Regarding the third point, those that are neither divisions nor categories: these include texts that mention the Pure Land, such as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

Furthermore, there are those that do not belong to any specific division or category, yet within them the exclusive recitation of the name is taught, such as the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetraguṇavyūha-sūtra* (Wen-shu p'an-jo).

Regarding "those that include [the topic]": besides those belonging to the same school and category, there are further sutras which, although they do not exclusively discuss the Pure Land, incidentally include exhortations and praises for rebirth there.
For example, in the *Avataṃsaka*, such as the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra" (*Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*), after the ten great kings of vows have been clarified, it concludes by stating:
"By means of these ten vows, one is led back to the Ultimate Bliss. Similarly, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*...
"To recite this sutra" means that at the end of one's life, one shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha;
this is as clarified in the section on "Arousing Faith" (*qixin*) within the aforementioned teachings. Regarding the term "and so forth" (*deng*):

it refers to how various sutras such as the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Shizhu duanjie jing*) mention the Pure Land in their expositions, layer upon layer and not just once. This is explained in detail in the subsequent commentary.
Cited from various sources. For a detailed discussion, see the section on "Holding the Name" in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

○ Eight: Explaining the Translation, Recitation, and Retention (Five Parts). First, explaining the translation; second, explaining the interpretation; third, explaining recitation; fourth, explaining retention;
fifth, concluding with an exhortation.
First, the clarification of the translations.

It is already known that this sutra belongs to a specific section and category, and its detailed or concise versions share certain similarities and differences. However, it remains uncertain as to when it was first translated and how many translations exist in total.

Furthermore, regarding the commentaries that have elucidated it, and the spiritual efficacy resulting from its recitation, chanting, and upholding—this shall be clarified first. First, the clarification of the translations:
There are two [versions]. The first is titled *The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha*. This is the present sutra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Regarding "Yao Qin": during the Zhou period there was the Ying Qin; during the Northern and Southern Dynasties there was the Fu Qin; and the Yao Qin—here, the term used is "Yao."
This distinguishes him from others of the Qin dynasty. As for "Tripiṭaka," it refers to one who is proficient in the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, and is equally skilled in both Chinese and Sanskrit.
As for "Dharmācārya" (Master of the Dharma), it refers to one who belongs to the Buddha-dharma and expounds it to instruct the multitude, serving as a model and exemplar.
Kumārajīva—whose name in full Sanskrit is Kumārajīvajaśa—the first five characters mean "Child-Life" (Tóngshòu) in Chinese; "Jiā" (什) signifies depth.
He was skilled in the scripts and terminology of this region (China). When the names of the Chinese (*Huā*) and Indian (*Fàn*) were mentioned together, he was called Kumārajīva.

"Translator" (*yì*) means "to change. It refers to changing the Indian language into the Chinese. According to the *Zhou Lǐ* (Rites of Zhou), the languages of the four quarters each had their own official; for the north, it was called the "Yì" (Translator).
Since these scriptures came from the West, the term "Yì" is used because the northern officials of the Han dynasty were also proficient in Western languages. Mā... [text fragment]
When Kumārajīva first arrived, he was subsequently given the title "Translator" (Yi), which remains in use today. According to his biography, the Master was a native of Central India;

his father’s name was Kūmarayāna, and his family had served as ministers for generations. Having renounced worldly glory to travel abroad, the King of Kucha took him as his brother-in-law by marrying him his own sister.
The Master was born from this union. From birth, he possessed divine spiritual power. At the age of seven, he accompanied his mother to a monastery and saw an iron alms-bowl.

He attempted to place it upon his head; suddenly, he felt that this bowl was exceedingly heavy and wondered how he could lift it. Finding himself unable to bear its weight, he immediately realized that all phenomena are but mind.
He was profoundly learned and possessed a powerful memory that none could equal. Because of his profound age and noble virtue, he was called "Child-Immortal" (Tongshou).
Having mastered the Tripiṭaka, he traveled east to Kucha, where the King provided him with a golden lion throne for him to occupy.
Fu Jian occupied the state of Qin and was about to launch a campaign against the West.

Just then, the Grand Astrologer reported that a strange star had appeared in the celestial division corresponding to the Western Regions, signifying that a man of great virtue and wisdom would enter to assist the Central Kingdom. Fu Jian said, "I have heard that there is one named Kumārajīva in Kucha;
could this not be him? He dispatched General Lü Guang, and as they were about to set out, he said to him, "It is not that I covet territory for its own sake..."

The general heard that Kumārajīva had profoundly understood the characteristics of dharmas and was a master for later students. He thought that if Kucha were conquered, he should immediately dispatch a courier to bring Kumārajīva back;
thus, upon the fall of Kucha, he took Kumārajīva with him on his return journey. However, midway, he heard that Yao Xing had already been killed by Yao Chang, so he stopped and did not return.
Consequently, Kumārajīva’s teacher never reached Qin. Later, Yao Chang also heard of the teacher’s reputation and sought him out.

He requested [the scriptures], but Fotudeng did not grant his permission. When Zhi Chang passed away, his son Zhi Xing requested them again, yet still received no consent. Consequently, he dispatched troops to attack Fotudeng;
only after Fotudeng’s nephew surrendered to the Qin did they finally succeed in welcoming the Master into Guanzhong and honoring him as State Preceptor.

The Master examined the old translations and found that their meanings were frequently erroneous and deviant, failing to correspond with the Indic originals. He then assembled over eight hundred *śramaṇas*, including Zhu Fashang, Daozhao, and Sengrui.
He translated over three hundred and ninety volumes of newly rendered sutras and śāstras, all of which elucidated the source of the spirit and brought forth their profound subtleties.
A few days before his passing, he gathered the assembly and said: "I pray that what I have proclaimed and translated may be transmitted to future generations and circulated by all together.
Now, before this assembly, I make a vow of sincerity: if what I have transmitted is without error, may I be permitted to perform self-immolation."
Thereafter, his tongue did not burn or wither. On the twentieth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of Hongshi, he passed away in Chang’an.
When the firewood for the cremation was exhausted and his body consumed, the root of his tongue remained solemnly intact. This very sutra was translated by Master Kumārajīva;
that his tongue remained unimpaired is in harmony with the Buddhas extending their broad and long tongues to praise this sutra.
Upon examining them, one finds that the Buddha’s words are not false; thus, one gains even greater faith.
Second is the *Sutra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Acceptance*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty.
These two sutras are compared side-by-side; they differ slightly but are largely identical. At that time, those who followed and esteemed them all propagated the Qin edition.
Master Xuanzang was a native of Goushi in Luozhou during the Tang dynasty; his secular surname was Chen.
Having encountered hardship in his youth, he followed his elder brother, Dharma Master Changjian, to enter the monastic order at Jingzhu Monastery.

At the age of eleven, he could recite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, establishing himself as a preeminent figure who did not conform to the trends of his time. At twenty-one, he lectured on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* without consulting the textual commentaries.
His eloquence flowed forth inexhaustibly, and he was then hailed as a "divine man. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, he traveled to the Western Regions to retrieve scriptures.
Having endured numerous hardships and traversed one hundred and fifty kingdoms, he eventually reached Śrāvastī, where he obtained over six hundred fascicles of sutras.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he returned to the capital and translated sutras and śāstras at the Yuhua Terrace, totaling one thousand three hundred and three [fascicles].
In ten fascicles. While lying ill, he beheld a great white lotus flower and the marks of a Buddha. He passed away with his right side down and his feet stacked one upon the other.
For two months, his countenance remained as if alive. Previously, on the day of his departure for the West, he had caressed the pines of Lingyan Temple and made this vow:
"When I go west, you shall grow long toward the west; when I return east, you shall turn toward the east. After the Master departed, the pines grew long toward the west.

It reached several *zhang* in height. One day, it suddenly turned toward the east. His disciples rejoiced, saying, "The Master is returning! And so it was. At that time, it was called the "Buddha-crested Pine. According to this, the Master’s vow was self-imposed and never faltered; it was a word of truth and a word of reality.

Furthermore, Master Kumārajīva’s tongue-root did not decay, which reflects the broad and long tongue-mark of all Buddhas. Thus it is said: [...omitted text... Regarding the phrase "the tongue-root does not decay," it refers to the broad and long tongue-mark (*prabhūta-tanu-jihvā*) of the Buddhas. It signifies that the Master’s speech was entirely truthful and his realization perfectly realized. As for the pine tree, it was a manifestation of the Master’s spiritual power, responding to his vow and appearing as a sign of his imminent return.

This account illustrates how the Master’s words were unfailing and how his spiritual efficacy was manifest even in the natural world. It serves as a testament to the profound connection between his resolve and the phenomena that arose in response to it.
How could one not believe this scripture when it has been translated? Regarding "linked translations," these refer to successive re-translations.

As for those that differ slightly but are largely the same, these are cases where the Indic sounds (*brahmanī*) vary somewhat, or where the language is more elaborate or concise—such as *Gaṅgā* versus *Ganges*, or "six directions" versus "ten directions"—yet the general meaning remains entirely consistent.
"All extensive [versions]" refers to the three translations of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, including the Qin edition.
It is widely prevalent. This scripture likewise has two translations.
Second, the explanation:

next, regarding the explanation of this scripture, there is the *Treatise on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life* by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu as the formal commentary (*śāstra*), and as the exegesis (*vyākhyā*)—

There are the *Cien tongzan* (Comprehensive Commentary by Cien), the *Haedong su* (Commentary from the Eastern Sea), the *Gushan su* (Commentary by Gushan), and even the *Dayou luejie* (Brief Explanation by Dayou), among others.
As for Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, he frequently entered the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* (Sunlight Samādhi) and ascended to the inner court of the Tuṣita Heaven palace to personally attend upon Maitreya.
There he composed the *Amitāyur-dhyāna-sūtra-śāstra-upadeśa*. *Upadeśa* is translated here as "analysis" (*fen*).
Another account: The Dharma Master Cien, whose name was Kuiji and whose surname was Wei-chi, was the adopted son of Jingde.
Master Xuanzang ordained him, and he became proficient in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings. He composed commentaries totaling approximately one hundred fascicles.

While explaining the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, two sets of seven śarīra relics appeared from his pen. Furthermore, he revealed the essential meaning of the Western Land. There is the *Mi...* [text ends].
The *General Commentary on the Śūraṃgama Sūtra* (Duo jing tong zan), one fascicle. The Dharma Master of海东 (Haedong) was named Wonhyo;

his commentary on this sūtra generally takes the [Daśabhūmika] Śāstra as its primary authority. The Dharma Master Yuan of Gushan produced ten commentaries for circulation, and this [present] commentary is one among them.
The various explanations provided by successive masters, such as Yiyuan, Jingjue, and Yuexi, have for the most part been lost or scattered.
Among them, only Master Dayou of the Yuan era composed a brief commentary; today, only the commentaries by Yuexi and Dayou from the land of海东 (Haidong) remain.
As time has passed and the teachers have passed away, the scriptures have become fragmentary and the teachings have declined, thereby causing such a vast [work]...
This profound and far-reaching Dharma-gate cannot be fully understood by every individual; how tragic this is!

Yet, those who have distantly inherited the Buddha’s intent and extensively expounded the secret doctrine—whether through treatises, prose, anthologies, records, biographies, verses, rhapsodies, or poems—they praise and extol one another, their elegance beyond counting. There is none among them who does not offer earnest and sincere exhortations.

Moved by deep emotion, I sing this lamentary song to universally exhort those wandering in delusion to return together to the path of enlightenment. If you have once set eyes upon it, how could you fail to engrave it in your heart?
The preceding text specifically refers to the commentary on this sutra; now, as for the other verses praising the Pure Land, their words are beyond counting.
As for treatises, there are such works as the *Ten Doubts Resolved* (*Shiyi Baowang*). As for literary compositions, there are such as those by Longshu Wuchan.

"Exhaustive" (jin) refers to works such as the *Juedi yizhi* (Resolving Doubts Regarding the Destination). "Collections" (ji) refer to works such as the *Jingtu zixin ji* (Collection on Self-Confidence in the Pure Land).
"Biographies" (zhuan) refer to works such as the *Jingtu luezhuan* (Brief Biographies of the Pure Land). "Verses" (ji) refer to works such as the *Jinglu xingdao ge* (Verses on the Path of Practice).

"Rhapsodies" (fu) refer to works such as the *Shenqi anyang fu* (Rhapsody on the Spirit Dwelling in An-yang). "Poems" (shi) refer to works such as those by various masters expressing their longing for the Pure Land. To address these, I say: they are earnest and sincere.
These words are intended so that others may believe and accept them, and put them into practice. To sing of them as "sorrowful" is to employ plaintive and poignant language;

perhaps this may move the heart and inspire one to arise [in virtue]. "Li" (麗) means number. That it is "not merely a hundred million" means that even a hundred million is insufficient to exhaustively describe them.
These are many words indeed. All these are the sages and worthies of the Pure Land;

through thousands of sayings and myriad phrases, they never weary of their prolixity, desiring nothing more than to ferry all sentient beings across the sea of birth and death to the other shore before they rest.
We ought to cherish this grace and repay this virtue, engraving it upon our bones and carving it into our hearts, circulating it ever further and exhorting one another; were we to set it aside...
Some do not read it; some read it but do not believe it. They call it either the instruction of a foolish and ignorant person, or a mere allegorical discourse.
What can be done about this alone? ○ Third, the Recitation.

Next, to clarify the benefits for those who recite this sutra: as if their tongue-roots were not impaired, celestial music will welcome them from the West; they shall resolve their karmic enmities and attain rebirth.
Before the scroll is finished, they may pass away while seated; their return [to the Pure Land] will be like entering meditative concentration.
At the end, they shall behold white lotuses, exchanging the silver terrace for the golden terrace, and receive subtle bliss in place of coarse pleasure.
Regarding "the tongue-organ not being destroyed," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: There was a bhikṣu who recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
As his life was about to end, he said to his disciples, "Amitābha Buddha, together with the great assembly, has come to welcome me.

Later, when he was cremated, his tongue-organ did not turn to ash; its appearance remained as it was. As for "heavenly music welcoming him to the West," this refers to Song Tangshiliang, who [recited the sūtra].
He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand times. One day, he said to his family members, "The Buddha has come to welcome me.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself and passed away while seated. That night, a practitioner of the Way was on Mount Daowei when he dreamed of a wondrous light from the west.
Banners and flowers were profuse, and the sounds of music were clear and resonant. A voice from the air proclaimed: "Tang Shelang has already been reborn in the Pure Land.

As for the one who resolved enmity and attained rebirth, he was Feng Min, a commoner of Shangyu during the Song dynasty. In his youth, he was devoted to hunting. One day, he saw a giant serpent; grasping his spear, he was about to strike it.
At that time, the serpent was at the foot of a cliff, intending to devour a yellow calf. Min pushed down a boulder to crush it.
This continued until his death. A snake repeatedly caused him harm, but because Hui-min practiced repentance and recited the name of the Buddha for years, the snake could not injure him.
One day, he invited fellow practitioners of the Pure Land to recite the Amitābha Sūtra; with palms joined, he passed away while still seated before his time was up.

The Dharma Master Zhixian of the Jin dynasty was titled Zhenjiao. He resided at Bailian Temple and for thirteen years recited the name of Amitābha ten times while facing west, never ceasing for even a moment throughout the twelve periods of the day.
One night, he fell slightly ill and instructed the practitioners of the meditation hall to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

Before the scroll was finished, Anran sat upright and passed away, returning [to his origin] as if entering meditative concentration. Shi Chuxian of the Song dynasty cultivated the Pure Land with great diligence.
One night, having finished reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he praised the Pure Land and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I shall be born in the Pure Land through non-arising. Then, as if entering dhyāna-concentration, he suddenly passed away. Those who finally beheld the white lotus were from the Song Jia... [period].
The Lady Zhong of Hejun recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* ten times every day and never ceased her practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
One day she said to her son, "I see countless white lotuses; the assembly of sages is welcoming me. Thereupon, she sat upright, straightened her body, and passed away.
Regarding the Silver Terrace and Golden Terrace: Chan Master Huaiyu was a native of Taizhou. He wore plain clothes and took but one meal a day; he remained constantly seated and never lay down.
He practiced the Buddha-recitation with such diligence that he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* three hundred thousand times.

One day, he beheld the holy assembly of the Western Paradise, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. One [deity] held up a silver terrace and entered through the window. Huaiyu said, "Throughout my life, I have practiced..."

He advanced, vowing to reach the Golden Terrace. When he asked why he had not attained it, the Silver Terrace suddenly vanished. Yu was moved to such an extent that he redoubled his diligent practice.
After twenty-one days, he saw Buddhas filling the sky and said to his disciples, "The Golden Terrace has come to welcome me."

"I have been born in the Pure Land. Having spoken this verse, he passed away with a smile. County Governor Du Gong was struck by this marvel and composed a poem in his praise, which included the line:
"The branches bend low only because they are entangled with the Golden Terrace. As for those who enjoyed both coarse and refined music, there was Chan Master Yuan Zihuā.
In the ninth year of the Dali era, at Guanyin Temple in Runzhou, he recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* six...
In the month of [Month], he suddenly fell ill. At night, he smelled a fragrant aroma and heard the sound of music. A voice from the air proclaimed: "Coarse pleasures have passed;

subtle pleasures follow in succession. You shall be reborn in the Pure Land. After a long while, he passed away while reciting the Buddha's name. An extraordinary fragrance lingered for days without dispersing.
Furthermore, if one transcribes [the scriptures], their transformative influence will reach the common people; if one expounds them, auspicious signs such as white cranes will manifest.

Regarding transcription: the Great Master Shandao of the Tang dynasty used all the offerings he received to transcribe one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and exhorted others to accept and uphold it.
There were also those who recited it up to one hundred thousand times, and even five hundred thousand times.
Monastics and laypeople alike looked up to him with devotion; there were even those who, moved by the utmost sentiment, offered worship by self-immolation.

Those who attained the *nien-fo* samādhi (Buddha-recollection samādhi) are beyond counting. Among his lecturers was Shen Sanlang of the Song dynasty. In his later years, he turned his mind toward Buddha-recollection;

when he fell ill, he requested a monk to lecture on the *Amitābha Sūtra*. He changed his robes and passed away; as he drew up his knees in an effort to rise, his two sons constrained him, bound by the dictates of conventional ritual (*mingjiao*).

Because the coffin was difficult to close, they pulled his legs straightened it. As they were about to place him inside for enshrinement, he suddenly raised his head, pushed aside the shrouds, and sat up with a start.
The entire family was greatly alarmed; his two sons hurried forward to support and guard him, but he struck them with his elbows and knees.
His sons said, "We were merely helping our father sit through his passing. He finally passed away while seated. During the cremation, twenty-nine white cranes appeared.
A single bird flew and sang above the clouds; after a long while, it departed toward the west.
As for manifesting such responses in the present, one may behold the precious land from afar; as for securing rebirth there, Nirvana is not its equal.
Such manifestations have been witnessed repeatedly throughout antiquity and the present.
Regarding the one who gazed afar upon the jeweled ground: Chan Master Da Xing of the Tang dynasty first practiced the *Samantabhadra Repentance*.

Later, he entered the Great Canon and, taking a scroll at random from his hand, obtained the *Amitābha Sūtra*. He recited it day and night until the twenty-first day, when he beheld the Buddha and the two Great Beings appearing before him upon a ground of lapis lazuli.
Emperor Xi Zong, having heard of these events, issued an edict for him to enter the inner court and bestowed [upon him]...
He was titled the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence (Chang Jingjin). Later, he was seen again upon the lapis lazuli ground. On that very day, his life ended;

for ten days, a rare fragrance lingered, and his physical body remained undecayed. As for the Dharma Master Daozhen of the Liang dynasty, who lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, his realization of nirvana was beyond comparison.
During the Tianjian era, he stayed at Mount Lu, where he admired Master Huiyuan’s practice of pure karma.

While sitting in meditation, he suddenly saw several hundred people on the sea traveling forward in a precious vessel. The Master asked where they were going, and they replied, "We are going to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
He then requested to be allowed to board, to which they replied, "Although you, Dharma Master, are skilled in lecturing on the *Nirvana Sutra*, you are also truly inconceivable."
However, as he had not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, how could he go together with them? The Master thereupon ceased his lectures and devoted himself to mindfulness of the Buddha.
He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* twenty thousand times. Forty-seven days before his death, at the fourth watch of the night, he saw a silver platform from the West arrive;
it was as bright in the sky as the midday sun. A voice proclaimed, "Dharma Master, you shall ascend this platform and attain rebirth in the Pure Land. At that time—
The multitude all heard celestial music and an extraordinary fragrance that did not dissipate for several days.

That night, the monks at the temple on the mountain peak saw from afar dozens of torches at the mouth of the valley, their bright flames blazing throughout the night. On the following day, they learned that the Master had passed away.

As recorded above, these were all instances of cultivating causes and realizing fruits, where this response was evoked by that stimulus, appearing repeatedly and emerging in succession from ancient times until now.
At present, it is not possible to enumerate them all.
Regarding the fourth, "Holding":
if one holds the Name, perhaps a single thought-moment emits a ray of light, or a single utterance brings forth a Buddha, or a resonance...

In the valleys of the Mi-lin forest, [the sound of their chanting] sometimes penetrated the imperial palace; at other times, they maintained mindfulness throughout the six periods of the day, while the assembly of the True and the Responsive filled the void.

At other times, they marked their hearts with the ten characters, as sages and worthies entered their assemblies. Down to the present enlightened era, there have continued to appear those of renowned character.
This section clearly explains the practice of upholding the Name. Most of the virtuous ones who have cultivated pure karma have not been recorded here in detail;

I shall briefly cite one or two examples that are vividly known to the ears and eyes of the world to serve as an encouragement. As for Feiguang (Flying Light), he was the Great Master Shandao of the Tang dynasty.
When someone asked him whether reciting the Buddha’s name would lead to rebirth in the Pure Land, he replied: "If you recite as you do now, you will surely attain what you seek."
He made a vow. Thereupon, Dao recited the name of Amitābha Buddha once, and a ray of light issued from his mouth;

when he reached ten and then a hundred recitations, the light did likewise, filling the entire room. When the Emperor heard of this matter, he decreed that the place where he resided be named Guangming Temple (Temple of Radiance).
Later, he climbed a willow tree, sat upright, and passed away. As for those who manifested the Buddha, there was Shaokang.
The Dharma Master was at Mount Wulong, where he established a Pure Land practice hall and exhorted people to recite the Buddha’s name.

When the assembly saw the Master recite the Buddha’s name once, a single Buddha emerged from his mouth; by the time he had reached ten recitations, ten Buddhas appeared in succession, like a string of pearls.
On the day of his passing, several rays of extraordinary light spiraled from his mouth, and he died suddenly. As for Xiangmi, he was the Tang dynasty Chan Master Daocuo.
During his daily life, he lectured on the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* nearly two hundred times for the assembly; everyone counted their beads while chanting the Buddha’s name aloud.
At times when the session dispersed, the sound spread through the forests and valleys, its resonance penetrating far and wide. As for Yinche, he was the Tang dynasty Master Fazhao.
While practicing the Five-Assembly Buddha-recitation at Bingzhou, he moved Emperor Daizong so much that the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name was heard within the palace.

The Emperor dispatched an envoy to search for him from afar; upon seeing the master’s flourishing efforts in exhorting others to practice, the Emperor subsequently issued an edict inviting him into the palace.

There, the palace ladies also practiced the Five-Assembly recitation, and he became known as the Dharma Master of the Five Assemblies (*Wuhui Fashi*). Regarding the "six periods" (*liushi*): Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty, while residing at Mount Lu, composed...
Regarding the *padma* water-clock: for six periods of the day and night, he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, purifying his mind and fixing his thoughts upon him.

Nineteen years later, on the final evening of the seventh month, while at the Prajñā Terrace, he was just arising from meditative concentration when he beheld Amitābha Buddha. His body filled the entirety of space;
within his circular halo were immeasurable transformation Buddhas and a multitude of bodhisattvas. From the flowing radiance, the sublime Dharma was proclaimed. The Buddha...
He said, "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you. Seven days from now, you shall be born in my land.

When the appointed time arrived, he sat upright and passed away. Regarding the "Ten Characters": Chan Master Zongze of Changlu in the Song dynasty had a profound realization of the principles of Chan and was well-versed in both the school's teachings and its expositions.
Following the regulations of Mount Lu, he established the "Supreme Assembly of the Lotus," the method of which was as follows:
Every day he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether a thousand or ten thousand times, marking each instance with a cross beneath the character for "day.
One night, he dreamed of a man wearing a black cap and white robes, whose appearance was refined and elegant. This man said to Zhe, "I wish to enter your assembly for Amitābha;
I beg you to write down my name. Zhe asked, "What is your name? He replied, "Puhui. He added further: [The remainder of the text follows.]
My elder brother, Puxian, also requested to have his name inscribed. Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished.

Fazhe realized this and informed the venerable elders, who all remarked that there were two bodhisattvas by those names in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātuparivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Thus they knew that the sages and worthies had secretly provided their assistance.
The two Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) are placed at the head of this record. As for "the present age," it refers to the current era.

For instance, Xizhai, Konggu, Tianqi, Dufeng, and others were all eminent monks of recent times who were deeply faithful and practiced with refinement; their excellence was equal to that of the ancients, and their succession has remained unbroken.
This can be seen in some detail within the *Wangsheng ji* (Anthology on Rebirth), though there, only one or two out of ten thousand have been recorded.

As for their protective response, long-standing grudges were resolved and malevolent spirits did not invade. As for their spiritual efficacy, the blind regained their sight and captives were released from hardship.
Regarding those whose grudges were resolved:
Shao Biao of Tang was a native of Zhenjiang. While he was a student, he dreamed that he arrived at a government office where the presiding official...
The official asked him, "Do you know why you did not pass the examinations? Biao replied that he did not know. Thereupon, the official had Biao led forward.
He saw a large cauldron in which a clam was speaking in human speech, calling out Biao’s name. Terrified, Biao then recited the name of Amitābha Buddha;
the clam transformed into a yellow wagtail and flew away. Later, Biao passed the examinations and his official career reached the rank of Pacification Commissioner (Anfushi).
Regarding the "Repelling of Ghosts": In the time of the Buddha, there was a kingdom bordering upon the rākṣasas. These rākṣasas devoured humans without restraint. The King issued a decree:

"From this day forward, each household within the realm shall provide one person in turn to be sent to them; do not commit wrongful killings. There was a family that served the Buddha who had only one son.
When it came his turn to be dispatched, the parents wailed in grief and exhorted him, saying, "You must recite [the Buddha's name] with a sincere heart."
The Buddha, by his spiritual power, prevented the ghost from approaching. When she went to look at dawn the next morning, she saw her son was still there;
she took him back with her. From then on, the affliction of the rākṣasa ceased. As for Muming (Blind Eyes), she was the daughter of the Song family surnamed Chong; she was born blind in both eyes.
He practiced the Buddha-recitation for three years with unflagging diligence. His two eyes regained their former clarity. Regarding those difficult to deliver:
at the end of the Yuan dynasty, Zhang Shicheng attacked Huzhou. The Chancellor of Jiangzhe fought him and captured forty men, placing them in cages to be executed.
While they were staying overnight at Niaoke Temple on West Lake, Chan Master Dayou was walking slowly along the corridor. The prisoners saw him.
The Master’s divine countenance was serene and elegant; he recited mantras without ceasing and thus sought to rescue and deliver them.
The Master instructed them to recite with a sincere heart, "Namo Jiumu Jiunan Amituofo. Among them, three men accepted his words and recited without ceasing.

When the prisoners were released at dawn and their shackles were changed, it was found that when it came to these three men, the instruments of punishment were insufficient, and they could only be bound.
By means of a rope, they were subsequently interrogated; upon learning that they were common citizens who had been abducted, they were finally released.
Furthermore, as for the wicked, through the ten recitations of the *Namo Amitābha* (Shanhe Shini), the hells appeared while transformation Buddhas came from the void to welcome them.

For those reborn as animals, the myna birds called out their names; when their carcasses were buried, lotus blossoms sprang up from the earth. How much more so for those whose bodies have committed no grave transgressions—their retribution [is not such].
It is most efficacious. If one cultivates with faith and aspiration, how could it ever be in vain?
As for the "evil man," he was Zhang Shanhe of the Tang dynasty, who made his living as a butcher of oxen. At the time of his death, he saw a herd of oxen coming to claim his life.
Stricken with great terror, he called out to his wife, saying, "Quickly invite a monk to recite the Buddha’s name for me. When the monk arrived, he instructed him, saying, "The Sūtra..."

Regarding the account in the *Zhong* [Zhongsheng jing] concerning one who manifested evil signs at the time of death: by reciting the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart, he immediately attained rebirth in the Pure Land.

Huo said, "When hell arrives, quickly bring the incense burner. He then held the flame in his right hand and grasped the incense in his left, facing west and reciting the Buddha’s name with single-minded intensity.
Before ten recitations were complete, he declared, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and then passed away by transformation. As for the animal realm...
This refers to Master Guan of Zhengeng Temple in Huangyan, Song, who kept a myna bird that constantly recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
One day, it passed away while standing atop its cage. Master Guan buried it, and subsequently, a single purple lotus emerged from the earth.

Upon searching within the soil, it was found that the flower had issued from the tip of the bird's tongue. Master Lingzhi Zhao composed a eulogy for it; this is an instance of "passing away while standing."
"Imprisoning [the mind] in a cage is but a trivial matter; to transform it into a purple lotus flower is truly marvelous"—these phrases are as cited above in the section on "Holding the Name.
From the passage beginning with "Light flies forth and Buddhas appear" down to this point, such instances are but one in ten million.
"Malice" (*tek*) refers to that which is evil hidden within the heart. "The most spiritual" (*saieki*) refers to humans being the most spiritual among all things. At the end, he again concludes.
It is said: "If even an evil person who recites the Buddha's name can attain rebirth in the Pure Land, how much more so one whose evil is not necessarily as great as that of Shanhe?
If even an animal who recites the Buddha's name can attain rebirth, how much more so a sentient being endowed with spirit who is called a human?
By such analogies, one knows that rebirth is certain. It is impossible for the practice performed through faith, aspiration, and cultivation to be in vain."
V. Exhortation by Way of Conclusion:
Thus, when the single voice first intones, the thousand Buddhas join in chorus. Whether they be eminent monks of the Three Studies or renowned virtuous figures of the Nine Schools;
whether obscure or manifest, whether sage or ordinary—they are like ten thousand rivers that do not fail to flow eastward, or like the myriad stars that all revere the North Star.
Compared to other paths, this is called the Universal Gate; how could it be a hollow claim? Those who resolve to seek rebirth there must not entertain hesitation or deliberation.
This concludes the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, which all sentient beings take as their refuge. "To chant" means to lead.
"Jiang" (to continue) means to carry on. The one who first sang was Śākyamuni, who revealed the Western Land; thus sentient beings first came to know the practice of pure karma.
This was the act of leading and guiding them. Those who joined in the continuation were those who offered praise from the six directions, as described in detail within the sutra text.
This means to continue and harmonize [the teachings]. As for the "Three Studies," they refer to the three schools of Chan, Teaching (Jiao), and Vinaya. Regarding Chan:

Yongming served as a pillar of the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) and was reborn in the highest grade; Yuanzhao alone upheld the single transmission and established his fame in the Lotus Land. Regarding Teaching:
Sengrui assisted Master Kumārajīva in propagating the Dharma and saw a lotus flower emerge from his seat; Siming... [text ends].

Zhongxing revived the Tiantai teachings and passed away while seated facing west; Lüru manifested as an *lingzhi* fungus and propagated the *vinaya*, passing away to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
Qingzhao extensively expounded the study of the *vinaya* and recited a verse before returning to the West. If one were to cite further examples, they would be beyond counting.
As for the "nine schools," these refer to Confucianism, Daoism, agriculture, craftsmanship, medicine, divination, and so forth. Regarding Confucianism, there was Wen Lu.
Lord Gong’s virtuous achievements filled the court, yet he established the karmic connection for a hundred thousand beings to be born together.

Su Changgong’s literary talent and conduct were unsurpassed in the world, yet he maintained the discourse on the "Western Inscription. Daoru was like Ge Jizhi, who abandoned the study of immortals to turn his heart toward pure karma;
Master Luan burned the scriptures of the immortals to focus exclusively on the practice of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. This extends even to Zizhang—

Qi Huang practiced medicine while reciting the Buddha’s name; Zhang Quan carried his plow and hoe while invoking the Buddha’s title. As for those in the unseen realm, the Lord of the Netherworld paid him respectful homage and the rākṣasas ceased their malevolence.
As for those who are holy, Mañjuśrī sought rebirth [in his land] and Samantabhadra vowed to go there. This being so, what need is there to mention the case of the manifest and the ordinary?
Those who face the east do so to realize the principle of ultimate convergence; those who face the north do so to honor the fundamental source. This serves as a metaphor for purity.
The earth is that which is reached by the True Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); its momentum necessarily tends toward it, not because it is forced to do so.

The "shortcut" and the "Universal Gate" are explained in the preceding text; these words are repeated here to conclude [the section], clarifying that they are not in vain. Regarding those who resolve their will, the *Daban* (Mahāvaipulya) says:
Suppose there were a great fire filling the trichiliocosm; one must pass through it to be born in that land.
Thus, one’s resolve is determined, free from any retreat or cowardice. Regarding "deliberation," the *I Ching* says: "Deliberate before speaking; deliberate before acting.
Now it is said that deliberation is unnecessary. As an ancient said: "Divination is used to reach a decision."
Doubt. If there is no doubt, what need is there for divination? To attain rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha, one simply needs to believe with earnest conviction and remain free from doubt;
why then engage in further deliberation?
*Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, Scroll One.
Commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, Fascicle Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou.
Part Nine: General Explanation of the Title (2). First, the meaning of the title; second, the translators.
○ Regarding the meaning of the initial title:
Having already understood the general purport of this sutra through the exposition of the eight topical sections above, we now wish to explain the text.
To provide a guiding framework, we first clarify the overall title; therefore, we follow this with a general explanation of the title.
The *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha* [Commentary]:
There are four points regarding the meaning of the title. First, the Buddha who speaks; second, the actual exposition; third, the Buddha spoken of; and fourth, the conclusion of the title.
It refers to Śākyamuni Buddha of this land speaking of the primary and secondary [rewards] of Amitābha Buddha in that land.
This is a sutra that adorns the aspiration for rebirth through faith. First, the general meaning is summarized; next, it is explained in detail.
[Commentary]: Regarding the summary: first, the entire text is briefly presented so that its underlying structure may be clearly connected and its significance fully realized.
Next, each point shall be analyzed and explained individually. Regarding the title "The Names of the Buddhas" and the mention of the "primary and secondary [retributions]" (*shōjō*):
while the *Contemplation Sūtra* concludes with the word "Buddha," the present work cites the "Names of the Buddhas" so as to encompass everything without exception.

[Commentary] Next is the analytical explanation. "Buddha" (Fó): in the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *buddha*; here it is translated as "The Awakened One" (*jùzhě*), because he is complete in the three types of awakening.

He is also called "The Wise One" (*zhìzhě*), because there is nothing he does not know. Furthermore, "Buddha" is one of the Ten Epithets. Moreover, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* elucidates ten meanings of Buddha;
Tiantai elucidates the six levels of "immediate" Buddha; and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* elucidates the ten bodies of Buddha. Thus, [it is called] Buddha.
"O Heaven among Heavens, Sage among Sages. Whenever the term "Buddha" is mentioned alone, it refers to our original teacher, Śākyamuni.
[Commentary: *Fan* (梵) means purity. It is contrasted with the Chinese name *Fan*; this refers to the distinction between the refined and the substantive. *Ju* (具) means complete or endowed. *Fan*...

In speech, one should say "Buddha. When the syllable *ta* is not mentioned, it is for the sake of brevity. Translated into the language of China (Zhendan), it is called "The Awakened One" (*Jue-zhe*).

This name is derived in contrast to those who are deluded. Regarding the three types of awakening: awakening oneself distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary people; awakening others distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles;

and the perfection of awakening distinguishes him from Bodhisattvas. Because these three types of awakening are all perfected, he is called "The One Who Has Perfected the Awakening of Self and Others."

Furthermore, being free from the mind is called self-awakening (*svabodha*); being free from form is called awakening others (*parabodha*); being free from both is called the fulfillment of awakening (*paripūrṇabodha*). These also constitute the meaning of the three types of awakening.
It is also said that "the wise one" (*jñānin*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), which is the very meaning of awakening. There is nothing that is not known. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"Knowing the number and non-number of all sentient beings, as well as the permanent and the impermanent, etc.—this is wisdom that knows nothing. This is what is meant by attaining "one" (*eka*).
It is precisely the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is the meaning of "awakening fulfilled. Regarding the ten titles:

although the World-Honored One of myriad virtues cannot be fully enumerated, to speak briefly, from Tathāgata to Buddha, there are ten titles in total. Among these ten titles, "Buddha" constitutes one;
because he possesses these ten virtues and is the sovereign lord of both the mundane and supramundane realms, he is named the World-Honored One (*bhagavān*).
The ten meanings consist of: possessing the two wisdoms; severing the two hindrances; awakening to the two truths; and attaining the two benefits for oneself and others.

These are combined with the two metaphors of waking from a dream and the blossoming of a flower to constitute the ten meanings. Regarding the six stages of identity (*liu ji*): they begin with "identity in principle" (*li ji*) and culminate in "ultimate identity" (*jiujing ji*).
Thus, at the beginning, there is total delusion despite total awakening; in the middle, there is awakening that is not yet complete; and at the end, there is... [no further text].

What has not been realized is now designated as "Buddha," referring to the ultimate state. As for the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), they range from the first, the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha-kāya*), to the tenth, the Buddha of Accordance with Wishes (*yathābhiprāya-kāya*).
These are detailed and fully explained in the *Lokottara-parivarta* (Chapter on Transcending the World). These ten bodies of the Buddha exist only in the *Avataṃsaka*.

Nevertheless, regarding its essential purport, it does not go beyond the meaning of the fulfillment of awakening (*bodhi*). Therefore, it is said that when the ten bodies are first fulfilled, perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is initially accomplished;
this is what is called the "Perfectly Complete Buddha" (*paripūrṇa-buddha*). As for the "God among Gods" (*devātideva*), there are four kinds of gods: first, worldly gods, such as various kings;

second, born gods, which are the various gods of the desire, form, and formless realms; third, pure gods, which are the [four] fruits and the [eighty] practitioners of the branches [of the path]; and...
The Buddha is such. The four types of devas and the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are surpassed by the Buddha; he is a deva among devas.
Among the sages—the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas—who have entered the realm of the holy but have not yet reached its excellence, only the Buddha dwells in the ultimate fruit;
he is the sage among sages. As for Śākyamuni himself, he must be designated as such in relation to the past and the future.
"A certain Buddha. This refers to Śākyamuni seen sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Since there can be no two Buddhas within a single world-system (*lokadhātu*), it is analogous to how one must mention the dynastic title of an emperor of a previous era, whereas the current Emperor is simply called "The Supreme Honored One" (*zhìzūn*), because there can likewise be no two sovereigns within a single kingdom.
Thus, we know that when "Buddha" is mentioned alone, it refers to the one accomplished by Siddhārtha during this Bhadrakalpa.
The fourth is the Buddha. [Commentary:

"To speak" (shuo) means "to gladden" (yue). It is so called because it gladdens that which is harbored within, and because the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*) proclaim and expound it.
All twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), up to the four *siddhāntas*, constitute the meaning of "speaking."

[Commentary]: "That which he cherishes in his heart" refers to his original vow to deliver sentient beings. Having encountered those with the capacity [to be saved], he preaches; thus, that which he cherishes is joyfully fulfilled. As stated in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra]:
when the World-Honored One wished to preach this sūtra, first his faculties were filled with joy and his countenance became extraordinary.

How much more so now, when one holds the Name and practices nianfo—encountering the capacity [of the practitioner] to preach, the resulting joy is easily understood. Regarding the "four types of eloquence": they are called *artha* (meaning) and *dharma* (teaching).
They are called *pada* (phrases) and *pratibhāna* (eloquence). These four are all unimpeded and are termed "exposition" (*deśanā*). The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"The Buddhas rely upon the two truths to teach the Dharma to sentient beings. Unimpeded knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) explains through the differentiation of conventional knowledge;

unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) explains skillfully through the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*). As for the [unimpeded knowledges] of meaning (*artha*) and phenomena (*dharma*), they are [discussed] subsequently.

Furthermore, because it encompasses the preceding terms as well as *pratibhāna* (eloquence) and the dharmas that subsume meaning, the "twelve divisions" (*dvādaśāṅga*) and so forth refer to what has been taught.
As for *siddhānta*, combining the Chinese and Sanskrit terms, it means "universal bestowal.

By means of the four gates of the worldly, the personal, the therapeutic, and the ultimate truth, it provides the four benefits of generating joy, producing goodness, extinguishing evil, and entering the Path; thus, the twelve divisions of the scriptures [serve this purpose]. One.

Regarding all dharmas, he teaches according to what is appropriate through immeasurable skillful means; these ultimately resolve into the four types of teaching, such as those concerning the world, so that people may obtain the four benefits, such as joy.
His discernment of capacities and bestowal of the Dharma is detailed and extensive; I have cited it only briefly and not in its entirety.
[Commentary] "Spoken by the Buddha" means that it is spoken in order to distinguish [this teaching] from five types of persons.

[Sub-commentary] The five persons are: first, Buddhas; second, Bodhisattvas; third, devas; fourth, rishis; and fifth, emanated persons (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*). These five are all capable of preaching the sūtras.
Now, this reveals that the present sūtra consists of the words established by the Ultimate Sage, personally uttered from his golden mouth, and is not like those [spoken by] bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva resides in the causal stage; devas belong to the class of ordinary beings; seers are mixed with non-Buddhists; and transformed persons are not real.
This is like the decree of a Son of Heaven, which differs from the speech of the hundred officials, ministers, and various kings.
[Commentary: "Amitābha" is the designation that reveals that Buddha. "A" in the Sanskrit language means "non-"; "Mita" in the Sanskrit language means "measure.
It is said that the Buddha's merits are inexhaustible, hence they are called "immeasurable" (*amita*).
As the sutra says regarding his lifespan and radiance, these two matters are cited as examples from among the immeasurables to encompass all remaining merits.
[Commentary]: "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) has two meanings: first, being numerous beyond calculation; second, being vast and without limit.
Furthermore, there are two other meanings: first, the "immeasurable" among the ten great numbers;
second, the immeasurability that is utterly inexhaustible. To briefly cite two examples, it is because "immeasurable" does not stop at [referring merely to] lifespan.
It is also illumination. This will be explained in detail later in the text.
[Commentary] "Sūtra" is the Sanskrit term *sūtra*; here it is translated as "Scripture that Accords with Truth" (*qi jing*). It has both general and specific meanings.

Furthermore, "accordance" (*qi*) has two meanings, and "scripture" (*jing*) has many meanings. Although "scripture" has many meanings, they do not exceed the four meanings of "pervasion," "gathering," "permanence," and "dharma."
[Commentary] Regarding the general and specific [meanings]: the teachings spoken by the Buddha are collectively termed *sūtra*; this is the general sense.
When analyzed, the name "Sūtra" refers to the *sūtras*, "Vinaya" refers to the discipline (*vinaya*), and "Abhidharma" refers to the treatises (*abhidharma*);

this is the specific sense. Furthermore, the term "Kie" (契) has two meanings: first, it accords with principle, meaning words that harmonize with the Way; second, it accords with the capacity [of sentient beings].

Regarding the teaching that adapts to the capacities of sentient beings, the characters for "seal" (*mudrā*) are here abbreviated; it is simply called a *sūtra* (*jing*) to economize on the text. Furthermore, the term *sūtra* has many meanings.
The *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) cites five meanings from the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*: first, giving birth; second, revealing; third, a spring;
fourth, a measuring line; and fifth, a string of flowers. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* provides two meanings: first, threading together; and second, upholding.
This term has four meanings: first, permanence; second, dharma; third, path; and fourth, scripture. Thus it is said to have "many meanings.

When it is stated that these do not exceed four meanings, this refers to the four characters *cháng* (permanence), *fǎ* (dharma), *jìng* (path), and *diǎn* (scripture). This is because the character for "sūtra" (*jīng*) is correctly translated in the Western Regions as "thread.
A thread possesses the sense of threading together and sustaining; "threading" refers to penetrating the principles explained [in the teaching], while "sustaining" refers to upholding them.
The beings to be converted—these two [categories] encompass the five meanings of "birth. Furthermore, the scriptures of this region are also called *sūtra*. *Sūtra* has the meaning of "thread.
Since threads are not highly valued here, they simply took the character for "sūtra" (*jing*) and added the character for "agreement" (*qi*).
This ancient designation is most appropriate. Moreover, "constant" (*chang*) means it does not change across the past and present; "dharma" (*fa*) means it is the same whether near or far.

"Venerable One, 'constant' (chang) means that which is practiced over a long duration; it carries the sense of a common path, and is thus termed a 'track' (jing). 'Dharma' (fa) means that which is regulated and rectified;
it carries the sense of a fixed standard, and is thus termed a 'classic' (dian). Furthermore, these two terms encompass all four. Thus, in the former region, they are collectively subsumed as such.
In this region, when the 'constant law' (changfa) is combined with them, the full meaning of the sūtra is exhausted within these four characters."
[Commentary] Furthermore, this sutra possesses both general and specific meanings. The single character "Sūtra" (經) is the general name;
the five characters "Buddha-spoken Amitābha" (佛說阿彌陀) are the specific name. This relationship between the general and the specific is likewise applicable to the teaching, practice, and principle.
These three correspond to the Three Virtues (triguṇa), which are perfectly interfused and complete, as described by Tiantai. By hearing the title alone, one gains such merit.

Immeasurable. If these are correlated with the three greatnesses, then the Buddha is the greatness of essence (*dharmatā-mahattva*); Immeasurable Life is the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*);
and Immeasurable Light is the greatness of function (*karma-mahattva*). As it is said in the teachings.

[Commentary] Regarding "teaching, practice, and principle": the fundamental principle establishes the teaching; one practices according to the teaching; and through practice, the principle is revealed.
Since all sutras possess these three—teaching, practice, and principle—they are called "universal. When referring specifically to this sutra, the Buddha’s discourse is the "teaching."
Holding fast to the name is practice (*caryā*); Amitābha is principle (*tattva*). Because it is restricted to this and differs from others, it is called "distinct" (*viśeṣa*).
As for its correlation with the three virtues (*triguṇa*): principle is the *dharmakāya*; teaching is *prajñā*; and practice is *vimukti*.

Furthermore, principle pervades both practice and teaching; the *dharmakāya* is thus *prajñā* and *vimukti*. Even so, practice pervades principle and teaching, and teaching pervades principle and practice.

To mention one is to include all three; this may be understood from the preceding examples. Regarding essence (*tǐ*), characteristics (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*): "Essence" refers to the universal essence.
Since the term "Buddha" is all-encompassing, the Buddha constitutes the essence. "Characteristics" refers to the characteristics inherent within the essence.

As the essence is inexhaustible, the characteristics are likewise inexhaustible; therefore, Infinite Life (*Amitāyus*) constitutes the characteristics. "Function" refers to the activity manifested from within the essence. There is nothing that the essence does not illuminate.
Functioning also has nothing it does not illuminate; therefore, immeasurable light constitutes its function. Whether considered generally or specifically, the principles are as illustrated above.
[Commentary] The titles established in various sutras all rely upon persons, dharmas, or metaphors—either singly or in combination. This sutra relies solely on the person. Regarding "person":
Furthermore, there are two [reasons]: because there are persons who have attained the fruit in both lands; and because, in reality, all three are mutually interpenetrating.
[Commentary] Regarding the single and the multiple: for example, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Great Vaipulya) possesses all three—person, dharma, and parable;

the *Mahā-upāya-buddha-pratyupakāra-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Great Expedient Means of Repaying the Buddha’s Kindness) contains person and dharma but lacks parables; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma) contains dharma and parable but lacks person.
The *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-sūtra* uses the person as a metaphor but lacks the dharma; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of the dharma alone without the metaphor of the person;
the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* uses the metaphor alone without the person or the dharma. As for this present sūtra, it uses the person alone without the metaphor of the dharma.

All other cases follow this pattern. Regarding the "fruition-persons" (*phala-pudgala*) of the two lands: the bodhisattva resides in the cause, while the Tathāgata resides in the fruition; therefore, the Buddha is designated as the fruition-person.
Now, this is the Buddha of this realm speaking of the Buddhas of other realms. As for "interfusion," it means that by taking up one, all three are present.

Thus, although the present sutra pertains to a single person, the Dharma is taught through the person; it is illustrated by way of the person. While the words may seem partial, the meaning is complete.
That they interpenetrate and mutually permeate is the natural state of principle.
[Commentary]: The original title of this sutra was *The Sutra Praising the Inconceivable Merit and Protected by the Mindfulness of All Buddhas*.
The current title was revised by Master Kumārajīva. There are two reasons for this: first, because it signifies that the Buddha encompasses the inexhaustible;
second, because it is a title that people delight in hearing.
[Commentary] Regarding "the meaning it encompasses is inexhaustible": as stated previously, when one speaks of the Buddha, it is all-encompassing;
thus, all meritorious qualities issue forth from the Buddha, for the Buddha is itself inconceivable.

Furthermore, the great name of Amitābha’s myriad virtues is that which all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time delight in—from the Buddhas who praise it above, down to the ghosts and animals below.
"Taking refuge" refers precisely to the inconceivable merit.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "shu-chao": a *shu* (commentary) explains the sutra, and a *chao* (sub-commentary) explains the *shu*, so that it may be easily understood.
[Commentary] Regarding the term *shu* (commentary): the ancients said it means "to set forth in sections. It also means "to record and annotate.

Today it is said that through this, the meaning of the sutra is set forth in sections so as not to be obscure, and is recorded and annotated so as not to be forgotten. Regarding the term *chao* (sub-commentary): the ancients said it means "to extract briefly."
Furthermore, it is a transcription. To take [the essentials] in brief, one sets forth their most critical points. Transcription is the clear recording of notes. "Ji" (冀) means to hope.

Since the *Sūtra* is difficult to clarify, one provides a detailed commentary (*shu*); since the commentary is difficult to clarify, one extracts its essence (*chao*). This is done with the hope that every person may understand the meaning of the *Sūtra*.
[Commentary: To accord with principle, self-nature awakening (*svabhāva-bodhi*) is the meaning of "Buddha. The immeasurability of self-nature awakening is the meaning of "Amitābha.

Self-nature awakening, comprising both the original and the initial aspects, is the meaning of the realized beings (*phala-pudgala*) of the two lands. The essence of self-nature awakening is all-pervasive illumination.
This explains the meaning of the sutra; hereafter, all cases shall follow this precedent.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "conforming to principle": it means that phenomena and principle are identical. That which is called the "total inclusion of the myriad existents" is precisely the One Mind.

Thus, how could the dependent retribution (*niṣyanda-vipāka*) and the primary retribution (*mūla-vipāka*) not be of the nature of self-nature (*svabhāva*)? Furthermore, as for "that which is principle" (*li*), phenomena are established in dependence upon principle.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "According to the purity of the mind, so is the Buddha-land pure. Now, the present sutra speaks of "single-mindedness without distraction," which is precisely the Amitābha of self-nature and the Pure Land of Mind-only;
this constitutes the great purport of the entire scripture. To speak in accordance with the profound principle, it is called "recitation" (*nien*).
This is the general principle. "Awakening" (jue) is the general meaning. Within the essence of awakening, all things are vast and fully present, inexhaustible and endless;

this constitutes the specific meaning. There are two aspects, the fundamental and the initial. In terms of temporal sequence, Amitābha is the ancient Buddha, while this Buddha [Vairocana] has newly attained realization.
This is the beginning of that which was originally so. That is to say, the self-nature is fundamentally the Buddha as its basis;

being shrouded by ignorance, it is only now that one breaks through delusion and realizes wisdom, which constitutes the beginning. In terms of cause and effect, this teaching of the Buddha directs one toward rebirth, whereby one is able to behold Amitābha Buddha;
thus, this is the beginning of that which was originally so. That is to say, the self-nature is fundamentally the state of having already attained Buddhahood.
Wisdom is the foundation. By relying on this foundational wisdom to seek the Buddha-wisdom, one attains Buddhahood; this is the beginning. Foundation and beginning are mutually integrated;
constant awakening is never obscured. It illuminates heaven and reflects the earth; it shines through antiquity and soars into the present. Thus he constantly preaches such a sutra.
Question: This sutra’s commentaries and sub-commentaries are intended precisely to elucidate the merit of holding the name and to universally exhort all people to seek rebirth in that land.
Why, then, does each point resolve back into the self-nature, turning it into a discourse on the ultimate principle?
If the Pure Land is nonetheless the mind, why must one abandon this and aspire for that? Answer: This is precisely the dual [approach].

It is endowed with two faculties and simultaneously destroys two delusions, as clarified in the preceding preface. This is because those of dull faculties consider themselves sufficient by adhering to phenomenal appearances (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
Contemplating this, one should realize that within phenomena there exists an underlying principle; do not become stagnant in phenomena and lose sight of the principle.
Those of sharp faculties revere the principle of nature and become attached to emptiness. Contemplating this, one should understand that the principle resides within phenomena;

do not seek the principle by transcending phenomena. Furthermore, this sutra fundamentally relies upon those names and titles to reveal one's own mind, which is identical in intent to the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*.
Thus, those who wish to awaken to the mind should properly practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth there. Moreover, the Bodhisattva...

One should still remain close to the Buddha, as explained in the previous section on "Arousing the Mind. Thus, for those who have already awakened their minds, it is precisely appropriate to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth [in the Pure Land];
what cause for doubt could there be? Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:

"Although one knows that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the Pure Land to teach and transform sentient beings. Therefore, the concern is simply not having awakened to one's own mind.
Listen. When the mind is awakened, not a single dharma exists outside of the mind; the mind is the environment, and the environment is the mind.

To be reborn in the Pure Land and wish to see Amitābha does not obstruct the principle of Mind-Only; how could it hinder one's own nature? Furthermore, he asked: "The ancients said that the Avataṃsaka is the ultimate teaching.
Is it possible that all its various dharma-gates are explained solely in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*)? As for the Vaipulya [teachings]..."
[The questioner] asks: "How can it also be based on contemplative practice? The ancient master answers:

"All teachings—whether of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) or of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*)—are of definitive meaning, because they are but the single mind. Based on this, when a person of perfect capacity encounters the teachings, what teaching is not perfect?
When the mind of principle engages with phenomena, what phenomenon is there that it does not encompass?
○ Second, the Translator:
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripitaka Master of the Yao Qin Dynasty.

[Commentary]: The Yao Qin dynasty established the era; the Tripiṭaka masters manifested their virtue; Kumārajīva produced his renown. The single character "translate" (yi) constitutes the person who is capable of performing the translation.
[Commentary] The origins and details of these sources have been fully set forth previously; they shall not be recorded again here.
The ancients referred to Master Kumārajīva as a translator of scriptures since the time of the Seven Buddhas. This is merely a brief mention, referring only to those seven.
Now, from Vipaśyin down to Śākyamuni, the period from beginning to end spans only two kalpas; yet Amitābha attained Buddhahood ten kalpas ago—thus, [his land] is adorned.
Prior to this kalpa, ascending further nine kalpas ago, how many tens of thousands of Buddhas have already been encountered?

Since none of the Buddhas of the six directions fail to praise this sutra, it must be that from the time of those ten thousand Buddhas onward, they all likewise preached this sutra, and there must likewise have been translators for each.
Furthermore, the sutra refers to the "Mother Buddhas," stating: "In birth after birth, when a Buddha is born, I am his mother; [you] are the Son-Buddha."

Another said: "In every successive lifetime since a Buddha appeared, I have been his son. Judging by this precedent, when Master Kumārajīva translated the scriptures, how could he have served fewer than seven Buddhas?
Yet this scripture has circulated for a long time; thus, one’s faith is further strengthened.
[Commentary] To speak in accordance with principle, the self-nature is a fusion of the manifest and the hidden; this is the meaning of the translation from Sanskrit (Fan) to Chinese (Hua).

[Sub-commentary] That which is Sanskrit can thus constitute the Chinese; thus, the manifest is not external to the hidden. Furthermore, that which is Chinese has never failed to be Sanskrit; thus, the hidden resides within the manifest.
It is as if there were light within darkness, and darkness within light, mutually obscuring and reflecting one another as they interpenetrate.
Entering into the layers upon layers, the wondrous essence is interfused, being neither identical nor different.
○ Third, the detailed explanation of the textual meaning (in three parts): first, the introduction; second, the main body; third, the dissemination.
I. The Introductory Section (2). First, the five phrases establishing the testimony; second, the listing of the assembly to establish the testimony.
First, the five phrases establishing the testimony:
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

[Commentary] Regarding the separate explanation of the textual meaning: We have already understood the general purport of the title as a whole, yet we have not yet examined which passages from beginning to end within the sutra elucidate what specific meanings.
Now, therefore, the text shall be divided into chapters and analyzed phrase by phrase, so that the *prajñā* of words may lead to the realization of the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
By means of finite expressions, the infinite is briefly revealed. This section is divided into three parts.

This now belongs to the introductory section (*nidāna*). "Introductory" (*xu*) means to narrate (*xu*) and also signifies a thread or beginning (*xu*). Before entering the main text, one first sets forth the opening thread of this sutra. There are two types of introductions:

the introduction of testimony and trust (*saddharma-śraddhā-nidāna*) and the introduction of the occasion for the teaching (*utpatti-nidāna*). Here, we consider only the introduction of testimony and trust.

Generally, all such introductions consist of six kinds of accomplishments (*ṣaḍ-vidha-sampad*). Following the convenience of the text and balancing its complexity and brevity, I shall divide it into two parts.
First, the five phrases are explained; subsequently, the assembly is described. Combined, these constitute six parts.
Herein, following the previous pattern, the general meaning is summarized, after which each part is analyzed individually. Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard this Dharma":
at one time, Śākyamuni Buddha was in the Jeta Grove in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. This was for the sake of the Buddha’s instruction to Ānanda. Thus...
The phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) has three meanings: first, to eliminate doubt; second, to cease dispute;
and third, to distinguish from the heterodox. [Commentary]: This refers to the *prajñā* of words and letters. Although *prajñā* is wordless, it relies upon words to be manifested;

therefore, the Buddha preached the sutras by means of words and letters, and we now likewise explain them through words and letters. However, the nature of words and letters is emptiness, which is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore...
The three kinds of *prajñā* are mutually integrated; they are not obstructed by words and letters. As for "briefly manifesting," it is called "brief" because words cannot fully exhaust the meaning.
Regarding the division of the six kinds of accomplishment into two categories, this is like the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the six sense bases (*āyatana*):
sometimes form is combined and mind is expanded, and sometimes mind is combined and form is expanded. This follows what is appropriate; there is no fixed rule.
Regarding "The Buddha’s Instruction": The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he instructed Ānanda, saying:

"At the beginning of all sūtras, it shall be said: 'Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in such-and-such a country, at such-and-such a place. This is because they were to follow the Buddha’s final injunction. Regarding "Dispelling Doubts":
When Ānanda was compiling the teachings, the assembly gave rise to three doubts: first, the doubt that the Buddha had arisen again; second, [the doubt that]... (text fragmentary).

There were three doubts: first, that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood; second, that a Buddha from another world-system had come; and third, [the doubt regarding the authenticity of the teaching]. Now, by stating "Thus have I heard," these three doubts are simultaneously dispelled.
To quell disputes, he says "I heard," indicating that this is not a fabrication produced by his own arbitrary views.
To distinguish it from the heterodox, he says "Thus" (*evam*), indicating that it differs from the *āgama* (scriptures) of the non-Buddhists. As the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Such a Dharma, I..."
Formerly it was heard that this was intended to avoid the faults of increase, decrease, and heterogeneity, and also to cease contentious meanings.
