[Commentary] "In this way" refers to the accomplishment of faith. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the two characters "ru" (如) and "shi" (是) further carry two meanings, for which there are many interpretations.
If one determines them according to the primary tenet (*zong*), then within the context of our own school, "single-mindedness without distraction" is what is meant.
"Suchness" (tathatā). It is only this that is not "not-so," which is why it is called "thus" (is).
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma can be entered through faith. Faith means saying, 'This matter is thus.'"
Those who do not believe say that this matter is not so. Master Zhao said: "Thus" (*evam*) is a term of faithful compliance;
therefore, when people of the world agree, they also say "thus. Regarding the two further meanings, these are again separate explanations for each of the two characters "thus.
As for the many interpretations, some hold that when the Sage preaches the Dharma, he merely manifests the "Suchness" (*tathatā*); it is only Suchness.
It is as such. As Liu Qiu has explained: "That which is 'as it is' (rú) refers to words that accord with principle;
'is' (shì) is a designation for the absence of error. As Master Sheng has explained: "The Tathāgata’s accordance with the capacities of beings is termed 'response' (yīng), while 'as it is';
and sentient beings’ lack of error in their response is termed 'is'. As Master Rong has explained: "There is the principle of the true mark (shíxiàng) from beginning to end..."
That which is not different is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). To speak according to principle is called "This. As Tiantai has taught, some take Suchness to be empty tranquility;
this is the "wondrous existence" (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*) that refutes the two views of annihilationism and eternalism held by non-Buddhists.

As Qingliang (Zhiyi) synthesized the various schools' explanations, there are many other theories; fearing prolixity, I shall not cite them here. Each of the above possesses its own significance. Briefly...
They differ in their broad categories, yet there is no mutual obstruction between them. To distinguish them according to their respective schools:

these two meanings are determined by following their respective tenets. Now, the tenet of this sutra is "one mind. This is because by upholding the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction, one attains this one mind.
Being one mind, it is neither born nor extinguished; it neither goes nor comes; it is serene and eternally abiding. Therefore, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Furthermore—
This single mind is free from the four errors and cuts off the hundred negations; therefore, it is called "this. Apart from what is clarified here, one cannot be said to have attained "this.
[Commentary] "I heard" refers to the accomplishment of hearing. "I" refers to the self; "heard" refers to hearing directly. It means hearing directly by oneself.
"I heard it directly; it was not through private instruction, nor was it from reading the ancients. [Commentary:
"Heard directly by myself" means that he distinguishes himself from others and distinguishes face-to-face transmission from hearsay;
it refers to teachings received personally and in person. Regarding "private instruction," Mencius said: "I have not been able to become a disciple of Confucius; I..."
"I privately admire others. The commentary states: This refers to Mencius, who did not personally meet Confucius, but was instead a successor to those who had studied under him;
he "privately admired" his Way to cultivate himself. Regarding the reading of the ancients:
when Duke Huan of Qi was reading in his hall, a wheelwright thought that what was being read was merely the dregs of the ancients.
The commentary states: Duke Huan was not face-to-face with the ancients; the ancients had already passed away, and he was merely one who read their bequeathed words.
Now Ānanda has personally encountered the Supreme Sage; this is not a matter of private instruction through his virtue.

This corresponds to the preceding "from myself. Ānanda heard the supreme teaching directly from his ears; this is not reading the ancients. This corresponds to the preceding "personally heard. From myself, personally heard—now, by means of this...
He addressed the assembly: "You should immediately believe and accept this;

what more need be said? [Commentary]: The Sage is without self (*anātman*); why, then, does he now refer to "self"? According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three reasons: first, to conform with worldly convention; second, to refute false views;
third, so as not to cling to the notion of non-self (*anātman*). By means of these three, he is not hindered from speaking of "self. Furthermore...
The true self of the Dharma-body may also be called "self.
[Commentary] Below this, the phrase "I have heard" is again divided into two parts; the separate explanations are the same as before. One interpretation says: "In accordance with worldly convention."

This means that the "self" (ātman) is spoken of within the context of worldly conventions (*saṃvṛti*), not within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is taught in accordance with worldly usage;
since it lacks any substantial reality, it does not contradict the ultimate truth. Second, regarding the refutation of false views:
this refers to the false self, the conceited self, and the nominal self. Worldly people possess the former two types of self, while practitioners (*śaikṣa*) possess the latter.
Second, regarding the self: for the noble ones (ārya), it is only the final self that is conventionally designated as "self" in accordance with worldly usage;
this is merely a name, and since there is no actual false pride, there is no fault. Third, regarding non-attachment to non-self:

the noble ones know the true nature of all phenomena (dharma) to be empty and without self, yet they do not cling to emptiness nor do they cling to non-self. Furthermore, according to the *Yogācāra*, there are four meanings of the great...

It is roughly the same as this. Regarding the third meaning: if there were truly no self, who would practice and train? People would give rise to fear; therefore, one does not cling to the notion of non-self.
Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Sutra* states: "If there were no self, there would be no hearing [the Dharma]; if there were no hearing, the path of transformation would cease.
In order that the transmission and transformation may never cease, we provisionally speak of a 'self. As for the true self of the Dharmakāya, it is established in relation to the fundamental."
He said: "Ānanda, I am also the Dharmakāya. Within the dharma of non-self, there exists the true self;
this is precisely the Dharmakāya self, such as the 'self' in the Nirvāṇa qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. How could this be obstructed by [the teaching of] non-self?"

[Commentary]: When the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) gives rise to consciousness, the specific [organ] is subsumed under the general [category]; hence it is said, "I have heard. Within the Mahāyāna, there are three [positions]:

in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), there is no hearing; in the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), one hears yet does not hear; in the Sudden Teaching (*tadaṅga-yāna*), there is neither hearing nor non-hearing. This is according to our own school.
Thus, the Sage who transmits the Dharma, by means of the true self of non-dual "no-self," and the wondrous ear wherein root and object are neither identical nor different,
hears the dharma-gate of the unobstructed nature of the Sahā world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Commentary] Regarding "setting aside the particular to follow the general": it is because one does not say "heard by the ear," but rather says "heard by me.

This is truly because "I" comprehensively encompasses the various faculties, consciousnesses, and so forth; since the general includes the particular, it is said "heard by me. As for the "Initial Teaching" and so on:
if one were to say that since the self is non-existent, hearing is also non-existent, this is the meaning of the Initial Teaching, which serves as the first gateway to the Mahāyāna. If...

To say that things are empty because they arise from conditions, yet do not destroy conventional designations—this is "hearing without hearing" and "hearing while not hearing"; this is the meaning of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*).

To say that subject and object are both quiescent, such that there is neither hearing nor non-hearing, and that [reality] is suddenly manifested apart from thought—this is the meaning of the Sudden Teaching (*tatkṣaṇa-naya*).
As for "self" and "non-self," it is "arising without arising" and "non-arising while arising," because it is the Dharma-body. Thus, the faculties...
Regarding the "object" (viṣaya): because that which hears the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and that which is heard are neither identical nor different;

because what is called the Sahā world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss—namely, the environment and its inhabitants of the Sahā world—is entirely situated within the self-mind of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
and because this section of the sutra is subsumed within the Perfect [Teaching], as it should ultimately return to the Dharma-nature.
[Commentary]: One might doubt that since the Buddha attained enlightenment long ago and Ānanda only began his monastic life later, how could they both say "I have heard"?
According to the ancients, there are four reasons for this: first, it is said that his hearing is unimpeded; furthermore, there are three types of Ānanda, some of whom hear and some of whom do not.
"Furthermore, because it is unimpeded. [Commentary]:
One might doubt this: "It has been twenty years since the Buddha attained enlightenment, and ten years since Ānanda entered the monastic order before he was appointed as his attendant.
Although he personally attended upon the Buddha, how could he have [memorized] the sūtras spoken by the Buddha during those thirty years prior?"
All state, "Thus have I heard. Regarding the four meanings of the ancient response: first, hearing through successive transmission. As the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states:
"Sutras that Ānanda did not hear himself, he heard from other bhikṣus," or as spoken by various devaputras, such as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which was circulated by the Bodhisattva Hongguang.
Second, the Buddha’s reiteration. As in the *Bao'en*... [text continues]

The Sūtra states that when Ānanda was appointed as the Buddha’s attendant, he requested three vows. Regarding the third, because he had not heard certain sūtras, he requested that the Buddha preach them again.

Thirdly, Ānanda attained realization for himself; as stated in the *Vajrapuṣpa Sūtra*, Ānanda attained the Samādhi of Sovereign Awakening to the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-avabodha-vaśitā-samādhi*), whereby he was able to personally remember and uphold sūtras he had not previously heard. This is also mentioned in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It is also said: whether present or absent, one is naturally able to understand and realize [the truth]. Fourth, "Pure Coolness" (Qīngliáng) synthesizes the preceding three.
It states that Ānanda was a Bodhisattva of great expedient power (*mahopāya-kauśalya*) who manifested as a shadow and an echo to propagate the teachings.
As the *Acintya-viṣaya-sūtra* says: "Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and even Ānanda and the others—all were Bodhisattvas of great expedient power manifesting as voices."

Regarding "hearing with the body," how could one be hindered by mere traces? It means that words do not constitute hearing. As for the three Ānandas: the first is named Ānanda (Joy), who compiled the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
the second is named Nandimitra (Friend of Joy), who compiled the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka; and the third is named Sāgarānanda (Ocean of Joy), who compiled the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Thus, Ānanda, by means of his great supernormal powers, taught and guided according to the capacities of beings.

One should know that regarding the teachings of the various periods throughout the Buddha’s lifetime, what this Ānanda did not hear, another Ānanda heard. How, then, could hearing or not hearing constitute an obstacle?

[Commentary: "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the perfection of time. When the master and disciple are in harmony and the matter of teaching and listening is completed for that occasion, it is termed "one time.
Because there is no fixed [limit] to teaching and listening, specific years, months, and days are not mentioned;

this is because the temporal divisions across the ten directions are not uniform, and the calendars of the two lands differ. According to our own school, it refers to the very moment of teaching and listening within the mind.

When objects vanish, ordinary beings and sages meet; when the environment and its inhabitants merge, the one and the many become equal. When all such dualistic phenomena are unified as one, it is called "one time."
[Commentary]: Regarding the lack of fixed duration for speaking and listening: either the speaker attains *dhāraṇī* and, in a single *kṣaṇa*, explains all dharma-gates within a single syllable;
or the listener attains the purified faculty of hearing and, in a single *kṣaṇa*, upon hearing a single syllable, encounters no obstruction regarding all other [syllables].
Or, the time of the speaker may be brief, while the time of the listener...

Much. Or, it may be that the time of the speaker is long while the time of the listener is short; the speaker’s supernormal powers (ṛddhi) can extend or shorten [time] as appropriate, while the faculties (indriya) of the listeners vary, being either sharp or dull.

The ancients maintained that the Buddhas’ bodies—whether of recompense (saṃbhoga-kāya) or transformation (nirmāṇa-kāya)—are perceived differently by those of the three vehicles, whether ordinary beings or sages.

Because the length of lifespans and the duration since the attainment of Buddhahood vary for each, we now simply take the moment when the Buddha and his disciples—teacher and student—encounter one another through their respective capacities and responses;
once the act of speaking and listening is complete, it is termed "one time.

As for the temporal divisions of the ten directions, since the ten directions pervade both the horizontal and the vertical—the vertical encompassing the heavens and the four heavens—[the text continues].
One day, the human lifespan was fifty years. As for the horizontal distribution across the four continents, it was three *yāmas* in Jambudvīpa, while in Godānīya it was midday;
thus, it could not be fixed [as a single time]. Regarding the "first month" (*zhèngshuò*) of the two lands, the day marking the beginning of the year is called the "first month.

In Zhendan (China) and the Five Indias, there was no mutual subordination. The Zhou calendar established the eleventh month (*zǐ*) as the start of the year, while the Xia calendar established the first month (*yín*). At that time, in Zhendan...
This belongs to the Zhou dynasty. However, when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Śrāvastī followed the *yǐn* calendar, which employs the Xia (Chinese) standard;
thus, the first month of the five Indian regions corresponds to the third month in Zhendan (China), and the second month of the five Indian regions corresponds to the fourth month in Zhendan.

Since these dates cannot be fixed, it is simply referred to as "one time. Regarding "mind and objects": it is the state where the single mind is undisturbed, because there is neither a subject that can think nor an object that can be thought upon. In general...

"Because the Noble One is gathered together in one place with all superior and virtuous people; because the 'reality and its basis'—the Buddha, as well as the water-birds and forest trees—all preach the sublime Dharma together;
and because regarding 'the one and the many,' when a single Buddha preaches a sutra, those in the six directions simultaneously offer praise."
The various pairs of dharmas mentioned above all become a single flavor; it is at this very moment that "one time" is established.
[Commentary: "Buddha" means the principal achiever. The explanation of the meaning of "Buddha" is found in the preceding text.

He is called the "Principal" because he is the common object of veneration for all sentient beings throughout this entire period. Furthermore, among the six kinds of accomplishment, he is the most preeminent.

[Commentary] Regarding "the shared object of veneration": throughout the duration of a single cosmic cycle (*kalpa*) since the Buddha appeared in the world, all sentient beings—the six classes of ordinary beings and the three types of sages—share him as their sole sovereign.

This is because, just as the myriad subjects and officials return to a single ruler, within the six factors of accomplishment (*ṣaḍ-vidha-siddhi*), the subject (the listener) encounters the time of the sovereign’s presence when facing him; they hear the sovereign’s speech when it is uttered, and receive it.
When the Master’s teaching is perfected, faith is established; when his life is concluded, his dwelling becomes a sacred site;

and when his transformation is complete, he forms a community. These six elements together achieve fulfillment, yet they all gravitate toward the Buddha; thus it is said that the Buddha encompasses all things.

[Commentary]: "In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park" refers to the perfection of the location. Regarding the word "in" (zài), Tiantai states that it carries the sense of "abiding.
There are four distinct types of such abiding: the celestial abode (deva-vihāra), the Brahma abode (brahma-vihāra), the noble abode (ārya-vihāra), and the Buddha abode (buddha-vihāra).
The Buddha dwells according to what is appropriate, even up to dwelling among the devas. In reality, however, the Buddha’s body is neither located anywhere nor not located anywhere.

[Commentary]: Regarding "dwelling in accordance with [the occasion]," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha is at a certain place, and having stated this, speaks of him being there temporarily or dwelling for a long time;

this generally establishes that it is a matter of intention. Now, I say that regardless of whether it is for a long or short duration, one simply refers to the specific location where the sutra was preached at that time.

This is precisely what is meant by "being present. Just as when a celestial son goes somewhere, it is called "traveling and being present. Regarding the four abodes: the Buddha gathers in sentient beings and dwells according to what is appropriate.
He may manifest the "abode of devas," which refers to the causes for the six heavens of desire; he dwells therein by means of generosity, precepts, and a virtuous mind.

Or he may manifest the "abode of Brahmā," which refers to the causes from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he dwells therein by means of the four immeasurables.
The mind abides. It may manifest as the Noble Abode (*āryavihāra*), which refers to the causes of the Three Vehicles and consists of abiding in the three samādhis;
or it may manifest as the Buddha-abode (*buddhavihāra*), which consists of the Śūraṅgama, the hundred-and-eight samādhis, and the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*).

The former three are abodes that conform to the intentions of others, while the latter one is an abode that conforms to one's own intention. Question: Why does the Buddha abide in the Celestial Abode (*devavihāra*)? Answer: To humble his supreme dignity.
He dwells in the most inferior places for the sake of delivering sentient beings. As for "neither dwelling nor not dwelling": because his essence is tranquil and solitary, he does not dwell;
because his essence is perfectly pervasive, he does not not dwell. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Buddha-body neither arrives nor does it not arrive."
Why is this? Because space has no body; the Tathāgata is likewise.
He pervades all dharmas and all lands of sentient beings, neither arriving nor not arriving—this is precisely the meaning. Thus, although the Buddha was in Śrāvastī...

Because it accords with those of inferior capacity, it is called the "abode of devas. However, speaking according to reality, why would it not also be appropriate to call Śrāvastī the "abode of Brahmā," the "noble abode," or even the "abode of the Buddha"?
[Commentary]: Śrāvastī is a Sanskrit term, also transliterated as Śrāvastī. In the language of China, it means "Hearing Things. It is so named because of its virtuous reputation;
alternatively, it is said to mean "The Hearing One," because it was named after a person.

[Commentary]: Regarding "virtue" (*guṇa*): the kingdom abounds in four virtues. First is the virtue of sensory objects (*viṣaya-guṇa*); the realm of the five sense-objects is full of beauty. Second is the virtue of wealth (*dhana-guṇa*);
there is no rarity among the seven treasures that is not possessed. Third is the virtue of the noble (*ārya-guṇa*); the holy Dharma of the Tripiṭaka is fully complete.
Fourth is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*); many people attain liberation, as they are unstained by desire.

For this reason, his reputation moved throughout the five regions; it was a fame that reached all things. He was called by the name of a person because there were many worthy men [there], and because a country is valued for its people.
[Commentary]: Regarding "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park": *Jeta* is the Sanskrit term, also called *Śītavana*. As for the word *Jeta*:
This is an abbreviation of the text. "Victory in Battle" (Zhansheng) refers to King Jeta; "Giver of Solitude" (Jigu) expresses his virtue and refers to Sudatta.
"Garden" (Yuan) is the Sanskrit term *saṃghārāma*, which means "gathering garden," so called because it provides a place for the assembly of monks.
Since Jeta donated the trees and Sudatta purchased the grounds, the name combines both elements; thus, it is called the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma.
[Commentary] Regarding "Victorious in Battle": When the Crown Prince of King Prasenajit was born, the king had achieved victory in a war with a foreign state;
he established the name [of the prince] out of joy. "Sudatta" is a Sanskrit term, which here means "Delighting in Giving.

He was a minister of King Vijitasena who took great pleasure in practicing charity, and thus the name became established for him. Regarding "Givaka" (the Solitary): one who has no father from childhood is called...

One who is alone is called "lonely" (*du*). One who is old and without sons is called "solitary" (*du*). Now, to be without support and without sustenance is what is termed being "orphaned and lonely" (*gudu*).

As for the partial mention of "orphaned and lonely," it is because the benevolence of Confucius reached those in urgent need, and the governance of the Duke of Qi prioritized the widowed and orphaned; it was not that his universal compassion was lacking, but rather due to the exigencies of urgency.
Regarding the term "garden" (*ārāma*) for a communal dwelling: because its forest shade is serene and secluded, it is a place where those who study the Way ought to reside.
As for the one who donated the trees and purchased the garden, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the elder Sudatta was originally a native of Śrāvastī and initially did not know the Buddha.
On account of seeking a bride, he entered the city of Rājagṛha. There, through Śāṇakavāsin, he encountered the Buddha and conceived faith; he invited him to return to Śrāvastī.
The Buddha instructed Śāriputra to select a suitable dwelling place for the community, and they obtained the Jeta Grove.

When the elder asked for the price, the prince jokingly replied, "If you cover the ground with gold, then I shall sell it to you. The elder spread the gold, and the prince was moved to deep admiration. Thus...
He exchanged his land and offered all the trees upon it to the Buddha, thereby establishing a vihāra.
Because both the elder and the crown prince gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and together accomplished this noble deed, they are mentioned here as a pair.

[Commentary] If the metaphors are to correspond to the scriptures, teachings, and principles, each has its own specific indication, as illustrated in the commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the metaphor corresponding to the scripture: for example, the city of Śrāvastī. The excellence of this city symbolizes that the Dharma-gate of this Pure Land is vast, profound, and the most supreme among all dharmas;
this is what Master Ci'en meant when he stated that the city of Rājagṛha—[the excellence of] the city...
"Victorious over other cities" signifies that the Dharma of the Lotus Sūtra surpasses all other teachings; the following cases are to be understood by this analogy.

"Jeta’s Grove" refers to the excellence of the trees, signifying that the Pure Land provides shelter for sentient beings so they may forever be free from the affliction of feverish distress. "Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park" refers to the excellence of the garden.
Prince Jeta represents the excellence of the seed, signifying that those born in the Pure Land will ultimately attain Buddhahood and perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas.

The Elder Sudatta represents the excellence of the person, signifying that those born in the Pure Land enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and are all superior virtuous persons. This is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The various manifestations of phenomena are all intended to reveal the One Mind; this is the essential meaning.
[Commentary] To speak in accordance with principle, the self-nature penetrates throughout the ten directions—this is the meaning of Ānanda hearing the Buddha’s teaching.
That the self-nature does not depart from its present location—this is the meaning of the Buddha being at the Jeta Grove.
[Commentary]: When the mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions, Ānanda is currently presiding over the compilation of the teachings;

when one sits within the house of the True Buddha, Śākyamuni has never actually resided in the Western Heaven. By reversing hearing to hear oneself, and reversing toward the Buddha to become the Buddha oneself, one should know that the single assembly at Jeta Grove remains solemnly undispersed—not only on Vulture Peak.
II. Listing the Assembly as Witnesses (three parts): 1. The assembly of śrāvakas; 2. The assembly of bodhisattvas; 3. The assembly of devas and humans. I. The Assembly of Śrāvakas (three parts): 1.
Clarifying their categories and numbers; 2. Indicating their ranks and virtues; 3. Stating their names and titles.
First, the enumeration of the assembly is clarified:
"Together with a great community of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
[Commentary] From this point downward, up to the phrase "together with the great assembly of devas," the assembly is established. The term "with" (yǔ) carries the meaning of "together with."
"Great" (*mahā*) excludes the "small" and possesses three meanings: namely, great, many, and superior. It is so called because it differs from other bhikṣus.

The stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*) likewise possesses these three meanings. *Bhikṣu* is a Sanskrit term; in this [Chinese] language, it has three translations: first, "mendicant" (*yācanaka*); second, "terrorizer of Māra" (*mārabhayajanaka*);

third, "destroyer of evil" (*pāpahantṛ*). *Saṃgha* is a Sanskrit term; its full form is *saṃgha*. When the syllable *gha* is omitted, it is for the sake of brevity. In this [Chinese] language, it is translated as...
"The assembly is harmonious; as for the one thousand two hundred and fifty persons, this is because the three Kāśyapas, Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and the five disciples are combined together.
The former clarifies their category as śrāvakas; the latter clarifies the specific number.
"Together" (俱) carries the meaning of "shared" (共).

[The *Chao*] states that regarding the meaning of "shared," Tiantai explains it through the "Seven Unities": namely, unity of place, unity of time, unity of mind, unity of precepts, unity of the path, unity of view, and unity of liberation.
This sutra [describes how] the Buddha and the great assembly dwell together in the Jeta Grove.
"Correct intention. This is explained at length as above. "Selecting those who are not minor" clarifies that these are not novice bhikṣus;

rather, they are those referred to below as "elders" (*sthavira*) and so forth. "Great, vast, and superior" means they are collectively revered by celestial kings and great beings, and do not possess merely meager virtue—thus they are called "great" (*mahā*).
Regarding both Buddhist and non-Buddhist scriptures, there is nothing they have not mastered extensively—thus they are called "vast" (*bahu*). They transcend... [text ends]
They transcend the ninety-six types [of heterodox paths] and are not inferior vessels; thus they are called "superior. They represent the ultimate pinnacle within the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Regarding the three meanings of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*): first, because their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) consists of the various *pāramitās* and they possess the most extremely sharp faculties, it is called "Great" (*mahat*).
Second, because they have all attained the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*), it is called "Great. Third, having all attained the lesser fruits, they proceed toward...

"Great Bodhi" (Mahābodhi): it is called "great" because it pertains to the Mahāyāna. Regarding the three types of *bhikṣu*: first is the *piṇḍapātika* (one who begs for food), which refers to begging for both food and the Dharma.
As for begging for food, one should distance oneself from the four wrong modes of livelihood (*mithyājīva*) and conform to the four right modes of livelihood (*samyagājīva*).

One should not engage in worldly affairs or laboriously amass wealth; rather, all external entanglements should be immediately stilled, and one’s will should be fixed solely on pure cultivation. The Saṃgha should sustain itself in this manner.

Therefore, it is said that begging for food sustains the body. As for begging for the Dharma, one visits teachers and seeks out friends, earnestly and with sincere devotion, inquiring after and seeking the sublime Dharma, aspiring to achieve the fruit of sainthood;
therefore, it is said that begging for the Dharma sustains the mind. Second, the terrifying of Māra.
If a person resolves to leave the household life, the King of Māra hears of it and gives rise to great terror;
for while Māra delights in birth and death, this person leaves the household life, abandons desire, and heads toward the unborn.

Because Māra loses his followers and feels such fear, he is "the third breaker of evil," being able to break the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of affliction and severing them all. Alternatively, it may be added that he is "pure in precepts."

Regarding "life," it constitutes five meanings. Of these, the present three meanings are as follows: by means of begging for food, one upholds pure livelihood; and by means of destroying evil, one upholds pure precepts.

As for the "harmonious assembly," it refers to those numbering four or more, up to an immeasurable number, all of whom perform the same *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) without mutual conflict or dispute, blending together like water and milk; this is called a harmonious assembly. As for the "Three Kāśyapas":
First was Uruvilvā, who had five hundred disciples at the Fire Dragon Cave;
second was Gayā, who had three hundred disciples at Mount Gajaśīrṣa; and third was Nadī, who had two hundred disciples at the Hiraṇyavatī River.
Later, they all returned to the Buddha, thus forming a multitude of one thousand. As for Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, each had two hundred and fifty disciples;
these also came to take refuge in the Buddha, bringing the total to one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
According to one tradition, this number was completed by the addition of fifty people, such as Yaśas and others, along with five people, such as Kauṇḍinya and others.
[Commentary] The reason for mentioning only the one thousand two hundred and fifty people is that they were his constant attendants.
[Sub-commentary] "Constant attendants" refers to the fact that when the Buddha appeared in the world, the number of Arhat bhikṣus he delivered was exceedingly great and immeasurable.
Why mention only these? It is because these one thousand two hundred and fifty people were the very first to take refuge in the Buddha, and they remained constantly by his side until his parinirvāṇa;

therefore, they alone are singled out. As for the others, though they may number in the thousands and face one another in conversation, their accounts are established according to outward traces and conventional records, which is but the natural way of things.
It is like the disciples of Zhongni (Confucius), among whom there were the worthy and the eminent.
His disciples numbered approximately three thousand, yet he singled out only the seventy disciples because they had long resided by the Si River,
accompanied him through the vicissitudes of Chen and Cai, and had constantly followed him.
[○] Second, [the section on] manifesting their status and virtues.
They are all great arhats, renowned and well-known to the assembly.
[Commentary: The first phrase manifests their status; the second phrase manifests their virtues. "Great" (mahā-) serves to distinguish them from other minor śrāvakas. The Sanskrit term is...
Arhat. This term has three meanings: first, one worthy of offerings (arhat); second, a slayer of thieves (arhat); third, one who is non-arising (arhat).

These correspond to the aforementioned fruits of the mendicant, the terrifier of Māras, and the destroyer of evil. Regarding "knowledge" (vidyā): to hear the name and admire the virtue is called "knowing";

to behold the form and pay respectful homage is called "recognizing. One interpretation states that seeing the form constitutes "knowing," while seeing the mind constitutes "recognizing. Another interpretation holds that knowing is itself recognizing.
Furthermore, he may be a person of renown within the assembly, acting as a guide for the multitude.

[Commentary] To distinguish him from others: those from the first fruit to the fourth fruit all belong to the stage of the *śrāvaka*. That he is called a "Great Arhat" here indicates that he is a *śrāvaka* who has attained the fourth fruit.
As for being "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*), ordinary persons possess no such merit, while those in the three preceding fruits do [possess it in part].

His virtue was not yet great, nor had he been named an Arhat (Worthy One). Now that his holy life (brahmacarya) is established and he has transcended the three realms, he is worthy of receiving offerings from gods and humans;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "By making offerings to an Arhat, one obtains merit in the present life.
He is a fertile field for planting blessings for gods and humans; because he accepts gifts without shame, he is called 'Worthy of Offerings' (Arhat). At the outset, he held his alms bowl.

He vowed to bring blessings to all sentient beings; now that he has realized the Way, it is logically appropriate that he receive offerings, which is why he is called a "Fruit of the Beggar" (bhikṣu).

Yet the Buddha is also named "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat); whereas the Arhat is restricted to being an object of offering for humans and devas, the Buddha is the one to whom humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas should offer.
As for "slayer of thieves": afflictions plunder the wealth of merit and wound the life-force of wisdom. Previously...
Although the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have been severed at the stage of the third fruit, the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) still remain.

Now, having severed these afflictions of cultivation, all seventy-two categories are exhausted, like turbulent currents entirely eliminated, so that the world is at peace; thus it is called "slaying the thieves. At first, one took evil as an enemy;
now that evil has been extinguished, it is called "shattering the fruits of evil. As for "non-arising" (*anutpāda*): the birth and death of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are immeasurable.

The fruit of the first stage involves seven more returns to birth and death; the second fruit involves one more birth in the desire realm; and the third fruit does not return to the desire realm but still takes birth in the form realm.
Now, as the conditions for birth have been exhausted and no further existence will be received, it is called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*).

At the outset, one vows to transcend birth and death, causing the Māras to give rise to fear; now that non-arising is realized, it is called the "fruit that terrifies the Māras. Upon hearing its name or seeing it...
"Form" refers to the pair of "intimacy" and "distance. "Knowing" means that upon hearing of it with the ears, one feels longing and wishes to see;
"recognizing" means that upon encountering it with the eyes, one serves it without fail. "Seeing the form and seeing the mind" refers to the pair of "shallow" and "deep.
"Knowing" means facing the radiant countenance in person; "recognizing" means a spiritual communion within the realm of the mind. For example, when two monks visited the Buddha, their...
When one dies, the Buddha encounters that deceased person first; this is what is meant by "seeing the mind. "Knowing" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*);
it is like saying they know each other or are acquainted with one another. Because his virtue was lofty and his reputation weighty, his fame filled the world;
everyone knew him and everyone recognized him. Therefore, it is said he was "known and recognized by all. According to another interpretation, within the entire assembly...
This person is one of great learning and vast knowledge; he is the eye of gods and humans, and is called a leader of the multitude.
When people today speak of a "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*), it also possesses two meanings. First, it is spoken in contrast to the "evil":
among those I know, there are both good and evil, and this person is a spiritual friend who is good. Second, this person possesses a clear and thorough understanding that stands out preeminent.
This consciousness is beyond the reach of ordinary people; it is because this consciousness is virtuous that it is so called.

[Commentary: According to principle, its self-nature is untainted (*anāsrava*); this is the meaning of "Arhat. Its self-nature is free from delusion; this is the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

[Commentary] If the source of the mind is fundamentally quiescent, then all outflows (*āsrava*) are entirely empty. If the substance of the mind is fundamentally luminous, then where are the various delusions?
The *Lotus Sūtra* refers to this as a true *arhat*; it is called "true and authentic knowledge" (*tattva-jñāna*).
Those who sink into emptiness as their quiescence and know through conceptualization are merely *arhats* in name; they possess false and delusive knowledge. Therefore, [this is] heterodox.
Delusive views and right view are of one substance; manifold wonders and manifold calamities share the same gate.
Only when the mind is stilled and the fundamental source is reached can one perhaps truly be called a śramaṇa.
III. Listing the Names (2): First, the individual names; second, the summary. I. Individual Names:
The Elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Mahā...
Kahulūla, Revata, Cūḷapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, Gavāmpati,
Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja, Kālodāyin, Mahākapphiṇa, Bakkula, and Aniruddha.
[Commentary: "Elder" (*sthavira*) refers to one who is aged in virtue or aged in seniority (*kalā*). Furthermore, one who possesses both virtue and seniority may also be generally termed an "Elder.
This term encompasses the sixteen venerable seniors mentioned below.

[Commentary]: Regarding *la* (臘): one year of renunciation is called one *la*. Because there is only one *la* within a full year, it is also termed "one summer" (*eka-varṣa*), the meaning being identical.
As for the general designation: as stated above, "venerable in both virtue and *la*," this refers to one who is preeminent in virtue alone, or who is senior in *la* alone;
such a person may also be called an *sthavira* (elder). As in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Dharma...
The "Elder by Nature" (*jāti-sthavira*) refers to those such as the "Elder by Birth" (*vayasthavira*).

Furthermore, the Chinese translation *jùshòu* (具壽, "Possessor of Longevity") combines both virtue and seniority, while the Wei dynasty translation *huìmìng* (慧命, "Wisdom-Life") refers exclusively to virtue. Although both terms may be used interchangeably, virtue must necessarily be regarded as paramount.
Among those listed in the present sutra, there are indeed those who possess virtue but lack seniority; however, there has never been anyone who possesses [seniority]... [text ends].
One who has reached the winter retreat (*pravāraṇā*) but lacks virtue is so called. As for the term "venerable elder" (*sthavira*), it is a title applied to those of seniority;
it is not used for Śāriputra alone, but extends even to Aniruddha—all such individuals are named elders and are all preeminent disciples.
[Commentary: Regarding Śāriputra: *Śāri* in the Sanskrit language means "paddy-owl" (*śārikā*); *putra* in the Sanskrit language means "son. Thus, he is called "Son of the Paddy-Owl" (*Śāripu-tra*).
He is also called "Son of the Body" (*Shenzi*) and "Son of the Pearl" (*Zhuzi*). There are many other names, but fearing prolixity, they are not cited here.
Among all the disciples, his wisdom is foremost. As for the designation "foremost," this merely highlights one particular virtue. As the saying goes:
"A gentleman is not a mere vessel; how much more so is an Arhat.
[Commentary] As for Śāriputra, his mother’s physical form was upright and graceful, and her eyes were as pure as those of a śārika bird; he was named after his mother.
It is said that he is the son of Śāriputra. "Śarī" (Body) refers to his upright physique and noble mind; "Putra" (Son) refers to his pure eyes and noble mind.
He has many other names, but they are not essential for the present context, so I shall not cite them at length. All subsequent instances follow this pattern. As for "Wisdom":
While still in his mother’s womb, he was already able to cause his mother to excel in debate over her maternal uncle. At the age of eight, he ascended the debating seat;
by sixteen, he was peerless in discourse throughout the great kingdoms. Within seven days, he attained complete mastery of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, he is called the foremost in wisdom.

To briefly manifest a single virtue is to clarify that it is not the case that all other Arhats outside of Śāriputra possess inferior wisdom, nor that Śāriputra alone possesses wisdom while others lack it.

Rather, this is merely citing one virtue from each to represent the infinity of the Dharma-gates, and also to attract those who have particular inclinations. As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra was at peace..."
Śāriputra sat there. Maudgalyāyana, wishing to rouse him from his meditative absorption, exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not move even a single sash of his robe.
It was often said that Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers were foremost; who would have known that Śāriputra’s supernormal powers could reach such a state?
"The gentleman is not a mere vessel" is a saying of Confucius. Just as a boat cannot travel on land and a carriage cannot travel on water, such things are "vessels.

A gentleman possesses manifold capabilities and does not stagnate in a single capacity; how then could it be said that Yan Hui and Min Ziqian lacked literary talent, or that You Zhuo and Xia Hou were deficient in conduct?

If this is true even for a gentleman, how much more so for those who transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, whose three insights (*trividyā*) are radiant and whose six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are pure?
"Ch'e. Is he not called an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted? Therefore, it is said that this merely manifests one virtue.
[Commentary] Śāriputra is mentioned first because this sutra is understood solely through wisdom.
[Commentary: The Sūtra states that the Buddha preached this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of sentient beings.
Because it is difficult to believe, only those whose wisdom is profound and far-reaching will believe it without doubt; therefore, he is mentioned first. Some may object:
"If the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* addresses Śāriputra alone, we know that Śāriputra’s wisdom lies in the understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), not in the Pure Land. Alas! Form...
This is emptiness; emptiness is form. Why do you not say that the Pure Land is emptiness, and emptiness is the Pure Land?
If one rejects the Pure Land, it is not true emptiness; if one does not understand true emptiness, it is not right wisdom.
The wisdom of Śāriputra would certainly not be like this.
[Commentary: Regarding Mahāmaudgalyāyana: *Mahā* means "Great. *Maudgalyāyana* means "of the clan of Maudgalya" (or, alternatively, "of the clan of Radish").
He was foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
[Commentary] Maudgalyāyana is his clan name; his personal name is Kolita. "Kolita" is the name of a tree; he was born after praying to the deity of that tree, and thus he was named after it.
As his lineage was numerous, he was distinguished by the prefix "Mahā" (Great). Regarding his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*):

when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, a venomous dragon obstructed him. Although the bhikṣus requested that he subdue the dragon, the Buddha did not grant permission to any of them. Then Maudgalyāyana—
He manifested transformations of various sizes; the dragon was terrified and eventually submitted.

Furthermore, he restrained the heretics who were moving a mountain so that it could not be shifted, lifted an entire city of Śākyas up to the Brahma Heaven, and stopped the chariot as well as burned the hall. For these reasons, he is called the foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
[Commentary] Mahākāśyapa means "Great Kāśyapa" (literally, "Great Tortoise-clan"). One tradition calls him "Drinking Light. He was foremost among those who practice *dhūta* austerities.
[Sub-commentary] As for "Great Tortoise": in a previous life while practicing the Way, a numinous tortoise emerged carrying a divine chart (*tuó*). Consequently, he took this as his clan name.
"Pippala" is also the name of a tree; it is called "Great" (Mahā-) to distinguish it from others of the same name, such as the three Kāśyapas.
As for "Drinking Light" (Kāśyapa): in a previous life, he was a goldsmith who, together with a woman, used gold to adorn a Buddha image.
Consequently, he was blessed with a body like gold in every lifetime; its golden radiance so brilliant that it eclipsed all other colors, thus he was named Piṅgala (Drinking Light).
*Dhūta* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "shaking off" or "straining out. There are twelve practices, namely:
first, dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyaka*); second, always begging for food; and so on, up to the twelfth, possessing only the three robes. By means of these ascetic practices...
To sweep away the dust of worldly entanglements is to clarify and purify body and mind. Kāśyapa was advanced in years, yet he did not abandon his *dhūta* practices.

The Buddha, pitying his physical decline, urged him to rest. Kāśyapa continued his *dhūta* observances as before, whereupon the Buddha praised him deeply, saying, "Where there is the practice of *dhūta*, my Dharma will endure for a long time. Thus, he was called the foremost in *dhūta*.

[Commentary: Mahākātyāyana is his clan name. This translates as "Ornamentation" (Wénshì), or alternatively "Indeterminate" (Bùdìng), or "Fan-rope" (Shànshéng), or "Departing from Existence and Non-existence" (Lí yǒuwú děng).
He was of the Brahmin caste from South India and was foremost in debate.
[Commentary]: "Ornamentation" (*wénshì*) refers to the refinement of literary elegance.

When ordinary people engage in debate, even if their minds clearly understand a principle, if they proceed directly without elegance or speak diffusely without refinement, their words will fail to convey the intended meaning;

such individuals are not skilled at debate. "Indeterminacy" (*bùdìng*) refers to the skillful mastery of various perspectives; this is the essence of being skilled at debate. "Fanning the cord" (*shànshéng*) refers to...

Because the child is bound to the mother, and because the "Hot Ball" (taptakalāpa) is broken into pieces to serve as the cord for a fan, one does not fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism, but rather manifests the Middle Way to remain free from existence and non-existence.
For example, when an outsider asks: "If a person who has died does not return, we know there is no other world;
since a person who dies undergoes suffering and ought to return, yet they willingly accept not returning, therefore there is no other world," he answers: "It is like..."
"Worldly sinners are detained in prison; can they ever return? He asked again, "Why do the gods not return either?

He replied, "If one has fallen into a latrine and escaped from it, would he willingly enter it again? Thus, through various such sublime explanations of meaning, the *Ekottarika Āgama* praises him, saying:
"He skillfully distinguishes meanings and expounds the path of the teachings; therefore, he is called the foremost in exegesis (*abhidharma*)."
[Commentary] Mahākauṣṭhila means "Great Thigh" (Dàxī). He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and was foremost in answering questions.

[Sub-commentary] He was called "Great Thigh" based on his physical appearance. As for being the "uncle," it is because he and the mother of Śāriputra were siblings; she was his sister. Previously, when debating, he surpassed his sister.
While she was pregnant with Śāriputra, [the boy's] intellectual eloquence emerged so rapidly that the brother could not keep up. Consequently, he became indignant and went abroad to study.

He vowed never to clip his nails. He studied eighteen kinds of sūtras and answered those who questioned him. Because of his diligent application, he attained the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*);
thus, he could answer any question that arose, earning him the reputation as the foremost in answering questions.

[Commentary] Upāli (Līpóduō) means "Constellation" (Nakṣatra). One source says it means "Room-Constellation" (Viśākhā). He is foremost in being free from error and confusion. [Sub-commentary] Regarding "Constellation":
he was born from a request for a son made to a star, and thus he was named after it. Regarding "Room-Constellation":
the "Room" refers to the thirteenth lunar mansion among the twenty-eight constellations; it may be because he prayed to this star. "Free from error and confusion" refers to the mind.
It is correct; therefore, it is not inverted. The mind is concentrated; therefore, it is not distracted. Hence, it is said to be "the foremost in being free from inversion and distraction.
[Commentary] Cūḍapanthaka means "Successor of the Path" (Jìdào). One interpretation says it means "By the Side of the Great Road.
Merely by retaining half a verse, he attained awakening and realized the fruit of the path.
[Commentary] Regarding "Successor on the Road" (Jidō): when his mother was pregnant, she returned home; however, she gave birth to him midway along the road.
Because he continued [the lineage] while on the road, he is called "Successor on the Road. Regarding "The Great Road" (Daidō): the mother gave birth to two sons, both by the side of the road.

He is called "Great" to distinguish him from the younger one. Regarding "Half a Stanza" (Hange): the elder brother had been a monk since childhood but remained ignorant and dark-witted, having long failed to attain understanding. The elder brother entered [the path] first.
The Master found him ignorant and, sending a messenger, returned him to secular life. He leaned against the gate of the Buddhist temple, sighing and weeping profusely.

The Buddha took pity on him and accepted him, instructing him to recite the word "broom. He recited it every day; he would remember one word and forget another. After a long time, he suddenly attained enlightenment.
With defilements and afflictions removed, he attained arhatship.
[Commentary] As for Nanda, this means "Good Joy. He is the cowherd Nanda.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the cowherd Nanda, there are three types of Nandas: Ānanda, Sundarananda, and [the cowherd Nanda]. Together...
This constitutes three [categories], because the cowherd is distinguished from the other two.
[Commentary]: Ānanda means "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi) or "Untainted" (Wuran). He was the Buddha’s maternal cousin and foremost among those of great learning (*bahuśruta*).
According to this sutra, while Ānanda heard the teachings on the Pure Land together with the assembly, he alone...
Through the power of dhāraṇī, he remembers and does not forget, thereby accomplishing the compilation [of the teachings].
[Commentary]: As for Ānanda, he was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment.

When the king, ministers, and citizens heard that the prince had become a Buddha and simultaneously heard that a son had been born in the palace, these two rare beauties were fulfilled at once; the entire nation rejoiced in celebration.

It was for this reason that he received his name. Furthermore, those who beheld his physical marks, heard his voice, or observed his majestic deportment were all without exception filled with joy; thus, he remained untainted.
It was likewise his nature that, following the Buddha, he entered the palaces of devas and nagas without his mind becoming attached to them.
As for the Buddha’s younger cousin: the Buddha was the son of King Śuddhodana, while Ānanda was the son of King Śuklodana. These two—

This is because the King’s brothers were [so]. As for the "One of Great Learning" (Bahusruta): Ānanda attended the Buddha for twenty-five years; not a single word of the Dharma taught by the Buddha did he forget.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Ānanda is titled the "Scholar of Great Learning. Furthermore, Kāśyapa praised him, saying:

"The great ocean waters of the Buddha-Dharma flow into the heart of Ānanda. This is precisely what signifies his powerful memory (*smṛti*). As for "hearing together yet remembering alone," this specifically represents his strong retention.
He transcends his peers; therefore, he is called the foremost in much learning (*bahuśruta*).
[Commentary: Rāhula means "obscuration" (*āvṛti*) or "grasper of the sun. He is the foremost in secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*).
[Commentary] "The Obstructor" (Pihana) was originally the name of an asura. He was called the Obstructor because he could use his hands to block the sun and moon;

he is also known as the "Seizer of the Sun. Regarding the two meanings of "obstruction": first, it is said that the Buddha was obstructed [by this being] and did not immediately leave the household life.
Because he had no son yet, his father-king did not permit his renunciation. Later, having conceived a child by means of her palm, he was finally able to fulfill his original aspiration.
Thus, the Buddha was obstructed by this. One account states: He remained in the womb for six years because in a previous life he had once blocked a mouse hole and confined them there for six days;
as a retribution for this, he now experiences six years [in the womb], meaning he was already obstructed by his own karma. Regarding "secret practice," a sutra says:
Rāhula’s secret practice is known only to me; it is known only by the Buddha, and is unknown even to the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, let alone ordinary people.
Because he accumulated his practices while remaining unknown to others, he is called the foremost in secret practice.
[Commentary] Gavāmpati means "ox-chewer" (niúchī). He was foremost among those who receive celestial offerings.
[Sub-commentary] As for "ox-chewer": in a past life, he mocked a śramaṇa; thus, as his retribution, he now chews like an ox.

Furthermore, because he had been an ox for five hundred lifetimes, even when not eating, he constantly made empty sounds like one panting. Since this residual karma has not yet been exhausted, he is so named.
Regarding the name "He Who Receives Celestial Offerings": this was the retribution for [his past life as] the horse-grain eater. He alone received offerings in the Śirīṣa Garden in the heavens.
Furthermore, ordinary people perceive only outward form and do not know how to contemplate virtue; many would have disparaged him.

Fearing public ridicule and the incurrence of transgressions, he constantly dwelt in the heavens where the various devas paid him honor. Therefore, it is said that he received the foremost celestial offerings.
[Commentary: "Pindola Bharadvāja. The first three characters are his name, which here means "Immovable" (Acala).
The last three characters are his clan name, which here means "Sharp Faculties" (Tīkṣṇendriya).

[Commentary] Regarding the practice of naming the personal name first and the clan surname last: there are eighteen such clans in total. Placing the name first serves to distinguish it from the others.

The *Nayāyika-vinaya* states that when the householder Jyotiṣka placed a sandalwood bowl atop a stūpa and announced to the assembly, "I shall give this to whoever can take it by means of supernatural power," the Venerable [Mahāmaudgalyāyana] manifested his powers and took the bowl. After the Buddha rebuked him, he issued a decree...
He caused [the Buddha] not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to remain in this body for a long time, so that he might serve as an object of offerings in the final age and act as a great field of merit.
[Commentary: Kālodāyin; this is translated as "Black Radiance."
[Commentary] Regarding "black light": because his facial complexion was coarse and dark; furthermore, because his black color shone with an extraordinary luster.

When he went out to beg for food at night, people were startled and terrified upon seeing him. It was on account of this that the Buddha prohibited walking about at night, and thus this rule was established.
[Commentary] Mahā-Kapphiṇa means "the lunar mansion Mṛgaśiras" (the Deer Head). He was foremost among those who know the stars and constellations.
[Sub-commentary] The lunar mansion Mṛgaśiras is the fourth of the twenty-eight lunar mansions. His parents prayed to this star when he was born.
One tradition says that when he first left home and was about to go to the Buddha, he encountered rain on the way and stayed to receive alms at a potter's house.
He left. Shortly thereafter, a bhikṣu came and stayed with him overnight. That bhikṣu was actually a manifestation of the Buddha; having heard the Dharma, he attained the Way.
As for the phrase "staying in a room," it refers to the fact that he stayed as a traveler in the house of a potter; this is one meaning.

Regarding "knowing the lunar mansions" (nakṣatras), it means he understood celestial phenomena without relying on a浑天仪 (armillary sphere) or other instruments; thus it is said, "he knew the lunar mansions. First.
1. [Commentary] Bakula means "Good Appearance" (Sanskrit: *Bakula*). He was foremost in longevity.
[Sub-commentary] "Good Appearance" refers to his upright and handsome countenance. Regarding "longevity," his lifespan reached one hundred and sixty years.
He is said to possess the foremost longevity because, having maintained the precept against killing in the past, his life did not end prematurely for ninety-one kalpas.
Furthermore, because he once gave a harītakī fruit to a sick monk, he experienced five instances of immortality; at his first birth, he manifested supernatural wonders.
The mother found this strange. She placed him on a roasting pan, but he did not die; she placed him in a cauldron, but he did not die;
she placed him in water, where a giant fish swallowed him. The fish was caught by a man, and when it was cut open with a knife, the child appeared, unharmed in the slightest.
Fire could not roast him, boiling water could not cook him, water could not drown him, the fish could not devour him, and the knife could not cut him. This is called [the "Unharmed One"].
Fifth, he was deathless. Furthermore, he delighted in solitude and had few desires; he restrained his six sense faculties. After his parinirvāṇa, his stūpa remained adorned with white conch shells.
Therefore, he always took pleasure in dwelling in seclusion and did not remain among the crowds; for this too, he is called the foremost.
[Commentary]: Aniruddha is also named Aniruddha. This is translated as "Without Poverty," also as "Without Cessation," and also as "As One Wishes.
He was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

[Commentary] Regarding "The One Without Poverty": In a former age during a time of famine, he once offered millet porridge to a Pratyekabuddha. For ninety-one kalpas, his resources were sufficient and abundant;
even until now, this merit has not perished, and whatever he seeks is fulfilled as he wishes. Thus, there are three translations, including "The One Without Poverty.
Regarding "The One Foremost in the Divine Eye": He was a monk who delighted in sleep. When the Buddha preached the Dharma, he fell into a deep slumber and remained unaware. The Buddha...
He was then rebuked and compared to a conch or a clam. Resolving to exert himself with fierce diligence, he did not blink for seven days and nights until he lost both his eyes.
The Buddha taught him to cultivate the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination;

he subsequently attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), observing the great trichiliocosm as clearly as looking at a fruit in the palm of his hand. Therefore, he is called the foremost in the divine eye.
II. Summary. "Such as these great disciples. [Commentary]:
"Such as these" concludes what has preceded. "As these" serves as an analogy for the remainder. "Great" encompasses the aforementioned grand significance. "Disciples" refers to...
One who studies after the teacher is called a *di* (younger brother); one who understands through the teacher is called a *zi* (son).
In such an eminent assembly as this, they may truly be called "difficult brothers" and "difficult elder brothers," excelling both in practice and in exposition.

[Commentary] "Concluding the preceding by analogy to the remainder" means that after the sixteen *sthaviras* were previously concluded, the following serves as an analogy for the twelve hundred [disciples].
"Subsuming the great meaning of the preceding" means that these great disciples are none other than the aforementioned great bhikṣus and great arhats;

thus, the single character "great" (*mahā*) subsumes the two preceding categories. "Learning follows the teacher" means that the one who awakens first and the one who awakens later are like an elder brother and a younger brother.

Regarding the phrase "the younger brother was later": this explains that he was born from the Teacher, meaning he was initiated, nurtured, and developed into a vessel of the Dharma—what is called being "born from the Buddha’s own mouth" and destined to succeed the lineage of the Buddhas, just as a child is born of parents.

As for the expression "the difficult younger brother and the difficult elder brother," ancient tradition says that Yuanfang was difficult to be the elder brother and Jifang was difficult to be the younger brother; this means the elder brother was noble and the younger brother was brilliant, such that there was no one to surpass them.
[This is] inferior. Now, we do not adopt that interpretation. Briefly, it is illustrated by taking the Buddha as the elder brother and the various Arhats as the younger brothers;

for both are difficult to encounter. Regarding "skillfully composing and skillfully expounding," ancient tradition praises King Wen for having King Ji as his father—the father acting before him—and King Wu as his son—the son expounding after him.
Now, we likewise do not adopt that interpretation. Briefly, it is illustrated [as follows].
The Buddha is the father; the various Arhats are the sons. Because the way of teacher and disciple is in harmony, [the commentary] states:
"In accordance with principle, the self-nature and the mental factors are mutually pervasive and integrated; this is the meaning of the Buddha and his disciples being together."

[Commentary] The Tiantai teachings state: "The Mind-King is the Tathāgata; the mental factors (caitta) are his disciples. The present explanation clarifies that "King" refers to the eight consciousnesses.
These eight consciousnesses govern the cycle of good and evil, acting as the sovereign ruler, just as a king directs his ministers or a teacher leads his disciples.
"Factors" refers to the fifty-one mental associates (caitasika). Each of these fifty-one is constant...
They arise dependent upon the mind; secondly, they are associated with the mind; thirdly, they are subordinate to the mind.

Regarding the eight consciousnesses, they are like ministers facing a sovereign, or like disciples serving a teacher. Furthermore, Zhi Jue said: "The ten great śrāvakas are all the ten wholesome dharmas of one's own mind.
A verse from the Abhidharma states: "Desire, perception, contact, wisdom, mindfulness, volition, and..."
Liberation consists of mental attention toward objects and meditative concentration through sensation;

this is known as Mahākāśyapa, whose mind desires to count [the breaths] and whose resolve is fixed on the essential way of transcendence, for he has abandoned worldly evil desires through the arousal of a virtuous desire.
Pūrṇa is one whose mental attention consists of perception; through perception he makes distinctions, for his eloquence is unimpeded. Kātyāyana is further...
The Category of Joy: Because questions and answers proceed back and forth, mutually interpenetrating so that the discussion never reaches an end;
thus even Śāriputra calls to mind Upāli, thinks of Rāhula, considers Suvīkṣaṇa, and directs his attention to Aniruddha.
"Samadhi! Maudgalyayana! Alas, Ananda and the others! 'Suffering' refers to sensation; it is the mind’s experience and reception.

The King must possess the numbers, and the numbers must return to the King. These two support one another to bring about awakening. Whether it be the King or the numbers, they do not exist apart from one's own mind.
One need only attain single-mindedness; then both the King and the numbers will be exhausted."
II. The Assembly of Bodhisattvas (three parts): 1. Clarifying their category; 2. Listing their names; 3. Summary conclusion. I.
Clarifying their category:
Together with all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
[Commentary]: The word "and" (*bing*) indicates that when the Buddha preached this sutra as mentioned previously, it was not only the śrāvakas who were present in the assembly;
the mahāsattvas likewise heard it together. "Bodhisattva" is a term from the Sanskrit language; its full form is *bodhisattva*. Here, only two characters are used [as a contraction].

This is an abbreviation of the text. Here, it is called "Awakened Sentient Being" (*bodhisattva*). There are three meanings for "awakening sentient beings. Furthermore, there is the meaning of "valiantly seeking.
As for *mahāsattva*, this is translated as "sentient beings of the Great Bodhi-mind," because they possess four kinds of greatness.

Moreover, since the six great elements of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the three greatnesses of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* do not exceed these four, [the term] *bodhisattva-mahāsattva* is used; it is simply called "Bodhi... [and so forth].
"Sa" refers to the Great Bodhisattvas. This is used to distinguish them from the various minor bodhisattvas.
[Commentary] "Not only śrāvakas" means that both those of the Small Vehicle and the Great Vehicle—all worthy sages—collectively hear this sutra.
Do not say that the Pure Land is something for which Bodhisattvas have no use. "Awakened sentient beings" refers to those who share in the awakening realized by the Buddhas;

"awakening" (*jue*) refers to what has been realized, while "sentimentality" (*qing*) refers to the fact that ignorance has not yet been exhausted. Furthermore, there are three meanings: first, the meaning of the objects of compassion and wisdom.
This means that "awakening" is the Buddha-way being cultivated, while "sentimentality" refers to the sentient beings to be transformed. Above, through wisdom...

I. Seeking [Enlightenment]. This refers to saving others through compassion. II. The Meaning of the Union of Subject and Object. It is said that "awakening" (*bodhi*) is the fruit sought, while "sentient beings" (*sattva*) are those who seek it;
by means of one's own mind, one awakens to the principle of the Buddha. III. The Meaning of Making the Benefit of Sentient Beings the Priority.
It is said that one extensively awakens all sentient beings; that is to say, before one can save oneself, one is first able to save others.

This refers to the person. Regarding those who seek with vigor: the śrāvaka who hastens toward quiescence for their own peace is called "indolent," whereas the Mahāsattva who is determined upon bodhi is what is meant by "great, powerful, energetic, and courageous.

As for the four meanings of "great," the *Qingliang shu* states: first, greatness of aspiration, because they seek great bodhi; second, greatness of practice, because the two benefits are accomplished...

Third, it is great in terms of time, because it spans three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). Fourth, it is great in terms of merit, because it is fully endowed with all the virtues of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the six greatnesses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: there is faith in the Great Dharma, understanding of the Great Meaning, and the arousal of the Great Mind.

To hasten toward the great fruit, cultivate the great practice, and realize the Great Way—these constitute the three aspects of faith, understanding, and aspiration, which are subsumed within the first [of the four] great vows.
"Hastening toward" is subsumed within the third, the great vow of time; "cultivating" is subsumed within the second, the great vow of practice; and "realizing" is...

The fourth [category] is subsumed within the greatnesses (*mahattva*). Regarding the three greatnesses of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*): first, the greatness of number; second, the greatness of qualities (*guṇa-mahattva*);

and third, the greatness of activity (*karma-mahattva*). The greatness of qualities can be understood as it stands. "Number" refers to the intention of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), and "activity" refers to the intention of practice (*caryā*).

Therefore, it is said that they do not exceed these four intentions. To distinguish them from those who are not of the Lesser Vehicle: Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others are all bodhisattvas at the stage of equality (*samatā-bhūmi*).
This is because it is not the initial stage of the five grades of faith, nor the stages of abiding, practice, or penetration.

In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, within a single world-system, beyond the Sahā world, there are thirteen world-systems as numerous as the atoms of dust surrounding it.
Now, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is but ten thousand *koṭis* of lands away; how could this be considered distant?
Second, according to principle, the so-called "ten thousand *koṭis*" is spoken only in reference to the mental capacity of ordinary beings caught in the cycle of birth and death.

Once pure karma is perfected, the mind in meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the mind that takes rebirth in the Pure Land. Furthermore, it is said that [the land] appears clearly before one's eyes.
The former is this very point. How could it ever be distant? "Time" refers to the past, present, and future; "place" refers to the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir.
A world is not established by time or place alone; it is the conjunction of time and place that is called a world.
There are many translations for *Sukhāvatī*, but the term "extreme" (*ji*) signifies the bliss of the ultimate limit; it is not [the bliss] of humans, devas, or any other beings.
Because it is comparable to bliss, it is specifically singled out. Regarding the four lands: the first is called the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-praśānta-ābhāsvara-kṣetra*).
As the Sūtra says: "Vairocana pervades all places; the dwelling place of that Buddha is named the Land of Constant Quiescent Light. This is the abode of those who have attained the ultimate fruit.
The second is called the Land of True Reward Adornment (*bhūta-vipāka-alaṃkāra-kṣetra*). By practicing the true Dharma, one elicits a sublime retribution; [it is adorned] with the seven jewels.
It is called "Adorned" because it is endowed with the five pure and wondrous sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

It is also called the "Unobstructed Land" because matter and mind are non-dual, such that a single pore can contain all lands. This is the dwelling place of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body. Third is the "Land of Skillful Means with Remainder."
The severing of the delusions of the four abodes belongs to the path of expedient means (*upāyamārga*). Because ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, it is called "with remainder.

This is the dwelling place of the noble ones (*ārya*) of the three vehicles. The fourth is the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages; this is where the four classes of sages and the six classes of ordinary beings dwell together.
Although these four lands differ in their degree of excellence, each may also be divided into pure and defiled. Now, as for the Land of Ultimate Bliss...
It is said that bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and humans share the same name as this Sahā world and dwell together within it.

Yet, while this region consists of earth, stone, thorns, and brambles, where the four realms of existence are in turmoil, that land possesses the eight virtues and seven treasures, with humans and devas gathered in great numbers;
thus, it is a "pure dwelling" (sahā-vāsa). Furthermore, it also encompasses the previous three types of lands, appearing differently according to the varying capacities of sentient beings.

There are differences. Some perceive the Land of Peaceful Light (*śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*) within the Land of Common Residence; some perceive the Land of True Reward (*vipāka-bhūta-kṣetra*) within the Land of Common Residence;
some perceive the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-kṣetra*) within the Land of Common Residence; and some perceive only their own original land within the Land of Common Residence.

As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "In this land of mine, there is peace and security; devas and humans are constantly filling it. And as the *Sūtra for Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma* says: "Within the assembly seated here today..."
Countless multitudes may see this place as mountains, forests, earth, soil, sand, or gravel; or they may see it as the seven treasures; or they may see it as the dwelling places of all Buddhas;
or they may see it as the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas—all these are merely different perceptions according to their respective capacities.

Regarding the three lands being the same as above: first is the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature land), which is the Land of Tranquil Light (*jigguang*); second is the *saṃbhoga-kṣetra* (Enjoyment land)...

Regarding the land of earth (*dhātu-bhūmi*), it is further divided into self and other, which correspond to the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*). The three lands of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) correspond to the first three [realms] and the fourth, the Land of Expedient Means and Common Dwelling (*upāya-sahāvaivartika*).

Thus, although the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) belongs to the realm of transformation, it may also be experienced as the Land of Enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) and the Land of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the "ten kinds of lands," these refer to the ten categories of provisional and real [realms] as distinguished by Zao Bo. Although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is provisional rather than real, this is merely stated according to a conventional distinction between the provisional and the real.
If one discusses them in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, there is no fixed status as provisional or real. Why is this so?
It is because that [text] speaks of Amitābha’s Buddha-land for the sake of a certain class of ordinary beings who grasp at signs. Unforeseen...

If one believes in the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and focuses their mindfulness upon it, their mind will become partially purified and they will attain birth in the Pure Land.

This is provisional and not ultimate. Thus, we know that this refers to those who grasp at signs, not to those who have entered into the principle. If one possesses single-mindedness in accordance with the principle, then the provisional is itself the ultimate;

therefore, it is said that there is no fixed distinction. Furthermore, the aforementioned four lands are also inherently complete by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*); one must not merely cling to them as fixed entities.
The Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*). If one has realized the Land of Tranquil Light, one may, according to one’s own mind, take refuge in any of the three lower lands;

in that case, one does not deny their existence. However, if one has not realized the Land of Tranquil Light yet denies the existence of the three lower lands, then there would be no land at all for one to inhabit.

This is a grave error. Thus, to disbelieve that there is a Golden World (*suvarṇalokadhātu*) in other directions is what the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* severely rebukes. To say that the Buddha has no land is [equally erroneous].
The *Jingtu chao* (Commentary on the Pure Land), in its fourteenth section, states: "From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one is eternally liberated from the burdens of form;
the illuminating essence stands alone, and the spirit has no fixed location. What need is there for a land? Moreover, as for the Buddhas, they truly have no land.

Yet, when it is said that they do, it is because the understanding of sentient beings is subtle and their delusions are heavy; therefore, by means of blessings and joy, they lead them to practice goodness. This is indeed the way of the sages."
This is merely a proximate manifestation for engaging with sentient beings; hence it is said that "it does not hinder the discourse on lands.
[Commentary] The specific indication of the West is because it is the definitive direction of inclination.
