thus, they should all be in perfect accord. Now, the reason it is explained that [the lands] are mutually present or absent is that although the wording differs slightly, the underlying meaning is fully complete. Furthermore, as the Vows of Dharmākara state: "When I become a Buddha..."
Within that land, all the devas and humans, as well as every object, were solemnly pure, radiant, and magnificent.

Their forms and colors were extraordinary, reaching the utmost subtlety and excellence, such that no one could measure them. Even those who possessed the divine eye could not discern their names or numbers.

Contemplating this, it is evident that both the primary retribution (*vipāka*) and the environmental retribution (*bhājana-loka*) are fully encompassed without exception; one must not be constrained by the literal text to limit the meaning.
[Commentary: According to the principle, the self-nature is determined to achieve Buddhahood; this is the meaning of being a "Successor in One Life" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
[Commentary] Guifeng said: "Now, knowing that the mind is the Buddha-mind, one will certainly become a Buddha.

However, since one has been a Buddha from the very beginning and this is not something achieved through effort, one merely perceives the adventitiousness of initial enlightenment (shijue) while remaining unaware of the inherent nature of original enlightenment (benjue).
This may be called: 'If it is to be supplemented, it is certainly supplemented; yet if it is already accomplished, it is truly not accomplished.'"
II. Correctly demonstrating the vows and practices so that one may know how to cultivate and realize them (four parts). 1. Initial generation of the vow;
2. Arising of the practice; 3. Realization of the fruit;
4. Concluding exhortation. I. Initial generation of the vow (two parts). 1. Exhorting the generation of the aspirational mind; 2. Revealing the reasons therefor.
First, the exhortation to arouse the aspirational mind:
"Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear this should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.
[Commentary] Having previously described the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—it is now said that those sentient beings who hear this should give rise to [the aspiration].
"Great vow! May I be born in that land. This constitutes the first instance of exhortation. Subsequently, it is reiterated and clarified again and again. [Commentary]:
Regarding "the first instance of exhortation," within the sutra there are four layers of exhortations—exhorting one to hear, to believe, and to vow. This refers to the very first.
It is the arousal of the aspiration upon hearing the discourse on the sublime and wondrous merits of the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants.
This refers to making a vow. Second, "hearing this teaching" means hearing the teaching that those who single-mindedly hold the Name will certainly attain rebirth, and thereby making a vow.
Third, "hearing this sutra" means hearing the teaching that by holding the Name one is protected by the Buddha and shall not regress from Bodhi, and thereby accepting it with faith.
The reason "vow" is not explicitly mentioned is that acceptance with faith is itself the vow. Fourth, [it] says...

"If there are those with faith"—this is a summary concluding that, having heard [the teaching], they believe with deep conviction. Believing that there is no saying that one who possesses a vow will not be reborn, they give rise to vows.
As they hear, their hearing becomes ever deeper; as they vow, their vows become doubly earnest. Though the words repeat themselves, the meaning is not redundant.
Their compassion for sentient beings is profound, and they never grow weary in instructing others.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, hearing encompasses the meaning of faith (*śraddhā*), and aspiration encompasses the meaning of practice (*caryā*). Thus, the three provisions (*sambhāra*) are all complete herein.

[Sub-commentary]: Only after hearing does one believe; if there were no hearing, from what would faith arise? Only after aspiring does one practice; without aspiration, how could practice be initiated?
The subsequent discussion of faith and practice takes this as their fundamental source. Faith, practice, and aspiration are the provisions for the Pure Land.
Provisions are abundant and lacking nothing. [Commentary:
Furthermore, the power of aspiration is inconceivable. That Buddha’s Pure Land also exists by virtue of aspiration;
rebirth there at the moment of death relies solely upon aspiration; and all causes and effects within the triple world follow entirely from aspiration. Thus it is for all the great Bodhisattvas.
"Because all [beings] vow to be born [there].

[Commentary]: Regarding that Buddha’s Pure Land, because Dharmākara, through his forty-eight vows made during the causal stage, has now attained the Way of the Buddha and extensively saved sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible merits all arise from those vows; therefore, it is said that they are "innumerable."
Regarding those who attain rebirth at the time of death, the *Chapter on Vows and Practices* states:
"When such a person approaches the end of life, all their faculties completely decay. Even their kinsmen’s power, elephants, horses, treasures, and so forth, are all dispersed and vanish.
Only the King of Vows does not abandon them, leading them before them at all times. (1)
In an instant, one attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; therefore, it is called inconceivable. Regarding the cause and effect of the three realms:
if one vows to receive celestial bliss, a poor woman may ascend to heaven; if one vows to become a Lord of the Underworld, a mountain deity may govern the ghosts.
Such various manifestations according to one's vows occur without deliberate effort; therefore, it is called inconceivable. This is the vow of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding birth, the *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-gāthā* states: "May I, when my life is about to end, be completely cleared of all obstacles;

may I behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss," continuing through "may I receive the prediction of enlightenment" and so forth, up to "widely benefiting all sentient beings.
This includes the verses spoken by Mañjuśrī regarding his aspiration for rebirth.
It is also said: "May I, at the time of my life's end, eliminate all obstacles, behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face, and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
This is in perfect accord with [the vows of] Samantabhadra. Other matters, such as those concerning Vasubandhu, Nāgārjuna, and others, have been extensively detailed elsewhere;
therefore, it is called "inconceivable."
[Commentary] To accord with principle means that one’s own nature returns to its original essence; this is the meaning of the vow to be born in that land.
[Sub-commentary] If one knows that the original essence is not separate from one's current location, then it is not a matter of being born in that land, but rather being born in this very land.

Although it is said that the journey spans ten thousand *billion* leagues, how could one have ever moved even a foot’s length? Thus, it is said that one reaches the Western Land without so much as a snap of the fingers.
If True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not maintain its own nature and the five paths follow conditions, then this impoverished son is merely a traveler lodging in a foreign land;
he ought to return to his native home.
[The text] provides two reasons for this. Why is that?
Because one is able to meet and dwell together with such superior and virtuous people in one place. [Commentary]:
This follows upon the previous point to raise a question: For what reason does the teaching urge people to make vows to be born there? It is because that land is [the abode of] these...
Those of the highest virtue who gather together will be born in that land; thus, one should seek birth there so as to enter such a sublime assembly.
[Commentary] The interrogation contains two meanings: first, since this Sahā world is also a Buddha-land, why must one necessarily distance oneself from one’s native country?

Second, regarding the inexhaustible Buddha-fields of the ten directions: if one asks why [the sūtra] specifically inclines toward the western direction, I shall now provide a response by synthesizing the reasons, which comprise three points.
First, there are certain lands where humans, animals, ghosts, and those in the hells cohabit;
it is not necessarily the case that they are inhabited solely by humans. Second, there are certain lands that, although inhabited exclusively by humans, [are not the focus].

Because it is not necessarily the case that all are virtuous. Third, there may be lands where, although they are inhabited by purely virtuous people, it is not necessarily the case that all are of the highest virtue.
When we now speak of "all those of the highest virtue," they are not merely the virtuous among men, but rather the most excellent among the virtuous.
This refers to those previously listed, from the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas up to those in their final birth (*caramabhavika*). This...

These and other such superior virtuous persons now attain rebirth there; they immediately gather together in one place—namely, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta walking hand-in-hand, and Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra serving as their noble companions.
This is like ascending to the Dragon Gate or the Azure Sea, for it is something rare in the world.
For this reason, even Great Beings seek to be inscribed in the registers of the lotus; how much more so for ordinary beings who seek to establish their dwelling there?
"If one chooses the company of the benevolent, how much more so when it concerns the study of the Way! In such a sublime assembly as this, can one not aspire to it?
[Commentary] Question: Those born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are of many different types; why can they be collectively designated as "those of supreme goodness"?
Answer: Because they have all attained the stage of non-retrogression.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the categories are not uniform": this means there are the noble and the ordinary, the great and the small, and the superior, middling, and inferior grades;
their respective stages are clearly ordered. Thus, the middle and lower grades are omitted and collectively termed "superior goodness. It is for this reason that the objection is raised.
Now, it is clarified that all those born as sentient beings are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive); therefore, they will ultimately all achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This is so.
The Buddha-realm; therefore, there is no distinction.
[Commentary] To speak according to principle, the myriad virtues of self-nature all converge. This signifies the meaning of meeting together in a single place.
[Commentary]: The hundred rivers converge in a single sea; myriad forms converge in a single emptiness.
If all those who are virtuous and excellent do not meet in this one place, where else could they possibly meet?
II. Initiating Practice (in two parts). First, excluding other practices; second, demonstrating the correct practice.
I. Excluding Other Practices.
Śāriputra, one cannot attain birth in that land through small roots of goodness, merit, or karmic conditions.

[Commentary: Building upon the preceding remarks, it is said that while ordinary groups are easily formed, virtuous assemblies are difficult to join; how much more so is a gathering of the most supreme virtuous persons?

How could one be born among them with but little goodness or little merit? Among these, the "Numinous Mushroom" takes roots of goodness as its primary practice, which belongs to the "Holding the Name";
it takes merit and virtue as its auxiliary practice, which belongs to the "Pure Karmas. These are the three blessings.
In the tradition of海东 (Haidong), it is held that performing many good deeds and accumulating much merit constitutes the "primary practice," which is said to be the arousal of the bodhicitta;

whereas performing few good deeds and accumulating little merit constitutes the "auxiliary practice," which is said to be the recitation of the Name. These two meanings appear contradictory. Now, I shall harmonize them both:
to be born in that land, one must indeed possess many good deeds and much merit; yet, the present practice of holding the Name is itself the most excellent among all good deeds.
This is the supreme goodness; it is the blessing among blessings. This is precisely what is called "arousing the bodhicitta," which serves as the primary causal condition for being born in that land.
[Commentary] As for the contradictions:

on one hand, the recitation of the name is categorized as the primary practice; on the other hand, the recitation of the name is categorized as an auxiliary practice. These two explanations are like a spear and a shield [in conflict].
Shield. Furthermore, the primary purport of this sutra emphasizes the practice of holding the name (*nien-fo*).

If holding the name were merely an auxiliary practice (*chu-hsing*), how could the meaning of the subsequent passage—“hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and upholding his name”—be reconciled? It is absolutely impossible for holding the name to be an auxiliary practice.
Moreover, if Lingzhi equates the three blessings of the *Contemplation Sutra* with these merits, then as for the third blessing...

To generate the bodhicitta is to constitute the auxiliary practice (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), whereas in the tradition of海东 (Haidong), the bodhicitta is considered the primary practice (*maula-pratyaya*).

These two views appear contradictory; however, since the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* regards the three types of merit as the direct cause for pure karma, it follows that there is no such principle regarding the bodhicitta as an auxiliary practice.
Now, to harmonize these two perspectives: one should take the recitation of the name as the primary practice, and furthermore, through that recitation...
What is called "arousing the bodhicitta" integrates and harmonizes the meanings of both schools. Regarding "roots of goodness":

according to the *Contemplation Sūtra*, it refers to the third merit for arousing the bodhicitta as mentioned above; according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (the Larger Version), it refers to the arousal of the bodhicitta by those in all three grades of rebirth.
Based on this, to arouse the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is what is meant by having no roots of goodness.
Those who give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka but do not give rise to the bodhicitta are said to possess few roots of goodness. Regarding "merit" (*puṇya*):

according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, it refers to filial support for one's parents and so forth; according to the *Larger Sūtra*, it refers to the cultivation of various meritorious virtues and so forth.

Based on this, all meritorious deeds—including giving, precepts, and even the building of monasteries, the casting of images, meditation, recitation, and ascetic practices—are set aside [as insufficient].
Not to perform [merit] is called having no merit. To merely perform this kind of merit plants the causes for the tainted (*sāsrava*) fruits of the human and celestial realms;
this is called having little merit. Regarding that which is the best among the good, there are five meanings, because it possesses the five bodhicittas of the Treatise on Wisdom (*jñāna-śāstra*).
First is the bodhicitta of generating the resolve (*utpāda-bodhicitta*), which means, amidst immeasurable births and deaths, generating the Great...
First is the Bodhicitta of Awakening Mind. By holding the name, one gives rise to great enlightenment precisely within the mind of an ordinary person caught in birth and death.
Second is the Bodhicitta of Subduing the Mind, which refers to severing all afflictions and subduing that mind.

By holding the name, right mindfulness is manifested, and the afflictions are naturally extinguished. Third is the Bodhicitta of Clarifying the Mind, which refers to thoroughly comprehending all phenomena.
It is the true mark (*dharmatā*). To hold the name is precisely this single mind, for it clearly realizes the true mark of all phenomena.
Fourth, "going forth to bodhi" means attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), departing from the triple world, and reaching omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
By holding the Name, one immediately attains the first, second, or third stage of patience (*kṣānti*), swiftly transcending birth and death to hasten toward omniscience.

Fifth, regarding "unsurpassed bodhi," this refers to sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attaining supreme perfect awakening. By holding the Name, one attains the stage of non-retrogression and proceeds directly until the attainment of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the *Haidong Shu* (Commentary from the East of the Sea) quotes the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter" (*Bodhisattvabhūmi-cittabhūmi-paṭala*), which says:
When bodhisattvas first resolve their minds [on awakening], they are able to encompass all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and sublime roots of virtue.
The thirty-seventh [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "The roots of virtue accumulated by a bodhisattva, through a purely singular, pure, and wondrous faith..."
Dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed bodhi. The tenth fascicle of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"All roots of goodness that have been performed are entirely dedicated toward unsurpassed bodhi; thus, one takes bodhi itself as the root of goodness.
In this present sutra, the practice of holding the Name is precisely the dedication of the roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi, for Amitābha Buddha is none other than unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, this is the most excellent among all that is good; it is called "abundant goodness. Regarding "the most blessed among all blessings," there are also two meanings.
First, Amitābha is the name of ten thousand virtues; as soon as this single name is uttered, the ten thousand virtues are simultaneously perfected.
One does not seek blessings, yet blessings are already complete. Second, through the power of upholding and reciting [the name], one naturally refrains from all evils. All...
"Practice it well. By means of this, one cultivates merit; because merit is easy to accumulate, this is the "merit within merit," termed "abundant merit.
[Commentary] Regarding "causes and conditions": Qingliang takes that which can personally initiate [the practice] as the cause, and that which assists in its initiation as the condition.

Now, this further has two meanings. First, roots of goodness serve as the cause, and merit serves as the condition. Second, both goodness and merit each have their own causes and conditions. [Commentary]:
Regarding "goodness as the cause and merit as the condition," the roots of goodness for enlightenment are the direct cause for entering the Path. As various sutras state: [text continues].

One must resolve to attain the Bodhicitta of perfect enlightenment. Although one may practice the six perfections and myriad deeds for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, one will ultimately not become a Buddha.
Therefore, know that the root of all wholesome virtues is this; it is called the "cause. Yet, all merit and blessings are required to assist in the accomplishment of Bodhi.
Using merit to support wisdom, and using phenomena to substantiate principle, one is aided and supported in entering the Way. This is...

Regarding the statement that "each has its own conditions": as for roots of goodness and merit, the origins from which they arise and the initial resolve from which they are generated are all termed "causes.

Furthermore, the arising of roots of goodness must necessarily be assisted by various kinds of wholesome conditions (*pratyaya*), and the arising of merit must necessarily be assisted by various kinds of meritorious conditions; thus, each possesses its own specific conditions.

[Commentary] Question: For what reason is the arousal of the bodhicitta placed as the third merit in the *Amitābha-sūtra*? Answer: Because merit comprises both the phenomenal (factual) and the noumenal (principle), and it does not consist exclusively of the phenomenal.

[Commentary] Regarding the three types of merit in the *Contemplation Sūtra*: first, filially supporting one’s parents, serving teachers and elders, possessing a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous deeds;
second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, being fully endowed with the various precepts, and not violating dignified conduct;
third, generating the bodhicitta, having deep faith in cause and effect, reading and reciting the Mahāyāna, and exhorting practitioners to advance. It is difficult to say...
How is it that the arousal of the bodhicitta is given the same name as "merit" (*puṇya*) as the two preceding types?
Herein, it is clarified that merit possesses both the phenomenal and the noumenal aspects. This bodhicitta is the merit within *prajñā* that is like space and inconceivable;
it is not the tainted merit of the human and celestial realms rejected by the Dharma. Therefore, the former two types of merit are still [merely] common.

Generally speaking, this [text] exclusively specializes in the Mahāyāna. However, why is it that the present commentary does not correlate [the bodhicitta] with merit (*puṇya*), but instead attributes it to the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*)?
This is because, while goodness and merit are two when distinguished, they are one when taken collectively.
To distinguish them specifically, the bodhicitta belongs primarily to the roots of goodness; yet, to take them collectively, the bodhicitta is also [merit].
It may be called "merit. In the *Contemplation Sūtra*, it is stated generally that merit is unimpeded. Question: The *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* states:
"Those who wish to see Amitāyus Buddha should resolve upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta and should further single-mindedly contemplate that land while accumulating roots of goodness.
Thus, the bodhicitta and the roots of goodness appear to be two distinct matters. Why, then, are the roots of goodness here directly attributed [to the contemplation]?
"Bodhicitta. Answer: That [text] merely speaks of "wholesome roots," whereas this speaks of "many wholesome roots. The single character "many" (duō) is not itself bodhicitta;
how, then, could it correspond to it?
[Commentary] Question: Is there any external evidence outside of this sutra that corroborates the claim that upholding [this name] constitutes "many roots of goodness and merit"?
Answer: There is abundant evidence. As stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-pāramitā-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and others.

[Commentary] Regarding the "realization of roots of goodness," the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "By the root of goodness from reciting the Buddha’s name even once, one enters the realm of nirvāṇa, which is inexhaustible.

It further states: "After my parinirvāṇa, in the country of Northern India, there will be a bhikṣu named Kīrtivibhāga who will cultivate immeasurable and most excellent roots of goodness; having done so, he will pass away and be reborn in the West."
After passing through hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds, he will attain Buddhahood in the land of Amitāyus Buddha;
his name shall be Vimalaprabhā Tathāgata. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra-śāstra*, there was once an old man who came to seek ordination during the Buddha’s lifetime.
Śāriputra and the other great disciples were all unwilling to grant him the precepts, as they perceived that he lacked roots of goodness over many kalpas.

Therefore, the Buddha himself delivered him, and he immediately realized the fruit of the Path. Consequently, he addressed the great assembly: "In the past, for immeasurable kalpas, this person was a woodcutter.
When a fierce tiger pressed upon him in extreme terror, he climbed a tree and cried out, 'Namo Buddha.

By virtue of these roots of goodness, he encountered me and attained deliverance. The tenth chapter on Dedication in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "May I remember [the Buddhas] of the immeasurable and boundless..."
The worlds of the past, future, and present—all Buddhas—[have taught this]. It further states: "By means of these roots of goodness from mindfulness of the Buddha...
All such passages serve as clear evidence that [this practice] possesses manifold roots of goodness. Regarding the proof of its merit, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

"If a person, even with a distracted mind, practices mindfulness of the Buddha, they shall likewise be freed from suffering, and their merit shall never be exhausted; how much more so [for those with a focused mind]?"
Focus the mind and contemplate. The *Sūtra on the Praise of the Merits of All Buddhas* states:
"If there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitāyus and, with single-minded faith and joy, uphold, recite, and keep it in mind, such a person shall obtain immeasurable merit."
They will forever be free from the three miserable realms. After their lives end, they will be reborn in that land. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For example, suppose there were a person who, as soon as they were born and fell to the ground, could travel a thousand li every day.

Even if they lived for a full thousand years and offered the seven treasures to the Buddha, this would not equal the merit of another person who, in the future evil age, recites the name of Amitābha Buddha even once; the latter's merit surpasses the former."

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If one were to provide the four types of offerings to all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, and another were to recite the name of the Buddha for even as long as it takes to milk a cow, the merit of the latter would surpass the former in an inconceivable way.
All such passages serve as clear evidence that upholding the name brings great merit. Furthermore, the nineteenth fascicle of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says: "At that time, one..."
Monks, having heard the Buddha extol the merits of the buddha-field of Akṣobhya Tathāgata, their hearts gave rise to craving and attachment, and they thought of being reborn there.
The Buddha said: "One does not attain rebirth there by means of a heart of longing and attachment;

rather, only by planting various roots of goodness and cultivating various pure practices can one be born in that field. Roots of goodness are the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*); pure practices are merit (*puṇya*).
Virtue. This also doubly demonstrates that holding the Name is clear evidence of having much goodness and much merit.
Since it is praised in various sutras, how could one not believe and accept it?
[Commentary] Question: For those in this land who practice the Perfect and Sudden [teachings] alone and do not aspire for rebirth [in the Pure Land], can they truly be said to have little goodness?
[Question: Is this so? [Answer: For a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, although they have realized the One Mind, they still remain subject to future existence (*punarbhava*).
It is precisely appropriate for such a person to seek birth in that Land and draw near to Amitābha. The late Master Qinggong’s clear precedent is evident here.

If one prides oneself on being a Perfect Person yet does not wish for birth there, one should know that this is likewise due to the thinness of one's roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), as stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
[Commentary]: "Subsequent existence" (*paścādbhava*) refers to the subsequent aggregates; that is, rebirth in a future life.

Although the realization of one who has perfected the stages (*yuanren*) may be equal to that of a Buddha, they have not yet completely eliminated the coarse and subtle *avidyā* (ignorance), nor have they fully realized the ocean-like inherent virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*).

Since there remains the defilement of delusion to moisten rebirth, how could there not be subsequent existence? As long as subsequent existence persists, there is a locus of birth, and one does not transcend the six realms of existence.
Excluding those who have already ascended to the stage of true retribution (*samyak-vipāka*), others may still not yet be free from the realms of humans and devas.
Yet, among these, desire is abundant in the heavens, while suffering is manifold among humans; those who fall back are numerous, while those who attain liberation are rare.

If one is not born in a Pure Land, where else can one go? Both Master Zhe and Master Qing were said to have attained awakening; however, in his subsequent life, Master Zhe was attached to wealth and status, whereas Master Qing—[in his subsequent life]... [text fragment ends].

Throughout many lifetimes, they have experienced much suffering and grief; all this is due to their failure to aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land, whereby they have lost the benefit of goodness for themselves and caused them to remain stagnant through many births, leaving the path to Bodhi desolate.
Is this not because their roots of goodness are meager and thin that they have come to such a state?
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter states that among the great śrāvakas in Vairocana’s assembly, those who did not see the Buddha were so because—
Because their roots of goodness differ, and because they have not originally cultivated the roots of goodness for seeing the sovereign power of the Buddha,
one should know that those who uphold the Name and vow to see Amitābha possess truly many roots of goodness, great roots of goodness, most excellent roots of goodness,
and inconceivable roots of goodness.
[Commentary]: To accord with principle means that the self-nature gives rise to all phenomena; this is the meaning of "roots of goodness.
That the self-nature is replete with all phenomena is the meaning of "merit."
[Commentary] How unexpected that the self-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally and spontaneously complete!
2. Showing the Right Practice:
"Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, uphold it..."
If for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days,
or seven days, you maintain single-mindedness without distraction.

[Commentary] Building upon the preceding discussion of "much goodness" and "much merit," [the text proceeds] up to the point of "that land. Yet, it is difficult to plant roots of goodness there, and difficult to cultivate merit;

how much more so to speak of "much" [merit], which requires diligent effort over many kalpas and remains beyond one's power to accomplish—such as the ten minds of the *Ratnakūṭa* or the ten vows of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Now, there is a single dharma that is direct, straightforward, and simple, yet constitutes "much goodness" and "much merit. Therefore:
This reveals the extraordinary merit of upholding the name.

[Commentary] Regarding the difficulty of planting roots of goodness: as in the previous case of Śāriputra, who conceived the mind of the Mahāyāna but subsequently fell back due to the Brahmin’s request for his eyes, and so forth.
Regarding the difficulty of cultivating merit: as stated in the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, concerning the five grades...

One cultivates the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) with the mind. That is to say, by practicing each of the ten wholesome actions at the lower, middle, upper, upper-middle, and uppermost levels, one achieves fifty.
When these are further distinguished as being cultivated at the beginning and at the end, they constitute one hundred blessings (*puṇya*). Thus, it is clear that blessings are not easily cultivated.

Regarding the ten mental states of the *Ratnakūṭa*, the first is to give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings and to have no mind of harm. The second is to give rise to great [compassion] toward sentient beings...
Compassion; a mind free from affliction—these three; a mind that delights in protecting the Buddha-dharma without begrudging body or life;
and so on up to ten: a mind that recollects all Buddhas while relinquishing all signs. By possessing these ten minds, one is reborn in the Pure Land.
As for the Ten Vows of the *Avataṃsaka*, they range from the first, "Prostrating to all Buddhas," to the tenth, "Universally dedicating [merit]."
One shall likewise be born in that land by means of these ten [practices]. All of the above constitute the vast and expansive wisdom-practice of a bodhisattva;

they are not easily planted nor easily cultivated. Now, regarding the merit of upholding the Name: even if the ten mental states are not yet complete and the ten vows are not yet uniform, [one shall still attain birth].
Once pure karma is established, one is immediately reborn in that land. Having attained rebirth there, this mind and this vow are spontaneously fulfilled.
Is this not the result of many roots of goodness and merit? Not passing through detours or complications is called "direct and straightforward.

Being free from all entanglements is called "simple and easy. Through being direct and straightforward, one attains profound realization; through being simple and easy, one gains vast benefits. As for other dharmas...
That which is beyond the reach of the gates is called "extraordinary and supreme.
[Commentary: Regarding "good sons and good daughters," "good" has two meanings: first, it refers to virtuous causes from previous lives; second, it refers to those of a virtuous nature in this life.
"Men and women" refers generally to both monastics and laypeople, those of sharp or dull faculties, and all beings within the six realms of existence.
This refers to sentient beings.

[The *Commentary* states: Regarding those with roots of goodness from past lives, the *Great Sutra* says: "The people of the world who performed good deeds in previous lives are able to hear the name and merit of Amitābha Buddha.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s name once, their hearts are filled with compassion and joy, and their resolve..."

Their bodies become pure; their hair stands on end; and tears immediately flow forth. These individuals have either practiced the Buddha-way in past lives, or they are bodhisattvas from other buddha-fields;
they are certainly not ordinary people. Thus, those who recite the Buddha’s name with faith are all those who have cultivated the roots of goodness in previous existences.
Those born as virtuous beings in this life are as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "It would be better to be in the various evil realms, yet constantly attain..."
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, one does not wish to be born in the good realms; for even a moment’s lack of hearing the Buddha’s name is avoided.

Now, if one does not regard the human or celestial realms as "good," but instead regards the hearing of the Buddha’s name as "good," then those who believe with sincerity and practice mindfulness of the Buddha are all members of the company of the virtuous.
Whether monastic or lay, whether of sharp or dull faculties, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land encompasses them all, just as in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra].

It is said: Regarding those of the "upper grade," there are both those who have abandoned their homes and left secular life to become śramaṇas, as well as those who have not abandoned their homes and left secular life—namely, the five groups of the ordained and the two groups of the laity.
As long as they simply practice mindfulness of the Buddha, all shall attain rebirth; this applies universally to both the monastic and the lay.
Furthermore, the lotus is divided into nine grades: the highest encompasses bodhisattvas of magnificent virtue, while the lowest extends even to...
Even ordinary people, and even those as wicked as the evil-doers, shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land simply by reciting the Buddha’s name;

this applies to both those of sharp and dull faculties. Furthermore, even those in the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings—whether female or male, whether cow or stallion—may all equally be called "men" and "women," and if they simply recite the Buddha’s name, they shall all attain rebirth;
this applies to all sentient beings alike. This is verified by the historical accounts in the *Wangsheng ji* (Anthology on Rebirth).
Now, I shall record one or two points here; I hope you will examine them in detail. [Commentary:

The subsequent text consists of three parts: first, the name of Amitābha, which designates the object of mindfulness; second, "holding it with a single mind," which clarifies the method of mindfulness;
and third, "one day or seven days," which specifies the duration of the practice.
[Commentary]: If there is no object, then the Dharma has nothing upon which to be bestowed. If it is not the Dharma, then the object is established in vain.

If there is no commitment, then even if the object is excellent and the Dharma is potent, one will remain indolent and complacent, and merit will not be swiftly established. Because these three factors are complete, one is able to ensure that pure karma is definitively accomplished.

[Commentary] Regarding the designation of the object of mindfulness: Since that Buddha has accomplished myriad virtues and, through his pure land, gathers in and nurtures sentient beings, the four characters of the Great Name "Amitābha Buddha" are taken as the object of mindfulness.
One practices in reliance upon this, for it provides a specific point of reference.

[Commentary] Regarding the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and its environment and inhabitants: the term "Buddha" already encompasses them all. Likewise, the ocean of the Buddha’s merits is fully contained within his name.
Therefore, one takes the four-character Name as the object of focus. Relying upon this object, one applies focused mindfulness (*dhāraṇā*).

Thereafter, one proceeds toward the land where he dwells; "to go" means to arrive, that is, to reach that country. Alternatively, it may be said that there is no object external to the mind; one contemplates the mind itself.
This is sufficient. Why then establish a specific object? It is because one does not realize that the mind and its objects are of one suchness, nor do they fail to arise in mutual interdependence.

The masters of old have said there are samādhis for directly observing the three paths to manifest the Buddha of original nature; there are samādhis that incorporate the recitation of mantras; there are samādhis that incorporate the recitation of sutras;
and there are samādhis that incorporate the mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*). Here, the object of mindfulness is designated; this is precisely the inclusion of mindfulness [of all these].

The Buddha’s samādhis all assist in manifesting the Buddha of one's own fundamental nature. Whether they manifest it directly or assist in its manifestation, their ultimate purpose is one and the same.
This is especially true for ordinary beginners whose defilements and obscurations are thick; they must rely entirely upon these sublime objects to awaken their wondrous mind.
This is truly an essential method for practice; it must not be neglected.
[Commentary] To clarify "mindfulness of the Dharma" (or mindfulness of the Buddha's name): once one has heard the holy name, the essential point lies in its retention.

"Retention" means that upon hearing this, one receives it with courageous resolve and decisiveness, so as not to be shaken or diverted. "Retaining" means that having received it, one guards it, remaining forever constant and steadfast.
Because there is no forgetting.
[Commentary] The analysis of the term "upholding" (*dhāraṇī*) is as explained above. When used alone, "upholding" includes "grasping.
In sum, it means to maintain focused mindfulness without forgetting. Furthermore, there are several types of upholding: first, "vocal upholding," which refers to reciting aloud. Second...
"Silent recitation" (*maṃtra-dhāraṇī*) refers to silent, mental recitation without sound. "Half-voiced, half-silent recitation" refers to reciting while slightly moving the lips and tongue;

this is what the practitioners of mantra call *vajra-dhāraṇī*. Furthermore, one may perform it while counting the repetitions or without counting them, as explained in detail in the Secret Teachings (*Guhyamantra*).

Either method is permissible according to convenience. Each, however, is distinguished by its respective aspect of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*); thus, one should maintain mindfulness without [distraction].

Continuous practice is called "retention of phenomena" (*shih-ch'i*). Investigating the essence without interruption is called "retention of principle" (*li-ch'i*). This shall be explained in detail below.
Taking this as the cause, the subsequent state of "single-mindedness without distraction" likewise possesses both phenomenal and principled aspects.

Those who do not understand this meaning hold that reciting the Buddha's name is for those of dull faculties, while investigating the Zen kōan is for those capable of awakening to the Way. When beginners hear this, they are unable to reach a decision for themselves.

Not knowing how to investigate the essence through nianfo (buddha-recitation), he observed that his approach closely resembled the method of the venerable masters of former generations who taught people to raise a *huatou* and give rise to the spirit of doubt (*yiqing*).
Therefore, he said: "In practicing Chan, there is no need to raise a separate *huatou*;
it suffices simply to apply oneself to the single phrase 'Amitābha Buddha. How wondrous these words!"
[Commentary] Furthermore, "to uphold" (*zhíchí*) is synonymous with "taking refuge" (*guīmìng*).

[Sub-commentary] "Taking refuge" is the Sanskrit term *namas*; its explanation may be found in the preceding Preface. If one does not surrender one's body in taking refuge, how can one uphold [the mantra] with a single mind?
Therefore, the meanings are identical. The two meanings of "returning" (*guī*) and "restoring" (*fù*) are also as explained in the preceding Preface.
First is the meaning of seeking refuge: to hold the name and direct one’s mind toward it with single-mindedness; this is single-mindedness in practice.
Second is the meaning of returning to the source: to hold the name and return to the single mind; this is single-mindedness in principle.

[Commentary] Regarding the two aforementioned categories of objective dharmas, there are further three meanings: first, hearing the recitation of the Buddha’s name constitutes the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā);
second, holding it within one's heart constitutes the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā); third, maintaining it without forgetting constitutes the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
[Commentary] Regarding "wisdom derived from hearing": although Amitābha Buddha possesses immeasurable merit, this merit cannot be known without hearing, nor can it be heard without being taught.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The attainment of the wisdom of non-arising first depends upon extensive learning. It further says:
"If the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, even those with wisdom cannot comprehend it. Alternatively, it refers to that which is proclaimed in the sūtras and śāstras.
Yang: Or, when one hears what has been revealed by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), it passes through the faculty of hearing once and becomes forever a seed for the Path;
this is called "hearing" (śruta). As for "wisdom" (prajñā), hearing itself is wisdom. This is said in contrast to wood and stone, which are dull and do not hear;

and in contrast to fools, whose hearing does not take up or grasp [the teaching], as if they had not heard it at all. Therefore, it is called "wisdom derived from hearing" (śrutamayī-prajñā). As for "wisdom derived from reflection" (cintāmayī-prajñā), since...
When [the teaching] enters the ears, it must be retained in the mind. To examine and contemplate it with precision—asking, "What dharma-gate is this?

What principle is this?"—is what is called "reflection" (cintā). As for "wisdom" (prajñā), reflection itself is wisdom. Although birds and beasts hear, they do not understand because they lack reflection;

although fools hear, the words merely enter their ears and leave their mouths because they do not engage in recollection and contemplation. Therefore, it is called the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) and the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
Having reflected deeply upon this, one should practice it with diligence; this is what is meant by "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). As for "wisdom" (*prajñā*), cultivation itself is wisdom.
Although a madman may reflect, because he obscures his essence and exerts his spirit without practicing it [in deed], he does not attain it. Question: Does this refer to the three types of wisdom?
What evidence is there for this? The answer is that the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva traverses the Pure Land by means of the three sublime wisdoms.

The commentary explains: "By means of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one attains entry into the Pure Land. Therefore, we know that the practice of nianfo (buddha-recollection) necessarily involves these three wisdoms.
[Commentary: Furthermore, there are three meanings. To hear the names of the Buddhas being spoken and not harbor doubt or hesitation—this is called faith (*śraddhā*).

Having believed, to grasp [the teaching] and give rise to a joyful aspiration in the mind—this is called vow (*praṇidhāna*). Having vowed, to maintain it with diligent exertion in the mind—this is called practice (*caryā*).
[Commentary]: Faith, Vow, and Practice shall be explained in the following text. [Sub-commentary]:
Regarding the Name: the four characters of "Amitābha Buddha" are the primary focus and do not include the physical form and other attributes.
This is as stated in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* and the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, because the physical form and other attributes are already subsumed within the category of the Name.
[Commentary]: "Not including physical forms and so forth" correctly clarifies that this sutra focuses exclusively on the upholding of the Name. The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* states:

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "One who wishes to enter the Samādhi of One Practice should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, not grasp at appearances, and bind the mind to a single Buddha, single-mindedly reciting His name. Following that...
Regarding the location: with body upright and facing forward, one is able to maintain the continuous succession of thoughts upon a single Buddha.

Within that very mindfulness, one is able to see all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. The merit of mindfulness toward a single Buddha is non-dual from the merit of mindfulness toward immeasurable Buddhas.
The Buddha-dharma heard by Ānanda still dwells within the realm of numerical limits; if one attains the three samādhis of a single practice...
He discerns each and every dharma-gate of all the sutras with clarity and understands them all completely.

Day and night he proclaims them, his wisdom and eloquence never ceasing. Even if Ānanda’s vast learning and eloquence were multiplied a hundred thousand times, they would not equal even a fraction of his.
The *Lun-zhu pípóshā lùn* (Treatise on the Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā) states: "The Buddha-dharma has immeasurable gates, just as there are various paths in the world."
That which is difficult to attain is made easy; that which is easy to practice leads swiftly to arrival. One should thus practice mindfulness of the Buddha and recite His name.
The Original Vow of Amitābha Buddha is as follows: it encompasses those who grasp the Name through two meanings. First, because a name must necessarily have a corresponding form (*nimitta*);

second, because both name and form are inseparable from the one mind. Thus, by raising the Buddha’s name even once, both the primary reward (*sambhogakāya*) and the environmental reward (*bhājanaloka*) are encompassed.
It is not exhausted. Why doubt the physical form?
[Commentary] When people today hear of the Buddha and are unwilling to uphold it, there are four obstacles.
Only when these four obstacles are eliminated can one uphold it, even to the point of single-mindedness.
[Commentary] "Obstacle" means to block. Because these four kinds [of obstacles] block the mindful mind, one is unwilling to maintain it;
therefore, they must be eliminated. As for the four obstacles: the first is the notion that "the mind itself is the Buddha"—why then should one abandon oneself to contemplate another?

This is because one does not realize that the Buddha is the mind, and thus fails to see that contemplating the Buddha is not precluded. Since the mind itself is the Buddha, how could it not be the Buddha?
This mind merely clings to its own thoughts and does not permit the recitation of the Buddha’s name; thus, the mind and the Buddha become two, and the meaning [of non-duality] is not established.
Therefore, because there is no mutual obstruction between recollecting the Buddha and recollecting the mind, why not recollect all Buddhas universally instead of recollecting only one?
It is because one does not know that when the mind is single-mindedly focused on one, samādhi is thereby accomplished. This is truly due to sentient beings...
Wisdom is shallow; if it is too complex, one cannot master it. Therefore, when the will is undivided, the spirit becomes concentrated;

when the mind is employed along divergent paths, its efficacy is lost. This is as when the Bodhisattva Puguang asked the Buddha: "If there are buddha-lands in all ten directions, why do you alone praise the Western Land?
The Buddha replied: "The people of Jambudvīpa have minds that are mostly distracted and chaotic. To cause them to focus their minds on a single object—"
One attains rebirth because all Buddhas possess the same Dharma-nature body; thus, by recollecting one Buddha, one recollects all Buddhas.
Third, it is said that while any Buddha may be recollected, why follow the recollection of just one, rather than necessarily recollecting Amitābha?
This is because it is not known that this Buddha has a particular affinity with sentient beings. This is truly due to the name of that Buddha.
The Name is that which people joyfully invoke. Even when an evil person, at some time, involuntarily utters the name of the Buddha,
or when a person encounters a good fortune and involuntarily recites the Buddha’s name with joyful praise,

or when a person encounters misfortune and hardship and involuntarily recites the Buddha’s name with piercing grief— such karmic responses and conditions arise spontaneously, without being prompted by anyone else.
For this reason, the fourth [point] asks: why not recollect the Buddha’s merit, wisdom, marks, signs, and radiance, but instead recollect only his name?
This is because one does not realize that holding the name is most suited to the capacities of beings in the Dharma-ending age (*mofa*), and because it is inconceivable.

Regarding "suited to capacities," the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are dull and ignorant; they cannot understand through contemplation. Therefore, simply cause them to recollect [the name]."
Through the continuity of sound, one naturally attains rebirth. As for the "inconceivable," it is as previously explained regarding the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi):
it does not merely accommodate those of dull faculties, for its divine function is unfathomable. As the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Yijiao jing) states:

"If the mind is controlled in one place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Now, by controlling the mind upon the Buddha-name and reaching the state of single-mindedness (*ekacitta*), how could this not be so?
[Commentary on] "Fixing the Period of Contemplation": From one day to seven days is the essential period fixed for the practice.

As for the seven-day period, both in the mundane and supramundane realms, those who take the matter seriously always rely upon the number seven; thus, reciting the Buddha's name for seven days is sufficient to avoid [rebirth in the evil paths].
Regarding the duration of seven days in hell, there are furthermore two meanings, each distinguished by the capacities of those with sharp or dull faculties. Moreover, many [periods] exist:

the ten-day period of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, the ten-day period of the *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda*, the forty-nine-day period of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, and the ninety-day period of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*, and so forth.

If it is brief, the fundamental principle is "one day. Regarding the *Contemplation Sūtra*’s mention of "ten recitations" and so forth, the term "day" is used because it corresponds to one complete cycle of the waxing and waning of the heavenly path.
[Commentary] As for the essential point: if one were to rely on the Tathāgata’s attainment of Bodhi, it would truly not be contingent upon days; thus, it would not be "day."

It is not a kalpa; how could there be seven days? If one were to base this on the bodhisattva’s cultivation of practice, which spans dust-like kalpas, it would be infinite and inexhaustible—how could it stop at merely seven days?

Now, the reason for establishing a fixed period is that when sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age cultivate various merits, diligence is always difficult to maintain while negligence is always easy. One must set a limit in order to give rise to a superior resolve. Seven.
That which is held in high esteem by the world is as follows: the ritual for repentance is said to last for seven nights; the recitation of mantras is said to be performed seven times;

the railings and rows of trees surrounding this sutra are said to be sevenfold; even the state records its ancestral lineages as consisting of seven temples; and the instruction of the people is said to take seven years.

To "exhaust one's sincerity" refers to practices such as the seven-day fast and purification (*śīla*). Regarding those who are spared from hell, the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya) states:
There was a king who murdered his father; he was destined to fall into hell after seven days. A venerable elder instructed him to recite "Namo Buddha.
The king then single-mindedly recited the name of the Buddha without ceasing for seven days. When his life ended, he arrived at the gates of hell and called out "Namo..."

There was no Buddha; all the sentient beings in the hells attained liberation. Regarding those of sharp and dull faculties, some say that for the sharp-rooted it takes one day, while for the dull it may take up to seven days.
Now, however, it is said that for both the sharp and dull faculties, the period ranges from one to seven days respectively.

This is because those of sharp faculties, due to their agile nature, achieve success in a single day, immediately attaining single-mindedness (*ekacitta*) and becoming free from distraction. As for those who are somewhat dull...

For two or three days, and even up to seven days, one finally attains single-mindedness. There are also those of sharp faculties who, for seven days, remain upright and one-pointed, never for a moment becoming distracted.
Those who are somewhat dull-witted may achieve this for only six, five, or even just one day, or they may become distracted immediately.
Therefore, there are respectively those of sharp and dull faculties; one should not categorize them exclusively [as one or the other]. As for the ten-day period, it is the great...

The original text states: "Those who maintain the purity of the precepts and fasts, and with single-mindedness constantly recite [the name] for ten days and nights without interruption, will certainly be reborn in my land at the end of their lives.
Furthermore, the *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* (*Ghoṣadatta-sūtra*) states:
"If one upholds the name of that Buddha, steadies the mind, and recollects it without forgetting for ten days and ten nights, setting aside all distraction, one will certainly behold that Amitābha."

Regarding "seven seven-days" (forty-nine days): the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that if a person single-mindedly recollects a Buddha of a particular direction, whether walking or sitting, until the forty-ninth day, they will see the Buddha in their present body and immediately attain rebirth there. Regarding "ninety days":
the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states that if a person makes a vow to themselves to constantly walk and stand for ninety days with a single mind...
By fixing the mind in samādhi, one shall behold Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

"If for ninety days one sits upright facing west and single-mindedly contemplates the Buddha, one will immediately attain samādhi. Regarding the period of a single day, the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* (Dafangdeng daji jing) states:
"If one fixes the mind single-mindedly upon me, even if it lasts for only a single day and night without interruption, [one shall surely attain rebirth]."

"Born in my land. Regarding "ten recitations," the *Contemplation Sūtra*, in its section on the lowest of the low grades, states: "That person, oppressed by suffering, has no leisure to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
yet by chanting the Buddha’s name ten times, etc. From this, one knows that from one day up to seven days—according to the number of days—one’s period for rebirth is certain;
it simply depends upon how much effort one exerts. "A cycle of darkness and light" refers to the time from the hour of Zi (midnight) to Wu (noon), which constitutes one full cycle of darkness.
It is bright from the hour of *wu* (noon) until the hour of *zi* (midnight), proceeding from light into darkness; this constitutes one day and night of the heavenly way (*tāndào*).

Now, the mind is indeed subject to momentary arising and ceasing—how could it be confined to a day and night? Within this single mind is what is called the continuity of thought-moments throughout the twelve periods of the day and night.
[Commentary: Furthermore, these seven days are not necessarily the seven days preceding death;
for anyone who possesses such power of meditative concentration during their ordinary life will certainly be reborn in that land.

[Commentary]: Regarding "during one's lifetime" (*píngshí*): fearing that people might cling to the scriptural passage concerning the "seven days" and claim that death must occur precisely from one day up to seven days before it can be called "the seven-day period," he says "either at the time of death or during one's lifetime.

This means that anyone who possesses the power of meditative concentration for even a single day or for seven days shall attain rebirth. This is what is meant by the saying: "Prepare during leisure; employ during busyness."
Later, when his life comes to an end, cause and effect will correspond, and he will surely be reborn in that land.
[Commentary] "With a single mind, without distraction" describes the ultimate state of upholding [the name]; this constitutes the essential purport of the entire sutra.

[Commentary] "Mind" (citta) excludes those who recite with their mouths but do not contemplate with their minds. "Single-mindedly" (eka-citta) excludes those whose minds, though contemplating, are not focused on a single object.
"Without distraction" (avikṣipta) excludes those whose contemplation, though single-minded, is at times not so.
When one is single-minded and without distraction, the essential task of the Pure Practice is complete.
[Commentary] To explain these four characters, first the general meaning is clarified, followed by a detailed exposition of the facts and principles.
The general meaning is that, at first glance, these are both direct and inverse expressions. The direct expression refers to single-mindedness; the inverse expression refers to being undisturbed.
[Commentary]: First, there is non-distraction. If one is distracted, there is no unity. Because there is that single mind and no distracted mind, it is said to be "positive" and "negative.
This is like saying "pure and single, not mixed," or "refined and singular, without duality," and so forth.

The fourth text of the *Ten Dedications* (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "That which is called non-distraction dedication, single-minded dedication. The commentary explains: "One..."

"Mind" refers to focusing intently on the correct object. "Not distracted" means not giving rise to deluded thoughts. This focus and absence of delusion constitute the meaning of "correct" and "opposite.
[Commentary] Next, to clarify phenomena and principle: a single word of the Tathāgata encompasses both phenomena and principle; therefore, they are equally termed "one mind."

There is the phenomenal aspect (*shi*) and the noumenal aspect (*ri*). As stated in the *Great Text* (*Daben*): "To bind the mind with single-minded mindfulness" is precisely what is meant by "single-mindedness without distraction.

Yet, the phenomenal and the noumenal are each distinct. First, regarding single-mindedness in the phenomenal aspect: it is as previously described—recalling [the Buddha] with each thought in continuous succession.

There is no duality of thought; the power of faith is perfected. This is called "single-mindedness regarding the object" (*nāmārtha-ekacitta*). It is subsumed under the category of concentration (*samādhi*), because wisdom (*prajñā*) has not yet arisen.
[Commentary]:
Within the preceding section on "retention," one investigates with mindfulness (*smṛti*), which is briefly divided into two types. Regarding mindfulness: having heard from the Buddha...

Regarding the name and title: constantly recollecting and constantly mindful of it, one traces it with the mind so that each syllable is distinct. From the preceding phrase to the succeeding phrase, they continue without interruption.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is only this single thought; there is no second thought. It is not confused by the various thoughts of afflictions such as greed and anger.
As stated in the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Accomplishing All Radiance*, this is what is called emptiness.

To unify the mind amidst solitude and stillness, and to unify the mind amidst the various afflictions—even regarding praise and censure, gain and loss, or good and evil—to unify the mind in all such circumstances is precisely this.
Although one attains success in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), one has not yet penetrated the principle (*li*);
because one possesses only the power of faith and has not yet seen the Way, it is called "one-pointedness of mind in terms of phenomena. As for the term "concentration" (*samādhi*), it is because...
"Because one subdues delusion. "Those without wisdom" are so called because they have not yet been able to shatter delusion.
[Commentary] "The principle of single-mindedness" is as previously investigated: having attained one's own fundamental mind, it is therefore called "single-mindedness.
Within this, there are further two aspects: first, realizing that the subject who recollects and the object recollected are not two separate things, but are solely the one mind; second...
It is neither existent nor non-existent; neither both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent. It is free from the four propositions because it is solely the one mind.

This is pure contemplation of principle (*tattva*), not focused on phenomenal characteristics. When the power of this contemplation is perfected, it is called "one mind through principle" (*li-yi-xin*);
it belongs to the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*) while simultaneously attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "thorough investigation" (tǐjiū): upon hearing the name of the Buddha, one does not merely recollect it; rather, as one recites, one turns the gaze inward to investigate and examine it thoroughly, tracing it back to its very source.
When this thorough investigation reaches its ultimate point, there is a sudden realization and accord within one's own fundamental mind.
Regarding the two meanings of the middle [verse]: first, it is the non-duality of suchness and wisdom; outside of the recollecting mind, there is no Buddha that is recollected by me.
Outside of this wisdom there is no suchness; outside of the Buddha whom one contemplates, there is no mind capable of contemplating that Buddha.
Outside of suchness there is no wisdom; it is neither suchness nor wisdom, and therefore there is only the single mind. These two are quiescent illumination, inconceivable.
If one says they exist, then the contemplating mind is empty in its original substance, and the contemplated Buddha is utterly unattainable. If...
If one says it is non-existent, then the mind that is capable of mindfulness is luminously unobscured, and the Buddha who is the object of mindfulness is vividly distinct.
If one says it is both existent and non-existent, then both mindfulness and non-mindfulness are simultaneously extinguished.

If one says it is neither existent nor non-existent, then both mindfulness and non-mindfulness are simultaneously preserved. Being neither existent, it is eternally quiescent; being neither non-existent, it is eternally illuminating. It is neither...

Both together, neither both nor not both—then there is neither stillness nor illumination; yet it is both illuminating and still. Beyond the reach of words and thought, it cannot be named or described. Thus, there is only the one mind.
In this state, the dichotomies of subject and object dissolve, and views of existence and non-existence are exhausted.
Within the essence that is fundamentally pure and quiescent, what further phenomena could there be to cause confusion? Because one has seen the truth, it is called the "Unity of Principle."

It is the mind. As for "wisdom," it is so called because it can illuminate delusion. As for "conjoined with concentration," it means that by illuminating how delusion is fundamentally empty, delusion is spontaneously subdued;
furthermore, this illumination can destroy delusion, not merely subdue it.
[Commentary: Furthermore, the teachings distinguish four types of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha), ranging from shallow to deep. This [practice] occupies the very beginning.

Although each subsequent stage is deeper than the preceding one, in reality, each preceding stage penetrates through to the subsequent ones. This is because the single-mindedness of principle (*li yixin*) is itself the true aspect (*shixiang*).

[Commentary] The four types are as explained previously in the introduction: first, invoking the name; second, contemplating the image; third, contemplating the visualization; and fourth, the true nature (*dharmatā*).
"Invoking the name" refers to this present sutra. "Contemplating the image" means establishing a sacred image and gazing upon it with focused attention.

As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Rising and joining the palms, contemplate the Buddha with a single mind. This refers to contemplating the Buddha who is presently manifest through his physical marks, signs, and radiance.
Alternatively, as King Udayana did when he fashioned an image of the World-Honored One out of sandalwood, this refers to contemplating Buddhas cast from clay, wood, gold, or copper;
hence it is called "contemplating the image" (*xiang*). As for "contemplating the visualization" (*xiangxiang*), it means employing one's own mind and eyes.
To contemplate that Tathāgata is precisely what is taught in the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations*.

As for "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it refers to recollecting the Buddha of one's own nature, which is inherently true and devoid of such characteristics as arising and ceasing, existence and emptiness, or subject and object.

It is likewise free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, if one wishes to see Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one sees him immediately according to one's wish—this is it.

Although these four [methods] are all equally termed "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*), the former is shallow and the latter is deep. Although the recitation of the name belongs to the initial gate, its...
The true meaning contains the inexhaustible. A single mind in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) is shallow; a single mind in terms of principle (*li*) is deep.

When phenomenon and principle are one, then shallowness and depth are one. Therefore it is said: "penetrating before and penetrating after. Why is this so? Because of what constitutes the single mind of principle.
The single mind is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), because the beginning is itself the end. Question: How can merely naming it constitute the true mark? Answer:
What is called the "true mark" does not necessarily require the extinction or removal of all marks; rather, it is the absence of marks within the very midst of marks. As the Sūtra says:
"The worldly language of governance is entirely non-contradictory with the true mark. Why is this so?
The vast and magnificent name of ten thousand virtues does not equal a single word for governing the world. To once invoke "Namo Buddha," one has already established the path to Buddhahood;
how much more so when one now attains the single-mindedness of principle! Furthermore, see the *Commentary on the Contemplation of the Buddha’s Marks and Signs*, Chapter Nine of the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
This directly refers to contemplating the Buddha’s Dharma-body. Since the marks and signs are themselves the Dharma-body, how could the name and title not be the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?

[Commentary] Furthermore, this principle of single-mindedness is the text for Mañjuśrī’s Single Practice Samādhi (*ekavyūha-samādhi*) and the *Avataṃsaka*’s Single Practice of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*).

At one time, there was mindfulness of the Buddha. Furthermore, as clarified in the *Awakening of Faith* regarding the True Suchness Dharmakāya, and as taught in various sūtras: [The *Commentary* states:
"As for the practitioner of the Single Practice of Mañjuśrī, he exclusively upholds the name of the Buddha with Prajñā-wisdom; this is seen in detail in the preceding text.

Regarding the practitioner of the Single Practice of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Commentary on the Dharma-gate of Mindfulness of the Buddha shown by Bhikṣu Meghaśrī* says: 'The Samādhi of Single Practice...'"
Contemplating his Dharma-body, one takes suchness as the object; there is no object that is not the Buddha.

Furthermore, the cultivation of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) is generally based on gradual practice—namely, first the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), then the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and finally the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). Now, however, one cultivates them all simultaneously.

Without passing through successive stages, there is a single practice and not two practices; there is a single moment and not two moments. Therefore, it is called "the single mind that is identical with principle.
Regarding the arising of faith in True Suchness (*tathatā*), the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"If one contemplates the True Suchness Dharma-body of that Buddha and constantly and diligently cultivates this practice, one will ultimately attain birth [in that land], because one abides in right concentration. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattva..."
One recollects the Buddha not by means of form, nor even by means of the four wisdoms or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is this?
Because these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. That which is empty of intrinsic nature has nothing to be recollected; that which has nothing to be recollected is [the true recollection].

This is what is meant by mindfulness of the Buddha. Furthermore, in the *Buddha-dhyāna-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "For one who abides in mindfulness of the Buddha, the seal of the mind remains unbroken.
The commentary states: To thoroughly understand one's own mind is called "contemplating the Buddha"; it means not being distracted by external objects.
It is called samādhi; its single essence is immovable, which is termed the "Mind-Seal" (*cittamudrā*) and so forth. Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
"To cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha with a single mind" refers entirely to the principle of the single mind.

[Commentary: Furthermore, although it is said to be "one mind," in reality, it fully possesses the three minds of the *Contemplation Sūtra*, the three minds of the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, the three minds of the *Treatise*, and even the ten minds of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the ten minds of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*. It likewise possesses the eight dharmas of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
It is also because of single-mindedness. The twenty-first gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Cloud of Virtue, likewise does not transcend this principle of single-mindedness.
[Commentary] Regarding the three minds in the *Amitābha Sūtra*: first, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; third, the mind of dedication.
The mind of making vows and the three minds for arousing faith are different in name but identical in principle.

This is because the "mind of utmost sincerity" is precisely the "direct mind" of the *Awakening of Faith* that correctly contemplates True Suchness (*tathatā*). Since this single mind is undisturbed, it is free from further delusion and free from further flux, as it accords with True Suchness.
The "deep mind" is precisely the "joyful mind" of the *Awakening of Faith* that delights in accumulating all wholesome dharmas.
The root is this single mind of non-distraction; because all myriad virtues return to it, those who dedicate their merit and make vows do so to give rise to faith and deliver all sentient beings.
This single mind of non-distraction suddenly dissolves the distinction between self and others.
The treatise clarifies three minds: first, the pure mind, for in this single mind there is no defilement that is not exhausted; second, the peaceful...
The mind of purity. Since this single mind, in principle, lacks nothing, it is the third. The mind that delights in purity.
Since this single mind, through compassion, encompasses all, it corresponds precisely with the two sets of three minds mentioned above.

Regarding the ten minds of the *Avataṃsaka*, these are the ten recollections of the Bodhisattva treasury, which clearly elucidate ten kinds of mindfulness of the Buddha: first, the recollection of tranquility; second, ... [and so forth].
Pure mindfulness, up to and including the ten unobstructed mindsets—now, when the single mind is unmoving, this is the mindful state of tranquility.
When the single mind is unstained, this is the mindful state of purity. When the single mind is identical with the *dharmadhātu*, this is the unobstructed mindful state.
Regarding the "ten minds of Ratnakūṭa," their explanation may be found in the preceding text. The preceding [section] referred to the difficulty of fully possessing these ten minds; now, however—
This means that once the mind is unified, what kind of compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, or equanimity—among the hundreds of thousands of varieties of mind—would it not possess?
Regarding the "eight dharmas of Vimalakīrti," it is said that when a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight dharmas, they act without blemish and are born in a pure land.
The eighth point concludes: "Always seek all merits with a single mind. Now that the mind is already unified, [one possesses] hundreds of thousands of kinds of dharmas.

What is not fully contained herein? Regarding the "Gate of Mindfulness of the Buddhas" by Cloud of Virtue (*Guṇamegha*), it is found in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Lokadhātupraveśa*) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Therein, the Bhikṣu Cloud of Virtue says to Sudhana: "I have attained the 'Dharma-gate of the Wisdom-Light that Universally Perceives the Realms of All Buddhas through Mindful Recollection.
This further unfolds twenty-one gates, beginning with the Arising of the Light of Wisdom that Shines Universally and concluding with..."
It abides in empty space. Now it is said that there are no objects external to the mind, no wisdom-illumination external to the mind, and no empty space external to the mind;
therefore, nothing transcends the single mind, for all things are fully present within it. As the *Naxian jing* says: "Among all virtues, the single mind alone is the foremost.
When one unifies the mind, all virtues follow it. This is precisely what is meant here.
[Commentary] Furthermore, this single mind constitutes these two meanings. [Sub-commentary] The *Contemplation Sūtra* states:
"When one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, this mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.
Now, it is said that when one holds the name with this single mind according to this sūtra, by virtue of this single mind, one will ultimately become a Buddha. From cause to fruit, this is termed...
It is said: "To act" means that this very one mind is, in its entirety, the Buddha; it is neither cause nor fruit, and is thus termed "this.
[Commentary] Furthermore, this one mind is the concentration within concentration.

[Commentary] Regarding "concentration within concentration," this is distinguished by means of the contrast between concentration and distraction. Those who practice other minor wholesome merits possess distracted goodness;
those whose minds are undistracted possess concentrated goodness. Furthermore, one may distinguish between concentration and distraction even within the state of a single mind:

"single-mindedness in terms of phenomena" (ji-ichinen) is the distracted goodness within concentrated goodness, while "single-mindedness in terms of principle" (ri-ichinen) is the concentrated goodness within concentrated goodness.
[Commentary] Furthermore, this single mind is precisely the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.

[Sub-commentary] One might suspect that in the *Bodhisattva-nianfo-sanmei-jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha) preached by the Buddha, there are no words concerning rebirth through faith and aspiration;
it merely states that correctly contemplating the true mark of all phenomena is called "mindfulness of the Buddha. This seems to differ from the present sutra...
Their meanings are contradictory. Now, it is said that the former focuses exclusively on principle (*li*), while this one encompasses both principle and phenomena (*shi*).

As for "principle and the one mind," mindfulness without mindfulness is precisely the true mark (*dharmatā*). Thus, the former enters through non-mindfulness directly, whereas this one enters through skillful means via mindfulness;
