their functions differ slightly, yet ultimately they are not distinct. For this reason, they are both called the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
[Commentary] Furthermore, this single mind is precisely the Chan of Bodhidharma’s direct pointing.
[Sub-commentary] Generally, those who speak of Chan avoid the Pure Land. Now, it is said that the Chan taught by Bodhidharma is the direct pointing to the self-nature of numinous awareness.
Since this principle of the single mind is precisely the self-nature of numinous awareness, it is not a matter of provisional arrangements for the sake of the teaching’s gateways.
They are the same; yet that which is realized is not two minds. How profound are the words of Zhongfeng:
"Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land; the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan. How much truth there is in these words!

Some may say that the Chan of direct pointing does not rely on words or texts, yet now we recite the Name—how can these be reconciled? This is because they do not understand the transmission of the Dharma.
To seal the mind with a four-line verse and to compare it with a four-fascicle sutra, the latter is even more prolix in its characters.
This is certainly not because the establishment [of truth] is achieved by the annihilation of words; rather, it is to be neither identical to nor separate from words.
Those who have attained realization accord with this.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding this single mind, one should know that neither the mind-king nor the mental factors are not unified.

[Sub-commentary] The explanation of the "king" (citta) and its "factors" (caitasika) is found in the preceding text. These eight [categories] and the fifty-one [mental factors] are diverse and not uniform.

They arise in a chaotic clamor, yet there is not one among their words that does not converge on the same point. This is truly because, although the objects of the King [the Buddha] are many, if one traces the current back to its source, they do not emerge from anything other than the single mind.

Now, when a person of nianfo first hears the name of that Buddha with the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), and subsequently focuses their mindfulness and recollection with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because of this concentrated mindfulness, the six sense faculties—eye, nose, tongue, body, and so forth—are all comprehensively gathered. Just as...
These six consciousnesses all cease to function. By contemplating them without ceasing, when contemplation reaches its limit, one forgets them.
That which was called "constant and critical deliberation" becomes tranquil. By forgetting them without ceasing, when forgetting reaches its limit, they transform.

That which was called "the union of the true and the delusive" has its delusion dissolved. Consequently, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses also cease to function. Once the master is no longer present...
It exists; those who follow it will naturally attach themselves to it. What need is there to discuss its fifty-one [mental states]?
At such a time, great waves and ripples alike become still water; thick clouds and thin mists all turn into a clear sky. There is only this single mind, with no other dharmas whatsoever.
Therefore, it is said that there is nothing that is not one.
[Commentary: Thus we know that a single sincere recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas;
this is truly because it correctly points to the principle of single-mindedness (*ekacitta*). As it is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*:

[Commentary] Someone may raise this doubt: "If one's offenses have persisted for many kalpas and the karmic hindrances are heavy and deep, it would require long-term diligent repentance and the gradual accumulation of merit before they could possibly be extinguished.
Yet, a single recitation of the Buddha's name extinguishes the sins of many kalpas; thus, the cause is minute while the fruit is vast."
This is indeed what I do not believe. What is now called "the utmost mind" (*zhìxīn*) is precisely "single-mindedness" (*yīxīn*).

If one practices with the single-mindedness of phenomena (*shì yīxīn*), although it can extinguish transgressions, its power is somewhat lax; thus, transgressions will likely reappear. A multitude of thoughts can only extinguish a small amount of fault.
This "utmost mind" properly belongs to the single-mindedness of principle (*lǐ yīxīn*). Once this single-mindedness is radiant, accumulated delusions are suddenly emptied. To illustrate:
Just as in a dark room a thousand years old, how could darkness not be swiftly extinguished by a single lamp?
Thus, a single invocation of "Namo Buddha" means that all have already attained the path to Buddhahood. This is not found only in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; the *Fahua Sanmei Guan Jing* states:
"If sentient beings of the ten directions invoke 'Namo Buddha' even once, they shall all become Buddhas. There is only this One Great Vehicle.
There are neither two nor three. All dharmas have but a single characteristic and a single gateway, namely: non-arising and non-ceasing, the ultimate mark of emptiness.
By practicing such contemplation, the five desires are naturally severed, the five hindrances are naturally eliminated, and the five faculties increase.

One immediately attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The commentary states: Regarding "attaining Buddhahood by a single invocation," it means that through single-minded devotion, there is nothing that does not lead to Buddhahood.
Apart from the single characteristic and single gateway of one’s own mind, there is no other dharma to which one can take refuge;
it is ultimately empty and quiescent. For one who contemplates in this way, the five desires are naturally severed, and even the six perfections and myriad practices are all fully accomplished.
It is as stated above: how could it be anything other than "one-pointedness of mind through improper means"? Furthermore, the *Buddhanāma-sūtra* states:

"Hearing the name of the Buddha even once extinguishes the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas. "Once" here does not require formal recitation; "immeasurable" does not stop at eighty billion kalpas.
Since the cause is more concise, the result is all the more vast. How could this be achieved without one-pointedness of mind through improper means?
This is the conclusion. One need only fear that the mind is not unified; what concern could there be that sins will not be extinguished?
[Commentary: Thus we know that from the ancient sages' discourse on the lack of universal knowledge and vision, down to their distinctions regarding the concentrated and single-minded mind.
This is truly because one’s mind is focused solely on the matter at hand; it is not because of a single principle.

[Commentary] Regarding "limited knowledge and vision," the *Huayan lun* states: "The Great Way of the One Vehicle is not the realm of Bodhisattvas who delight in being born in a Pure Land, for they harbor attachments to purity and defilement, and thus their knowledge and vision are not universal. Now, I say this refers to those who have merely attained...
Regarding "single-mindedness in practice": if one attains single-mindedness in principle, then through wondrous awakening one realizes single-mindedness; what defilement or purity could there be?
Nevertheless, although one knows that within the equal Dharma-realm there are no beings to be saved, one constantly cultivates the Pure Land to teach and transform sentient beings.
This is precisely what is called the Great Way of the One Vehicle. What is more universal than this in terms of knowledge and vision? Furthermore, [the vows of] Samantabhadra Bodhisattva...
Sāramati is the eldest son of the Avataṃsaka; is this not the realm of the One Vehicle?

Yet, if one wishes to see Amitābha face-to-face and attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī while claiming that the mind still harbors distinctions between the pure and the defiled, can this truly be called "single-mindedness"?

Yongming said that the nine grades, from the highest to the lowest, do not transcend two types of mind: first, the concentrated mind (*samādhi-citta*), such as when practicing meditative concentration and cultivation of contemplation—this constitutes the highest grade.
First, superior rebirth; second, single-mindedness. For example, by merely reciting the name, one may achieve the lowest grade [of rebirth].
Now, since it says "merely reciting," the word "merely" (但) specifically refers to having attained the fact (事), but not yet having attained the principle (理).

[Commentary: Therefore, we know that when the ancients spoke of "fools seeking the practice of purity," they were referring neither solely to the single mind of principle nor to the single mind of phenomena.

[Commentary] Ancient worthies have said that there are those whose Zen practice lacks efficacy; they abruptly change their former causes and, morning and evening, count their prayer beads, seeking pure karma.
Others say that by reciting the Buddha’s name a certain number of times, one hopes to escape the iron staff from the hands of Old Man Yama. Such is the conduct of the foolish.
Those who cling to these words give rise to doubt and slander, failing to realize that this [practice] is merely because their resolve for Zen practice was not firm.
To return to the point: the explanation that one who suddenly changes their path [is a fool] is not intended to disparage pure practice;

it merely states that fools recite their prayer beads morning and evening seeking pure practice, but does not say that fools seek pure practice with a single mind and without distraction morning and evening.
The *Amitābha Sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra) says: "Merely hearing the names of the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas can extinguish immeasurable births and deaths."

It is a transgression, let alone to dwell upon it. To "dwell upon" refers here to single-mindedness regarding a specific object. If one knows that even focusing on a single object is no longer the way of a fool, how much more so is it when one focuses on the single principle?

[Commentary: Thus we know that those who cultivate pure karma further neglect other practices; it is not merely that they do not understand the oneness of principle, but they are also still unable to maintain one-pointedness of mind regarding phenomena.
[Commentary] To recollect the Buddha in every thought-moment without any other distracting thoughts is called "single-mindedness.

To recollect the Buddha with a single mind, and yet also to cultivate various other dharma-gates with a single mind—this constitutes two minds. Now, one who is free from distracting thoughts has merely attained the single-mindedness of phenomena (*dharma*), which we have not yet achieved;
how much less so the single-mindedness of principle (*li*)? Therefore, those who practice the recollection of the Buddha must maintain their resolve without duality.
Do not, because samādhi is difficult to achieve, hastily change your practice to other disciplines. As the former scholars said:
"One must not, because benevolence is difficult to mature, willingly accept that another path has already achieved success. This is precisely what it means.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, if these four characters are explained through the method of *li-he* (separating and combining), they are identical in essence; thus they are called "one mind. They are distinct in appearance;
thus they are called "not chaotic."
[Commentary] Regarding "identity" (*xiāngjí*): this means that emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are identical. This is as previously explained.

Herein, the subject that recollects and the object recollected are simultaneously existent and non-existent, simultaneously non-existent and existent. Both extremes are unobtainable, and even the middle does not persist.

The three virtues (*triguṇa*) are perfectly integrated and cannot be differentiated; this is called "one mind. Regarding "non-identity" (*xiāngfēi*): the provisional is not the same as emptiness, and emptiness is not...

This is the provisional. Within this, the middle is not provisional, and emptiness is not provisional; thus, both the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated are simultaneously extinguished, accomplishing the virtue of *prajñā*.

When both the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated are simultaneously established, the virtue of *vimukti* (liberation) is accomplished. When they both exist and both vanish, the Middle Way is revealed, accomplishing the virtue of *dharmakāya*.
These three virtues are distinct and clearly defined, never to be confused; this is called "non-confusion."

[Commentary] Furthermore, this "single-mindedness without distraction" is also divided according to the five teachings. It is not discussed here because it specifically points to the Sudden and Perfect [teachings].

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the division into five teachings: since the lotus has nine grades, there are naturally distinctions between the Small and Great Vehicles, as well as between the shallow and the deep.

...and so forth. In the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the mind that creates karma and thereby brings about external objects is taken as the "one mind. In the Initial Teaching (Prathama-yāna), that which is transformed by the *ālaya-vijñāna* is taken as the "one mind.
In the Final Teaching (Paryanta-yāna), where consciousness and its objects are like a dream, only the *tathāgatagarbha* is taken as the "one mind.

In the Sudden Teaching (Aksara-yāna), the simultaneous sublation of both defilement and purity is taken as the "one mind. In the Perfect Teaching (Pūrṇa-yāna), it is taken as the comprehensive inclusion of all.

All phenomena are but the one mind. Yet the Buddha preached this sutra primarily for ordinary beings of the lower realms, so that by merely reciting the name of the Buddha, they may directly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression and proceed straight to Buddhahood; this precisely belongs to the category of sudden and perfect [teaching].

Furthermore, because those with the seeds of the two vehicles do not arise [in this teaching], the first three stages are omitted and the five stages are no longer divided. The four teachings of Tiantai follow this same principle.
[Commentary] Furthermore, this matter of the two modes of upholding—phenomenal and noumenal—is fully present within the *Awakening of Faith*.

[Sub-commentary] The Treatise states: "By single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha, one immediately attains rebirth. This is spoken with reference to both the phenomenal and the noumenal simultaneously.
It further states: "If one recollects that Buddha’s Dharmakāya of True Suchness," and again: "Even though one recollects, there is nothing [to be recollected]."
"Being able to recite" and "that which can be recited" both refer to the single-mindedness of principle (*li*).
[The Commentary] Furthermore, these two forms of upholding—of phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*)—correspond to the two approaches of Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism.
[The Sub-commentary] The four-character name consists entirely of Sanskrit; merely reciting it without forgetting is identical to the practice of mantra-recitation (*dhāraṇī*). This is called...

It is called "Esoteric" (Mi). To contemplate and investigate while observing the mind and probing into principle is called "Exoteric" (Xian). While the gates differ slightly, their return to the source is the same.
Thus, Exoteric and Esoteric are perfectly interfused, and phenomena and principle are without obstruction.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding these two modes of upholding—phenomena and principle—although their relative superiority has been detailed above, there are those who focus exclusively on phenomena and those who focus exclusively on principle;
yet their spiritual capacities are mutually compatible, and one need not harbor doubts or obstructions.

[Commentary]: This is intended for those who fear that by merely practicing the recollection of the Buddha as a ritual act, they may doubt that their inherent nature (li-xing) is not clarified, and thus worry that their practice is of no benefit.
Therefore, it is said that the practice of the phenomenal (shi) can penetrate the principle (li) in order to resolve such doubts. As the *Great Power* chapter on "Complete Penetration" states:

"Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. Master Konggu said: "Do not investigate 'Who is this that recites the Buddha's name? Simply maintain a single, pure thought."

"Go! There will also be a day of awakening; this is it. Furthermore, fearing that those who focus solely on the principle (li) might doubt themselves for reciting the Buddha's name too little and thus fall into emptiness, he stated that the principle can be realized through practice (shi) to resolve their doubts. In every thought-moment, the principle is one.
This is the Amitābha of every thought-moment. Is it not great, then, to recite his name?

Therefore, the two modes of nianfo—concentrating the mind and realizing the nature of the mind—are mutually interpenetrating in both the phenomenal and the noumenal, for they are fundamentally non-dual.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding these two types of upholding—of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*)—one may enter them either gradually or instantaneously, depending on the individual's capacity;

thus, they are not fixed. [Sub-commentary] "Gradual entry" refers to those whose faculties are somewhat dull: they first diligently practice the upholding of phenomena and later gradually investigate the principle.

If one’s faculties and nature are of great sharpness, they proceed directly to the upholding of principle; this is called "instantaneous entry. Although their methods of application differ slightly, when they achieve success, they are one and the same.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the passage "with a single mind, without distraction," some editions add the twenty-one characters "exclusively holding the Name.
This is not adopted here because the phrasing and meaning would be inconsistent. We instead rely on the ancient edition and do not add them;
however, the intent of "many roots of goodness and merit" is implicitly included therein, which is most appropriate.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the text is not settled": since the four characters "upholding and reciting the Name" (執持名號) already appear in the preceding text, one cannot further add the single phrase "singlemindedly upholding the Name" (專持名號).
To do so would result in redundancy between the preceding and following sections, failing to constitute a coherent textual meaning.

It is traditionally transmitted that these twenty-one characters are from a stone inscription in Xiangyang; one should know that these were the words of a predecessor’s commentary on the sutra. [The Xiangyang edition].
These have erroneously entered the main text; they are merely written together without distinction. One who is skilled in literary meaning will naturally perceive this for themselves.
[Commentary] To speak according to principle: self-nature is neither recollecting nor forgetting—this is the meaning of "retaining.

It is neither now nor yesterday—this is the meaning of "seven days. It is neither one nor many—this is the meaning of "one mind. It is neither fixed nor distracted—this is the meaning of "non-distraction."

[Commentary] Fundamentally, there is neither arising nor ceasing; how, then, could there be recollection or forgetfulness? The essence is devoid of coming and going; who could establish "today" or "yesterday"?
Even "one" does not constitute one; how much less can "many" exist? Since concentration (*samādhi*) has no fixed form, where could distraction (*vikṣepa*) find its lodging?

If one realizes it in this way, throughout the day one recites the Buddha’s name, throughout the day one contemplates the mind; throughout the day one contemplates the mind, throughout the day there is no-thought—this is precisely the mind.
This is precisely the Buddha. It is neither Buddha nor mind; this is what is called the true practitioner of Buddha-recollection.
*The Commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha*, Fascicle Three.
*The Commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha*, Fascicle Four.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Temple in Ancient Hangzhou.
III. Receiving the Fruit (2). Part One: The Buddha Appears Before Me; Part Two: I Go to the Buddha’s Abode.
"First, a Buddha appears before me.
When that person is approaching the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy ones, will appear before them.

[Commentary] "That person" refers to the practitioner who holds the Name. Based on the preceding statement that they are able to maintain single-mindedness without distraction, at the time of their death—

The Buddha will certainly manifest before them. This is because their own power and the Buddha’s power interact through the path of resonance, as described in two sections of the sutras and various other scriptures.
[Commentary] Regarding "one's own power":
when an ordinary person’s life comes to an end, there is that which is about to pass away and that which has not yet been born; throughout one's lifetime, one's wholesome...

Evil naturally manifests before one; as when the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes manifest as the hells, or stinginess, greed, and jealousy manifest as the realm of hungry ghosts, and so on, up to the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds manifesting as the realms of humans and devas.

Now, if one focuses exclusively on the Buddha with a single mind without distraction, then pure mindfulness will be accomplished. Within such a pure mind, how could the Buddha not manifest before one? (*Śūraṅgama Sūtra*)
It is said: "If one recollects the Buddha and contemplates the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.
As for the power of the Buddha, the *Great Sutra of the Dharma-Treasury Vows* states:

"When I become a Buddha, among the gods and people of the countless worlds throughout the ten directions, should there be those who resolve to attain Bodhicitta, cultivate various merits, and vow to be born in my land—at the time of their final passing, I..."
[The Buddha] appears before that person together with the great assembly. Furthermore, regarding the three grades of rebirth, it is said:

"When that person’s life is about to end, the Buddha and the holy multitude will all come to welcome and escort them. In the nine grades of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, some say that Amitābha Buddha comes before the practitioner, while others say he comes to the person's location;
both express the sense of appearing before one's eyes. As for what is stated in various sūtras:
The *Sūtra on the Praise of the Merits of All Buddhas* states:

"If there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitāyus and believe and rejoice in it with a single mind, at the time of their death, Amitābha Buddha, together with his bhikṣus, will stand before them;
Māra shall be unable to destroy their resolve for perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, the *King of Drum-Sound Sūtra* states: "If there are members of the fourfold assembly..."

If one is able to correctly receive and uphold the name of that Buddha, at the time of death, Amitābha Buddha will immediately appear before that person together with his great assembly, enabling them to behold him.
Furthermore, the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata has ten kinds of buddha-activities. The first is that if there are sentient beings who mindfully recollect him with single-minded devotion, he then manifests before them."
...and so forth. This refers to the fact that the Buddha "grasps and does not abandon" sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
If one relies on *prajñā*, there are again two internal powers: first, the power of mindfulness; second, the power of the intrinsically existing Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

When combined with the power of the Buddha’s grasping, these constitute three powers. The intrinsically existing [Buddha-nature] is like a boat; mindfulness of the Buddha is like the sail and oars; and the Buddha’s grasping is like...
[The practice of] *bianfeng* (expedient means) is complete in three respects; one will certainly ascend to the other shore.
[Commentary: "The Buddha and the assembly of sages" refers to the Buddha, including both the *saṃbhoga-kāya* and *nirmāṇa-kāya*, and the assembly of sages, including both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

[Commentary] Regarding the inclusion of both the *saṃbhoga-kāya* and the *nirmāṇa-kāya*: the *Contemplation Sūtra* clarifies the Buddha by first mentioning sixty trillion [yojanas], subsequently opening up the sixteen-foot [form], and further stating that a *nirmāṇa*-Buddha comes to welcome those of the lower grades.
Thus, one knows that what is seen by the nine grades is not uniform.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also states that the *saṃbhoga-kāya* is seen only upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*), becoming increasingly subtle and wondrous as one progresses. Here, however, it simply says "Buddha" without distinguishing between the *saṃbhoga* and *nirmāṇa* bodies.
Because "one encompasses many," this includes both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. As stated in the *Amitābha Sūtra* regarding the highest grade of the highest birth:

"The Buddha, together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, the great assembly of Śrāvakas, and immeasurable devas, appear before that person.
Yet, there are also cases where the Buddha does not come to welcome them, but a Bodhisattva does; this is as follows:
Generally speaking. [Commentary] Question:
When the Buddha appears at the moment of death, are there also māras? Answer: The ancients said there are no māras; however, it is possible that they might appear.
The essential point lies in discernment.

[Commentary] Regarding those who are free from demons: if one practices meditative concentration alone, the *skandha-māras* (demons of the aggregates) may arise, as is explained in great detail within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, and various other sūtras and śāstras.
Now, it is said that for those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, there is the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the power of the Buddha’s original vows.

Within the Great Radiance, there will certainly be no demonic activities (*māra-karman*). Nevertheless, for those with deep-seated past obstructions (*pūrvāvaraṇa*) or those who do not apply their minds skillfully, it is possible that demons may arise;

this cannot be taken for granted. One must therefore identify them in advance. As explained in the sūtras and śāstras, when a practitioner sees a Buddha, there are two ways to discern [the nature of the vision]:
first, if it does not accord with the sūtras (*sūtra*), it is a demonic activity; second...

That which does not accord with what was originally cultivated is a work of Māra. Why is this so? Because for a person who practices meditation alone, the cause originally cultivated is "mind-only without external objects";
therefore, even if a Buddha appears externally, it is entirely disregarded, as the fruit does not correspond to the cause.
Now, for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they recollect the Buddha throughout their lives and see the Buddha at the moment of death; this is the correspondence between cause and fruit.

This is consistent [with reason]. How can you categorically dismiss this as the work of Māra? If you are still unable to reach a definitive conclusion, simply continue to discern and examine it as previously described.
Question: Since you say it is not Māra, it must be the True Buddha. Yet, the ancients said that the Buddha neither comes nor goes.
How then can there be a Buddha appearing before one? Answer: Through the mutual resonance of cause and response (*ganying*), it is not a hindrance for the Buddha to appear without having come.
Come! To see without seeing is to see. Thus Yongming said that if one regards things as illusory and not real, then both mind and Buddha are forgotten;
yet because illusory appearances are not non-existent, mind and Buddha are not destroyed. He further stated that the Dharma-body, the true Buddha, fundamentally has no arising or ceasing.
Arising from the Truth to manifest transformation, the Buddha guides those with deluded faculties; this is the merit of the Tathāgata’s original vows.
It causes sentient beings who possess the karmic affinity to focus their thoughts and mindfulness, enabling them to see the Buddha coming to welcome them within their own minds.

This is not because the Buddhas actually dispatch transformation bodies to come and receive them; rather, the Buddha-body is profoundly still and eternally quiescent, yet sentient beings perceive its presence.
Coming and going are like forms in a mirror—neither internal nor external; they are like events in a dream—neither existent nor non-existent. Furthermore, a sutra says:
"To those who should be saved by a Buddha-body, he manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them.

This is precisely that meaning. Therefore, when the water is clear, the moon comes of its own accord; when the mind is pure, the Buddha appears of its own accord. This is what is meant by "resonance" (kan).
The convergence of the Way should be understood as inconceivable.

[Commentary: Thus we know that the practice of setting up an image and assisting with recitation at the moment of death is recorded in the sacred scriptures and transmitted from the Western Regions; one should not harbor doubts or obstructions regarding it.
[Commentary] The *Verses on the Fifteen Sutras of the Avataṃsaka* states:

"Seeing those who are at the point of death, one should encourage them to practice Buddha-recollection (*nienfo*) and further show them sacred images to inspire reverence and veneration, so that they may develop deep faith and devotion toward the Buddha; by this means, one attains this radiance. The Sub-commentary (*Shu*) says:

According to the Dharma of the Western Regions: for one who wishes to relinquish their life, they should be positioned facing west. A standing image should be placed before them, also facing west, with the top of a banner hung from the finger of the image.
The patient is made to grasp the end of the banner with their hand and cultivate the visualization of being reborn following the Buddha.
Simultaneously, incense is burned and a chime is struck to assist in the recitation of the Buddha’s name. It is not only that the deceased attains rebirth; [the living also gain merit].
Even before the Buddha, one will ultimately behold the Buddha’s light.

As for those whose spirits roam the great universe, free from obstruction in both going and staying, let them be set aside as beyond ordinary discourse. Otherwise, you must strive in this practice as described above;

even when one has specially established an image to assist in rebirth, how much more so when, through single-mindedness without distraction, the Buddha appears before one? To then suspect this is a demonic manifestation and harbor self-doubt is a grave error.
[Obstruction]. [Commentary]:

To speak in accordance with principle, when delusive self-nature is exhausted and the true nature is revealed, this is the meaning of the Buddha’s manifestation at the moment of death. [Sub-commentary]:

When the deluded mind has not yet been fully extinguished, it remains deep and lingering; this is what is meant by the life-root not having been severed. When afflictions are severed, one realizes emptiness.
Affections dissolve and views fade away; the person perishes and the family is ruined; smoke vanishes and ashes fly—this is what is meant by the end of life.
When all delusions are exhausted, what need is there for anything that is not true? If one seeks the Buddha and he does not appear before one, he cannot be found.

Nevertheless, the Buddha’s compassion is limitless; why must he necessarily appear at the moment of death? Therefore, he reveals himself at all times to those of this age, yet people themselves fail to recognize him.
Second, when I go to the place of the Buddha,
at the time of this person's death, their mind will not be inverted, and they shall immediately attain rebirth in Amitābha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Commentary: The previous mention of "approaching" refers to the period when one is about to die. The present mention of "the time of death" refers precisely to the moment when warmth has ceased and consciousness departs.
"The mind is not inverted" means that because the mind is undistracted, it is not inverted;
because it is not inverted, one is not reborn in other realms. "Attains immediately" signifies its swiftness.
[Commentary] Regarding "inversion": because throughout their daily lives they have followed after deluded thoughts and failed to cultivate right mindfulness, their minds are largely distracted.
As previously mentioned, when the sensation of warmth is about to depart, all that was done during a lifetime manifests simultaneously;
their spirits are terrified, and their movements become frantic and unsteady. Those who ought to enter hell perceive the mountain of knives and the forest of swords as gardens and groves.
Those who ought to fall among the animals may enter the womb of a mare or a donkey, yet they perceive it as a hall or a dwelling;

even if they perform good deeds and are destined for rebirth in the human or celestial realms, they cannot avoid the feelings of aversion and attachment toward their parents. Even those at the initial stage of a Lesser Sage (śrāvaka) are still unable to correctly discern their entry and exit [into the womb];
all such states are termed "inversion. Driven by these inversions, one undergoes the fruits of karma throughout the three realms and seven destinies.
Now that you have attained single-mindedness without distraction, your inner thoughts will be concentrated on right mindfulness and you will externally invoke the Buddha’s welcome.
Upon casting off this retribution-body, you will proceed directly to that land. As the Buddha said: "According to the purity of one's mind, so is the purity of the Buddha-land.
He further stated: "All lands are sustained solely by perception; when pure perception is perfected, one will certainly attain rebirth. Of this there is no doubt.
There are three types of "other places": first, the Sahā world; second, other Buddha-lands; and third, the border regions of those lands.

All of these are now excluded. Regarding "speed," it means not passing through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and not being separated by days or time, as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* as being like the snap of a finger in generating rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Furthermore, the Wise One said: "At the moment of death..."
The mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is itself the Pure Land. When thoughts stir, that is the time of rebirth in the Pure Land.
What is called "being in concentration" refers to the present mind being free from delusion; what is called "stirring of thought" refers to the subsequent aspiration to be born in that land.
[Commentary] The Great Sūtra states: "Their bodies are not the bodies of worldly people, nor are they the bodies of celestial beings.
They are all bodies of natural non-substantiality, formed by the accumulation of the virtues of manifold good deeds.
They are born through transformation within lotus flowers, and there is no one to nourish them with milk."
[Commentary]: "One who has accumulated goodness" refers to a body perfected by roots of goodness and merit.

It does not take desire and craving as its cause, nor do the four great elements constitute its substance; therefore, it does not pass through the womb or the hells, but takes form within a pond of lotuses. Furthermore, there is no nursing;
this clarifies that growth occurs spontaneously, unlike the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, who still require milk produced from the tips of fingers for nourishment.
[Commentary]:
Those who attain rebirth therein do so by virtue of the single-mindedness that is undisturbed, which constitutes the three sets of nine causes.
If these were to be further subdivided, they would likewise be immeasurable.

[Commentary] Regarding "the three groups of nine": this refers to the three grades of the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] and the nine ranks of the *Contemplation Sūtra*. By means of a single mind, one distinguishes between the phenomenal (*shi*) and the noumenal (*ri*);

furthermore, within both the phenomenal and the noumenal, there are distinctions of superior and inferior. One attains rebirth in the Pure Land according to these causes, and one's rank is determined accordingly.
As for the "three grades," as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya*: those of the "upper grade" are they who have resolved their minds on Bodhi and exclusively recite the name of Amitābha.
Amitābha Buddha. Having cultivated various merits and vowed to be born in that land, when his life is about to end, the Buddha and the assembly of sages will appear before that person.
Thereupon, they shall be born by transformation within a lotus flower inside a pool of the seven treasures, abiding in the stage of non-retrogression.

Possessing courageous wisdom and mastery of supernatural powers, their dwelling—a palace of the seven treasures—will be situated in the midst of space, at a distance from the Buddha [equal to the width of a hundred thousand koṭis of worlds].

This is called being "near," which refers to those of the highest grade who are born [in the Pure Land]. In relation to the preceding categories, these are those who have attained both the single-mindedness of practice and the single-mindedness of principle.
As for those of the middle grade, they are unable to extensively cultivate meritorious deeds, yet they likewise resolve their minds on Bodhi and single-mindedly dedicate their merits toward rebirth.
Upon the end of their lives, they are born there. In terms of merit and wisdom, they rank next to those of the superior grade; these are called those born by the middle grade.
If one correlates this with what precedes it, they achieve a surplus in terms of practice (*dharma*) but fall short in terms of principle (*tattva*).

As for those born by the lower grade, they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds, yet they give rise to the bodhicitta and single-mindedly and exclusively recite [the Buddha's name], even as few as ten recitations, and are thereby born there.

The palaces and halls exist only upon the ground. Furthermore, as for those of the middle grade, who are termed "those born of the lower grade," when compared with the former, they have attained only the phenomenal (the *shi*) and have not yet attained the noumenal (the *li*). Regarding the nine grades:

as for the three upper grades mentioned in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, there are those who, upon being born there, immediately attain hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates, and there are those who remain for one small kalpa.

Regarding those who attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there is a sūtra stating that after three minor kalpas they attain the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas" and dwell on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
When correlated with the preceding [categories], this constitutes attaining both the single-mindedness of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*);

yet, because there are degrees of depth, they are formed into three grades, following the analogy of the "upper grade. As for the three grades of the middle [grade], some are born in that land and immediately attain the state of an Arhat, while others...
Regarding those who attain Arhatship after half a kalpa: there are those born there who attain Arhatship after one full kalpa.

If these were assigned to the preceding category, the facts would exceed the principle and the logic would be deficient. Furthermore, because of the differences in depth and shallowness, they are established as three grades, following the pattern of the middle grade.
As for the three lower grades, there are those who are reborn in that land and, after ten small kalpas, enter the first bhūmi; there are those who... [text continues]
It was only after six kalpas that the lotus flower opened. For those who resolve upon the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, it takes twelve great kalpas;

for those who resolve upon bodhicitta, this is applied to the preceding [period]. Thus, there are three grades based on the presence or absence of principle and phenomena, as well as their depth or shallowness.
The "lower classes" are exemplified here. As for their detailed classification, as in the preceding section on stages and grades, they are further subdivided;

thus, there are hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of inexhaustible classes and grades, all arranged in sequence according to the depth of realization attained through phenomena and principle.
[Commentary]: According to the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the highest grade of the highest birth (*śreṣṭha-uttama-upapatti*) is said to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Tiantai judges this to belong to the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). However, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that there are varying degrees of depth within the patience of non-arising itself;
thus, even within the highest of the high grades, there are many levels of faith (*śraddhā*), let alone the other grades.

[Commentary] Regarding "shallow and deep": the sub-commentary on the section concerning the "pure patience" (*śuddhakṣānti*) of the eighth stage states: "The patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) is briefly of two kinds:
first, in terms of phenomena (*dharma*); second, in terms of practice (*caryā*). In terms of phenomena, all principles of non-origination and non-activity are termed 'non-arising'."
The wisdom-mind rests here; therefore, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). In terms of practice, the retributive conduct becomes fully matured;

wisdom merges with principle, being signless and effortless, as vast as empty space and as serene as a still ocean. When delusive afflictions of the mind and consciousness no longer arise in stillness, this is precisely what is called "non-arising.
The former explanation applies generally to all stages, while the latter refers specifically to the eighth stage. The rest is as previously stated.

This was already distinguished in the preceding introduction; therefore, one should know that within the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there are inherent gradations of depth.

Thus, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the eighth, many categories are already accommodated within the "superior-superior" grade alone; the rest may be inferred accordingly. Therefore, they are subdivided in detail.
They should likewise be immeasurable.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the three grades and nine levels, the two sutras correspond with one another, though various explanations differ slightly. As explained by Fuzheng, these should be harmonized.
[Commentary] The *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra) states: "The nine grades of this sutra are intended to clarify the relative heights of the stages of consciousness;

these correspond to the three classes (*sanbei*) of the *Maha-sukhavati-vyuha*. Gushan (Fazhi) maintained that the three classes of the *Maha-sukhavati-vyuha* only correspond to the six [upper] grades of the *Guanjing*, because those three classes exclusively clarify virtuous conduct and do not include evil persons.
Lingzhi (Zongxiao), however, judged that the three classes correspond only to the upper grade, hence he said:
Various explanations differ slightly. Cao’an’s *Supplement to the Correct Interpretation* states:
"Tiantai’s identification of the nine grades with the three ranks is based on the identity of their stages and positions (*wei-cì*), not on the identity of their causal practices (*xíng-yīn*).
Thus, neither Gushan nor Lingzhi contradicts Tiantai. This is because, when Tiantai speaks merely in terms of stages and positions, the ranks and grades are indeed identical."
The two masters speak solely in terms of the causes of practice; thus, their positions are consistent with the middle and superior grades respectively, each having its own basis.

Because they adopt different meanings, there is no contradiction. To speak according to the ultimate reality, afflictions are not different from bodhi. How could an initial evil state hinder a final goodness?
Since an evil person has already become good, how could they not be categorized as equal to the sages and saints? This is precisely the case for the three grades and nine levels.
They are thus mutually integrated; what cause for doubt could there be?

[Commentary] Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, the number [of recitations] is equal to the mind. This refers precisely to the principle of the three grades and nine levels, wherein the results differ according to the causes.
[Commentary] Regarding "the number of minds" and so forth: the twenty-third scripture of the *Avataṃsaka*, in the verses of the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, states:
"Taking the Buddha as one's object of focus, if one maintains mindfulness without abandoning it, this person shall behold the Buddha; their number shall equal that of their own thoughts."

The commentary states: "The number is equal to the mind" means that [the manifestations] appear according to one's recollection. There are two types of recollection: first, recollection according to the quantity;
the Buddha likewise conforms to this, such as when with a single recitation of the Buddha's name, a single transformation-Buddha emerges from his mouth, and so forth.
Second, recollection according to the depth; the Buddha responds accordingly, such as when seeing the Buddha at the time of death, where there may be superior or inferior visions.
"Such as these," referring to the varying degrees of shallowness and depth, is the classification according to their respective categories.
"This person attains the vision of the Buddha" means that Amitābha Buddha appears before them. "Single-minded recollection" means being undisturbed by a distracted mind.
[Commentary] Furthermore, the two types of pure karma—*zhi* (aspiration) and *yan* (vision)—also possess the meaning of the three grades and nine levels.

[Sub-commentary] Master Zhiyan stated: "In the single gate of rebirth, there are two types of pure karma: the first is called 'correct contemplation' (*zhengguan*), which is the silent illumination of the fundamental mind;
the second is called 'auxiliary practice' (*zhuxing*), which is the comprehensive cultivation of myriad virtues. When both matters are attained, one attains realization."

One attains the four pure lands. For those who merely achieve mundane goodness, they will be born nearby in the Land of Common Residence (Sahā), while in the long run, it serves as the cause for the three [other] pure lands.
Thus we know that the pure lands are the realms ascended by Bodhisattvas who have fundamentally investigated the principle, yet they are also inclusively accessible to ordinary sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said: "The perfect capacity embodies the Way; this is the supreme pure karma. If one further adds a vow..."
Guide them. Even those of the most ignorant and simple sort who merely recite the Buddha’s vows will be reborn there;

thus, when one contemplates this single gate of the Pure Land, one sees that no being is abandoned by the sages. According to what is called "correct contemplation," it applies to those of superior and middling capacities;

according to what is called "auxiliary practice," it applies to those of middling and inferior capacities. Furthermore, this treatise by the Dharma Master is exceedingly excellent. Those who contemplate it should not...
[Sutra]: Suddenly.
[Commentary]: Some say there are nine grades, asserting that eight arise from lotuses because the first grade is called the "Vajra Terrace.
Now, synthesizing the sutras and śāstras, we maintain that all nine grades equally arise from lotuses.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "eight [grades] born from lotuses": according to the text on the "Highest Grade of Highest Birth" in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, it says, "One sees oneself riding upon a vajra pedestal," and the two characters for "lotus" (*padma*) do not appear. Therefore, it is said that those of the eight lower grades are born from lotuses.
Nevertheless, as clearly explained in the sūtras and śāstras, it is stated repeatedly that all who are reborn in the Western Land are born from lotuses. Great!

The Vows of Dharmākara state: "In worlds of infinite measure, from the devas and humans down to the most minute insects, all who are born in my land shall be born by transformation within lotus flowers inside ponds of the seven treasures.
By saying "all," he refers generally to those of the nine grades. It further states: "Great Bodhisattvas from other directions who wish to see Amitābha Buddha [shall go] directly..."

Within the seven-jeweled ponds of that land, one is born by transformation from a lotus flower; to speak of a "Great Bodhisattva" necessarily implies they are neither of middling nor inferior capacity.

Furthermore, it is said that those of the "upper grade," when their lives are about to end, will be met and escorted by the Buddha and the assembly of sages, and shall immediately be born by transformation from a lotus flower within the seven-jeweled pond. To speak of the "upper grade" refers precisely to those of the highest (superior) category.
Furthermore, there is no intention whatsoever to surpass the Lotus Sūtra. Moreover, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Those who hear this scripture and practice according to its teaching shall, at the end of their lives, go directly to the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), the dwelling place of Amitābha Buddha surrounded by great bodhisattvas, where they will be born within a lotus flower and attain the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva and the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Now, as for attaining the non-arising...

Is patience not the highest of the high grades? Furthermore, in the *Chapter on Vows and Practices*, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva leads [practitioners] back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss by means of the ten great kings of vows, saying:
"The assembly of that Buddha is entirely pure; at that time, I shall be born within a supreme lotus flower.
Is the rebirth of Samantabhadra not the highest of the high grades? Moreover, the *Ratnakūṭa* clarifies the dedication of the ten minds.
Subsequently, one is born through transformation within a lotus flower. Now, are not Bodhisattvas of the ten stages indeed those of the "upper-upper" grade?
Judging by this, there is clear evidence. Question: If that is so, why does the "Upper-Upper" section refer to it as the "Vajra Terrace"?

One might ask: "Why is it not called the Lotus [Rebirth]? The answer is: because the wording alternates between presence and absence, and it would be insufficient to insist on a single term. How is this known?
Even those of the highest grade who are born in the middle rank are said to "mount a purple-golden platform," yet they are also said to "arise from within the lotus" seven times.
This being so, how much more so for those of the lowest of the middle grades, who are merely said to "at the end of life, like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, immediately be reborn"?

In the description of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), the two characters for "lotus" (*liánhuá*) do not appear in the text. Furthermore, how could it be said that "six [beings] are born from lotuses"?
Now, if it is held that being "non-lotus" constitutes superiority, then why would those of middling or inferior grades not be non-lotus?
Furthermore, regarding the "upper-middle" grade, it mentions only the "lotus pedestal" (*padmāsana*). Is this similar to the "vajra pedestal" or the "purple-gold pedestal"?

Or is it similar to the lotus itself? The arrangement is inconsistent and lacks a systematic basis; yet, one clearly knows that while the textual descriptions may be mutually deficient, the underlying meaning must be comprehensive.
In my humble opinion, each [grade] possesses its own lotus, each flower has its own pedestal, and each pedestal is distinct.

It is the same; however, the *vajra* (diamond/thunderbolt) is the most excellent among the pedestals (*maṇḍala*). This can be verified by the case of Huaiyu’s Silver Terrace, where the Gold Terrace arrived subsequently.
Furthermore, there are two meanings of "terrace" (*tai*): first, the terrace as a foundation, in which case the terrace is situated beneath the flower.

This is like the practice of carving images in the secular world, where a precious terrace is fashioned at the bottom, a flower is placed upon the terrace, and a Buddha is placed upon the flower. This is it.

Furthermore, regarding the second type, the "calyx-platform" (fángtái zhī tái): here, the platform is situated within the calyx (huá). As stated in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), the lotus represents the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).
Reaching the passage on "such retribution," it says: "The arms are like the seeds of a lotus surrounding the calyx-platform. It further states: [and so forth].
The "receptacle" (*tāla*) refers to the seed-vessel. The "seed" refers to the lotus seed; that which is hidden within the receptacle is what is commonly called the "lotus pod.

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the passage on the Lotus of the Ten Stages, states: "Lapis lazuli forms the stem, sandalwood forms the receptacle, agate forms the filaments, and Jāmbūnada gold forms the petals.
These are all referred to as the stem, receptacle, filaments, and petals. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* likewise...
It is said: For example, when the stalk, petals, filaments, and pericarp combine, they form a lotus flower. What is here called the "pericarp" (tái) refers to the seed-vessel and its base;
this is the intended meaning of using *vajra-vaiḍūrya* and *cintāmaṇi* jewels for the pedestal.

Observe this, and you will understand that in the "Contemplation of the Lotus Seat" within the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, it first states one should form the mental image of a lotus flower, and subsequently mentions *śakrābhilagna* jewels.
If one considers it to be the platform [within the lotus], it refers to the platform inside the flower.

Furthermore, it is said that each is golden in color and manifests transformations everywhere—sometimes appearing as a diamond (vajra) platform, or as jeweled nets, and so forth—which refers to the platform beneath the flower.

Therefore, regarding those born by the middle grade of the superior class, it first mentions the "purple-gold platform," and subsequently states, "Beneath their feet there are also lotus flowers made of the seven treasures. Thus...
It is clear that the purple-gold pedestal (*vajra-pīṭha*) exists beneath the lotus flower. Where there is a flower, there must be a pedestal; where there is a pedestal, there must be a flower.

When the "Vajra Pedestal" is mentioned without mentioning the flower, or when the flower is mentioned without mentioning the pedestal, these are merely variations in the phrasing used throughout the text to clarify the meaning.
However, those of the highest grade are born within the lotus, whereupon the flower immediately blooms, they immediately behold the Buddha, and they immediately realize the Way. As for the others...

Then the blossoms will open later, the sight of the Buddha will be delayed, and the realization of the Way will be increasingly distant. Through such distinctions, one knows that the "Supreme of the Supreme" (Anuttara) is uniquely victorious;
it is not that there are no lotuses. If one were to consider the absence of lotuses as superior and the presence of lotuses as inferior, this would be a disparagement of the lotus.
Why then take up the Lotus Land? For when one contemplates the Lotus Throne, it is clearly seen that the Buddha sits upon a lotus flower. Thus, the Buddha...
That too would be inferior. How then can this principle be reconciled? Question: Regarding the nine grades of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, eight arise from lotuses.
Why does Zhiyi (Siming) say otherwise? Answer: Zhiyi merely states that eight arise from lotuses; he has not stated that those who do not arise from lotuses belong to which grade.
This is because the middle and lower grades likewise lack lotus flowers. If it were the case that the highest grade does not arise from a lotus, then—
There must be a reason why he merely opened the beginning of this matter without completing his explanation. Why is this? Perhaps these eight characters are a scribal error;
who knows that they might not actually refer to the nine grades of rebirth in Sukhāvatī, where one is necessarily born from a lotus?
I await further discernment from those of superior intelligence.
[Commentary] Question: Apart from the inferior grade, there is also womb-birth (*jarāyuja*). Does it truly exist? Answer:
Because the power of their faith is not firm, womb-birth does not truly exist.

[Commentary]: Regarding those who are not born from a womb: the *Mahāvaipulya* states that the Buddha told Maitreya, "If there are sentient beings who cultivate various merits and vow to be born in that land, yet do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom and their resolve remains hesitant, they will only regret their past transgressions when their lives are ending.
Because of this, they are born there; as soon as they enter the borderland, they see a city of the seven treasures and immediately settle there. In this regard—
Padmasambhava also experiences natural bliss, like that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
yet, though he dwells within the city for five hundred years, he is unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma, and it is because of this that it is called "womb-birth" (*garbhaja*).
It is not a literal gestation like that of humans. Furthermore, it is said: "If a son of a Kṣatriya commits a crime, he is imprisoned..."
The inner palace was situated within magnificent pavilions, with tiered towers and ornate halls adorned with rare treasures.
Precious curtains and golden beds—provisions for his clothing and carriage—were all provided in abundance; yet, his two feet were bound with chains of Jambūnada gold, depriving him of freedom.
This is the analogy for birth from a womb. Furthermore, it is said: if one recognizes one’s fundamental transgression and deeply reproaches oneself, seeking [liberation]...
Leaving their original abodes, they immediately arrive at the place where Amitāyus Buddha resides. Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva Womb Sūtra* (*Pusa chu tai jing*) states:
"To the west of this Jambudvīpa, twelve billion nayutas away, lies the realm of *Kṣānti-māndya* (the Realm of Indolence).
Its land is composed of the seven treasures, and its pleasures are beyond compare. Yet, those who have resolved to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha remain attached to this world."
They are unable to advance; they are also like those dwelling on the outskirts or borders of the city. All such cases arise because their faith is not earnest.

[Commentary] Question: Since it is said that [the period for the ten recitations] is seven days, whereas the "ten recitations at the moment of death" lasts but a mere instant, how can one attain rebirth there?

Answer: It is precisely because of the power of a single moment of mind. As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom). Furthermore, regarding self-power and other-power, as stated in the *Milindapañha* (The Questions of King Milinda).
[Commentary]: The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* asks: "How can the mind for a brief moment at the time of death surpass the power of a lifetime of practice? The answer says:
Although the duration of time is brief, because the power of the mind is so sharp and intense, this final thought is called the "Great Mind.
One should know that this is precisely because it is a state of single-mindedness without distraction. The *Nāgasena-bhikṣu-sūtra* records:

The King asked Nāgasena, "If a person commits evil throughout their life but recollects the Buddha at the moment of death, they can be reborn in the Buddha-land. I do not believe these words. Nāgasena replied, "It is like holding a large..."

A stone placed upon a boat does not sink because of it; likewise, although a person may originally be evil, by virtue of recollecting the Buddha, they do not fall into hell but attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
This is also the case here: it is through the power of one's own mind and the power of the Buddha’s vow.
"They mutually constitute one another. [Commentary] Question:
Since it is said that one "attains birth" (wang-sheng), yet ancient masters have also stated, "If one is born, one is certainly born;
if one departs, in reality one does not depart," this implies there is birth but no going. Now you speak of "attaining birth"; these two meanings seem contradictory. Answer: Because one is born...
Because it is one's own mind, one goes without going; this is called "birth in the Pure Land. As the Elder Vimokṣa says in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: [The Commentary states:
"The layered and manifold dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka* does not transcend the single mind. The ten directions of empty space in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* are all within your own mind.
Thus, we know that birth in Sukhāvatī is born from one's own mind. Since the mind has no boundaries, there is no 'West.'"
There is no east. To what place does one go? Its appearance is such that it is defiled yet pure, sheds the old yet becomes new, and leaves one state to attain another;

it seems as though there is a destination, and thus it is called "going. How could this be said to be like the worldly notion of going from here to there, such as traveling through cities and villages as described in secular scriptures?
As for that which is spoken of as liberation, it is the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter, concerning the Elder Vimokṣa.
It says: "Those Tathāgatas do not come here, nor do I go there. If you wish to see Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Peace and Bliss, you shall see him at will.
Since it says "at will," one is born in that land without transcending a single thought-moment;
thus we know that while the manifestation of attaining birth is termed "going to be born" (*wang-sheng*), in reality, there is no place to which one goes. Not so.
To abide and yet go—this does not preclude speaking of "going. To speak in ultimate terms, there is not only no going, but also no arising.
Yet, arising from non-arising—this does not preclude speaking of "arising."
[Commentary] Question: In the past, people also aspired to be reborn in the Inner Court of Tuṣita; why now do you specifically point toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Answer:

Because of the difficulty or ease of the cause, because of the superiority or inferiority of the realm, and because of the relationship between master and disciple. Furthermore, [one might ask]: What about the world of the Victorious Lotus?
[The Pure Land of] Ultimate Bliss is exceedingly transcendent; why then do you not go there? Answer: Because the Land of Bliss is near, one should not seek what is distant.
[Commentary]: The intent of the question is likely that Maitreya also currently preaches the Dharma, and his Inner Court is likewise pure and adorned.
And yet one does not seek birth there; for what reason? The answer is that there are three points. First, regarding the difficulty or ease of the cause:

those who are born in the Inner Court must necessarily possess the merit of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) to be worthy of the company of the sages; it is not as in Sukhāvatī, where one merely seeks birth.

When pure mindfulness is perfected, one’s wishes will surely be fulfilled. This disregards the influence of afflictions and karma. Formerly, Master Xuanzang remarked that rebirth in the Inner Court (Tuṣita) is easy to achieve;
this is because the distance from Tuṣita to the human world can be measured in *yojanas*, whereas the distance from Sukhāvatī to the Sahā world is immeasurable.
The former traverses many Buddha-fields and discusses the stages (*bhūmi*) while not discussing the causes; the present [text] discusses the causes while not discussing the stages.

Each has its own intended meaning. However, to speak of the ultimate: Master Xuanzang was for the sake of a certain class of practitioners at that time, whereas this sutra is the path to be constantly practiced throughout ten thousand ages.
Regarding the superiority or inferiority of the two realms: the Inner Court does not transcend the midst of the triple world (*tridhātu*).
The Land of Ultimate Bliss transcends the three realms; even in the City of Doubt within that land, there are no women.

Yet, in the Inner Court for those born externally, the five desires exist. Therefore, it is said that being reborn there is still superior to the celestial palaces. Regarding the three masters and their disciples:

Amitābha has perfected the fruit of myriad virtues and has already realized the state of a Tathāgata; Maitreya, honored as the "Successor," still dwells at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

As the Sūtra says, "Among them, many are those who are in their last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*)," meaning that Maitreya is currently in the same position as Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, attending by the side of the Teacher.
Thus, they are called "Teacher and Disciples. Therefore, to see Amitābha is to see [the Teacher].
"Maitreya, seeing Maitreya does not necessarily mean one sees Amitābha. Furthermore, there is a saying by an ancient virtuous master:

'First be born in the Western Land, and later be born at the Dragon Flower [Tree Assembly]'; this too possesses great道理 (principle/reason). Is it not fitting, then, to seek the Ultimate Bliss with singular focus?
Regarding that which surpasses the lotus flowers, see in detail the previous section on the Lifespan. Now, when comparing the lands in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, [the Pure Land of] Sahā..."
Thereafter, it is said that [the land] is "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). Farther and yet farther, reaching a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, it is then called "Supreme Lotus.
Thus, Ultimate Bliss is a neighboring state, while Supreme Lotus is a distant realm. This is like the analogy of the famine in Yue and the harvest in Wu:
if one sets foot in Wu, yet abandons Wu to go instead and longingly admire Yan and Qin from afar, such delusion is truly extreme.
[Commentary] Question: We observe some who practice nianfo for a lifetime yet do not necessarily attain rebirth at the end of life; why is this? Answer:
This is truly because their lifelong nianfo was not performed with single-minded devotion.
[Commentary]: As for those who are indifferent and lax, they spend their entire lives reciting the Buddha’s name;
that is to say, although they do not slacken, they are not yet diligent, and because they have not attained single-mindedness, they do not attain birth [in the Pure Land].

If, however, one truly applies the mind even if it is not yet pure and unified, although one may not be born there in this life, one plants the cause for birth and will surely achieve samādhi in a future life to attain birth.
As it says in the Brahmajāla Sūtra: "One may not obtain the precepts, yet one obtains the benefit of receiving them.
This refers to what the Chan school calls "awakening to a thousand truths upon hearing a single word" as soon as one emerges from the depths.
Be careful not to use such cases as excuses to say, "So-and-so recited the Buddha’s name in vain and gained no merit," and thereby slander the holy teachings as unworthy of trust.

[Commentary] To accord with principle means that self-nature has no form; this is the meaning of being non-perverted. That self-nature is stainless is the meaning of giving birth to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Sub-commentary] The Sixth Patriarch said: "I have a thing that has neither head nor tail, neither back nor face. This is what is sought.
Since even correct characteristics (*samyak-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be found, by what means could one designate "inversion" (*viparyāsa*)?
The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* states: "The characteristic of all phenomena is emptiness; it is neither defiled nor pure. Thus, even when seeking a characteristic of purity, it cannot be found.
Where, then, could one point to and call this "Sahā" (the world of endurance)? Abide in full body within the lotus of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Platform. As soon as delusion arises, you should contemplate the Sahā world:
the mind is the land, and the land is the mind. The West is not far from here.
4. The Conclusion and Exhortation:
"Śāriputra, it is because I see these benefits that I have spoken these words. If there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make a vow to be born in that land."

[Commentary] "This benefit" refers to the aforementioned seeing the Buddha and attaining rebirth. "These words" refer to the statement that one should single-mindedly hold the Name because one perceives this great benefit.
To not wish to go [to the Pure Land] would be to render the Buddha’s teaching in vain;
this constitutes the second level of exhortation.
[Commentary]: Words that lack benefit are not spoken by the Buddha. Merely holding the Name results in rebirth [in the Pure Land], which brings great benefit to all sentient beings;
therefore, the Buddha taught it. This is because having attained rebirth is called "self-benefit.
Once born in that land, one hears the Dharma and attains the Way, thereby able to extensively deliver immeasurable sentient beings; this is called "benefiting others."
Because it possesses these two benefits, it is called "great benefit. Regarding the second exhortation:

the initial statement that "sentient beings who hear" refers merely to their hearing of the sublime and wondrous adornments of that land, whereby they give rise to aspiration and joy; it does not yet clarify how one actually attains birth there.
Now, the underlying principle is set forth: it is said that by single-mindedly holding the Name, the Buddha comes to welcome and lead one, whereby one attains birth in that land.
Thus, one's vows should become even more earnest; hence, these are called the "two exhortations."

[Commentary] Furthermore, the mention of "benefit" serves as an inverse illustration of the harm incurred by not aspiring for rebirth there, thereby demonstrating what is to be rejoiced in and what is to be loathed.
[Sub-commentary] Practicing in this land, one may rise and fall through many kalpas without attaining liberation; now, by means of the practice of calling the Name, one attains rebirth there.

Thus one ascends to the stage of non-retrogression. When weighing their respective benefits and harms, it is as clear as looking at one's own palm: benefit consists of all forms of happiness, while harm consists of all forms of suffering;
therefore, one should cultivate joy for the former and revulsion for the latter.
[Commentary] Furthermore, the phrase "what I say" correctly clarifies that this is an unasked spontaneous teaching (*anāpṛṣṭavyākaraṇa*).
[Sub-commentary] Seeing such great benefit, I hasten to point it out, fearing that sentient beings might lose this advantage through delay;
therefore, I do not wait for a formal inquiry.
[Commentary] To accord with principle means that one’s own nature is fully replete; this is the meaning of "benefit" (*li*).
[Sub-commentary] Examine one's own nature: what is lacking? Upon the essence of numinous awareness, Amitābha and the assembly of sages are ever-present throughout the day;
within the realm of eternal quiescent light, the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is never not being entered. Alas, how is it that the Buddha perceives this?

Benefit. If sentient beings were blind, the Buddha would say this is a benefit; if sentient beings were deaf, although it would require the labor of his golden mouth to proclaim it, one must personally see it at least once before it can be attained.
III. Mutual Citation of the Buddha’s Words to Eliminate Doubt (2). Part One: Clarifying that the Buddha Jointly Praises the Two Explanations of the Sūtra and That They Should Be Praised.
(1) Part One: Clarifying that the Buddha Jointly Praises (2). Part One: The Original Buddha’s Praise; Part Two: The Other Buddhas’ Praise.
First, the Buddha’s own praise:
"Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable benefits of the meritorious virtues of Amitābha Buddha..."
[Commentary]: Building upon the preceding, it is not only I who perceive this benefit and speak these words; all Buddhas of the ten directions likewise perceive this benefit and speak these words.
"Praise" means to extol; "admiration" means to express profound wonder. Regarding "inconceivable":
whereas previously it was said that I perceive this benefit, now it is stated to the utmost degree that this benefit is no ordinary benefit.
The text contains three turns of praise. First, it is not without benefit; therefore, it is called "benefit. Second, it is not merely the benefit of worldly merit;
therefore, it is called "the benefit of merit. Third, it is not merely the benefit of merit;
therefore, it is called "the benefit of inconceivable merit. It is for this reason that this praise is not given in vain.
[Commentary] "To extol" means to proclaim and praise the vast merits of that Buddha, causing people to take refuge in and believe in them.
"To express admiration" means to be moved and sigh with emotion, thinking: "This Dharma is rare among humans and devas; it is difficult to encounter throughout kalpas.
It causes people to feel both sorrow and joy. "Joy" refers to rejoicing at having heard it; "sorrow" refers to grieving that one has heard it so late. It is inconceivable.
This is the original title of this sutra; its meaning is found in the preceding preface.
As for the name of the sutra being "Inconceivable," it is precisely because Amitābha Buddha possesses these inconceivable great merits. Regarding the threefold repetition of the text:
Within these benefits, much is contained, unfolding in ever-deepening and expanding ways. First, regarding the benefit of ritual merit:
because it cultivates merit based on formal characteristics and constitutes a mundane cause, it is called "small benefit. Second, regarding the benefit of spiritual merit:

because it constitutes a supramundane cause, it is called "great benefit. Third, regarding inconceivable merit: because it constitutes the supreme among the supramundane causes, it is called [inconceivable benefit].
It is the greatest among great benefits. For although merit surpasses worldly fortune, within it there are further distinctions of superior and inferior;
some are conceivable, while others are inconceivable. This is now an inconceivable merit;
therefore, it is called the greatest among great benefits.
[Commentary: It is inconceivable. As stated in the *Ghoṣarāja-sūtra*, all the Buddha-dharmas existing in that Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) are inconceivable;
the manifestation of supernatural powers and transformations is inconceivable.

If one can believe in such matters, it should be known that this person is inconceivable, and the karmic retribution they obtain is likewise inconceivable. Furthermore, regarding the environment and its inhabitants...
Cause and effect—these four are all inconceivable.

[Commentary] This section is divided into four parts: first, the merit of the vastness of the bestowed Dharma, namely, immeasurable life, immeasurable light, the Three Jewels, the factors of the path, and so forth;
second, the merit of the pervasive spiritual transformations, namely, the water birds...

The groves all proclaim the sublime Dharma; clothing, food, and utensils for use are provided spontaneously. All sentient beings possess the marks and signs of excellence as well as supernatural transformations.
Third is the merit of the roots of virtue from past lives through which they have accepted and believed [the teaching];

that is to say, regarding a Dharma that is difficult to believe, those who are able to accept and believe it must have cultivated immeasurable roots of goodness in previous lives. Fourth is the merit of the victory over karmic retribution; that is to say, namely—

One attains rebirth; that is, one immediately enters the assembly of supreme goodness and immediately attains the stage of non-retrogression, ultimately achieving Buddhahood, and so forth—all of which transcend ordinary perception and are therefore called "inconceivable. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is also inconceivable. This refers to the cause and effect of both the primary and secondary [retributions].
"Abode" refers to co-residence, which is itself the Land of Quiescent Light; "Correct" refers to the Response Body, which is itself the Dharma Body;

"Cause" refers to the completion of merit in seven days; and "Fruit" refers to non-retrogression in a single lifetime. Furthermore, these transcend ordinary sentiment; therefore, both are inconceivable.
Formerly, Master Ying lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* forty times in the Eastern Capital. Consequently, he entered [the state of] Chuo...

The Chan Master, at his Pure Practice Monastery, entered deeply into samādhi and sighed, saying: "I have long regretted that for many years I have merely sought out textual commentaries, only to weary my body and mind in vain.
Who would have expected that the inconceivable power of Buddha-recitation is so profound?"
[Commentary] To accord with principle means that the self-nature is free from the characteristics of mind and speech; this is the meaning of "inconceivable merit.
[Sub-commentary] The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "This mind, from the very beginning, is free from the characteristics of mental objects and free from the characteristics of verbal expression."
Therefore, to raise the mind is immediately an error; to stir a thought is immediately a deviation. Those who cling to phrases are deluded; those who rely on words perish.
If this is so, then what should one do? Even if one were to seal the mouth and forget all mental activity, one would still fall into the state of non-discrimination (*avyākṛta*).
This is what is called "the inconceivable."
II. Praise by Other Buddhas (six sections). 1. East; 2. South; 3. West; 4. North;
5. Below; 6. Above. I. East (three sections). 1.
Listing names to manifest vastness; 2. Manifesting signs to represent the true; 3. Generating [faith].
This is called "Exhorting to Believe.
First, the names are listed to manifest their vastness:
